en/evidence/CLM-027/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-027 Evidence record Three observed survey waves, not an annual series What does this evidence establish? The World Bank has published three observations of account ownership in Yemen: 3.7% in 2011 (accounts at financial institutions only), 6.4% in 2014 and 11.9% for 2022, from the 2021 Findex wave. This resource treats them as separate observed survey waves, not an annual series. What does it measure? Account ownership among adults aged 15 and over in Yemen, as published by the World Bank for three separate survey waves (2011, 2014 and 2022); the three values do not form an annual series. Who or what does it apply to? Adults 15+ under each source wave's survey coverage When was it measured or observed? 2011 / 2014 / 2022 How current is it? The latest of the three waves is the 2021 Findex wave, reported by the World Bank for 2022 (Yemen fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023); the Global Findex 2025 edition adds no newer Yemen observation. The series should not be read as describing any later year. What this evidence does not establish It does not establish values for the years between waves or a smooth growth path, and 11.9% is not a 2026 rate. Limits of the measure The 2011 comparator counts accounts at financial institutions only, which differs from the later account definition that also counts mobile-money use; the 2014 values are rounded; the 2022 value comes from fieldwork in November 2022 to January 2023 that excluded areas holding about 23% of the population. en/evidence/CLM-028/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-028 Evidence record Historical borrowing patterns in 2014 What does this evidence establish? In the 2014 World Bank weighted country profile, 65.9% of adults reported borrowing any money, while 51.7% reported borrowing from family or friends, 15.0% from a private informal lender and 0.4% from a financial institution. What does it measure? Shares of adults aged 15 and over who reported borrowing any money, or borrowing from particular sources, as published in the World Bank's 2014 weighted country profile for Yemen. Who or what does it apply to? Civilian non-institutionalized population age 15+; some channel measures use sender, recipient or account-holder sub-groups When was it measured or observed? 2014 How current is it? The values refer to 2014, from the World Bank's 2014 country profile for Yemen. No weighted value from a later Yemen wave is available in this resource for these measures, so they should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The indicators overlap and are shares of all adults, not of borrowers: they cannot be added up to 100% or read as a breakdown of borrowers, and they do not describe borrowing today. Limits of the measure These are historical values, not current ones. In the source, '..' means no observation. Saving and borrowing indicators can overlap. en/evidence/CLM-030/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-030 Evidence record Domestic-remittance pathways in 2014 What does this evidence establish? The 2014 World Bank weighted country profile reports 18.3% of adults receiving domestic remittances. Among recipients, 31.1% received via a money transfer operator, 2.0% via a financial institution and 0.0% via mobile phone in that source profile. What does it measure? The share of adults aged 15 and over who received domestic remittances in 2014 and, among those recipients, the shares who received them through a money transfer operator, a financial institution or a mobile phone, as published in the World Bank's 2014 weighted country profile for Yemen. Who or what does it apply to? Civilian non-institutionalized population age 15+; some channel measures use sender, recipient or account-holder sub-groups When was it measured or observed? 2014 How current is it? The values refer to 2014, from the World Bank's 2014 country profile for Yemen. No weighted value from a later Yemen wave is available in this resource for these measures, so they should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The channel values are shares of adults who received domestic remittances, not of all adults; they do not show what share of the money flowed through each channel, and the profile does not describe the current situation. Limits of the measure These are historical values, not current ones. In the source, '..' means no observation, and remittance-channel values are shares of a sub-group, not of all adults. en/evidence/CLM-031/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-031 Evidence record There is no single latest year for all people-side evidence What does this evidence establish? The people-side evidence here does not have one latest year: account ownership has a latest verified Yemen aggregate in 2022, while weighted public evidence currently available here for account use, saving, borrowing and domestic-remittance behaviour is centered on 2014; latest-wave resilience and barrier values remain unpublished until the required weighted computation is complete. Historical results stay separate from any newer estimate until that computation and its verification are complete. What does it measure? An evidence-timing comparison showing that different people-side measures have different latest observation dates. Who or what does it apply to? People-side evidence by financial function; each function keeps its own survey wave, population base, denominator and publication status. When was it measured or observed? Function-specific people-side evidence: weighted public evidence on financial behaviour centered on 2014, with the latest verified account-ownership value from the Findex 2021 wave and Yemen fieldwork in 2022–2023. How current is it? Each function has its own latest observation: account ownership refers to the 2021 Findex wave, with Yemen fieldwork from November 2022 to January 2023; account use, saving, borrowing and domestic remittances refer to 2014. Each is updated separately when newer comparable evidence is published. en/evidence/CLM-032/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-032 Evidence record Same reference year, different published value What does this evidence establish? Annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) publish materially different remittance values for the same reference year. For 2024, the 2024 annual report gave USD 6.245 billion, while the 2025 annual report restated 2024 at USD 3.42 billion. This is a same-year restatement, not evidence of economic movement between years. What does it measure? A revision in the published value for the same reference year across different editions of the publication. Who or what does it apply to? The remittance series published in the balance of payments of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); its exact territorial and conceptual mapping to the IMF reconstruction for areas under the internationally recognized government remains open When was it measured or observed? Reference years 2020–2025 in the 2022–2025 annual reports; IMF method work 2024–2025 How current is it? The record covers reference years 2020 to 2025 as published in the 2022 to 2025 annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); the restatement concerns 2024, first published in the 2024 annual report and restated in the 2025 annual report. It should not be read as describing a later edition unless a newer annual report is published. What this evidence does not establish The same-year revision is not an economic collapse and not a change between years. Limits of the measure The method reconstruction is strongly supported, but no public crosswalk states exactly how the levels, geography and statistical concepts of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and the IMF correspond. A same-year revision remains distinct from change over time. Original source and verification Open the source record here, or go to the original document where a public link exists. en/evidence/CLM-033/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-033 Evidence record A measured banking jump can partly be a valuation change What does this evidence establish? The same 2022 consolidated banking positions are published at materially higher levels from the 2023 annual report onward, alongside a documented January 2023 shift to market-exchange-rate valuation of foreign-currency positions. The published difference therefore does not by itself establish economic change of the same magnitude. What does it measure? A methodological or valuation break that changes reported levels without necessarily representing the same-sized economic change. Who or what does it apply to? Consolidated commercial and Islamic bank balance-sheet stocks When was it measured or observed? 2022 positions as published in the 2022 annual report and as restated from the 2023 annual report onward How current is it? This record applies to the 2022 positions as published in the 2022 annual report and as restated from the 2023 annual report onward. It should not be read as describing later positions. What this evidence does not establish The restatement is not evidence of an asset, deposit or credit boom, or of any change in solvency. Limits of the measure A method or valuation break materially changes the values for the same reference year; changes in individual lines can be attributed to valuation only as far as the documented valuation note supports. The pattern refers to the remittance series as published in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025. It may change if CBY-Aden revises the series or publishes a newer annual report. What this evidence does not establish The pattern does not establish smoothing, interpolation or low real-world volatility. The comparison is limited to those exact labels, not all aid or external finance. What does it measure? The ratio of the remittance item to the donor-financing item for the 2024 reference year, calculated within each of two editions of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) annual report. Who or what does it apply to? Two balance-of-payments items of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), labelled by the source as remittances and donor financing, within each annual-report edition; not all aid, official development assistance (ODA) or external finance When was it measured or observed? 2024 reference year compared in the CBY-Aden Annual Reports 2024 and 2025. How current is it? The comparison refers to the 2024 reference year as published in the 2024 and 2025 annual reports. It is recalculated if either item is revised in a later annual report. What this evidence does not establish The ratio does not describe all aid, official development assistance or external finance, and it does not rank flows that are defined differently. en/evidence/CLM-036/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-036 Evidence record A reconstruction programme is documented; the exact CBY formula is not What does this evidence establish? IMF documents a 2024–2025 external-sector statistical reconstruction effort with CBY-Aden, including a demographic-behavioural personal-transfer model where informal-channel data were limited. This establishes method context, not the exact formula or scope used for every remittance value in the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025. What does it measure? This record describes the documented work of the IMF with the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) in 2024–2025 to reconstruct external-sector statistics, including a model of personal transfers; it reports no value. Who or what does it apply to? The IMF's analytical framework for external-sector statistics for areas under the internationally recognized government; component scopes and source methods vary When was it measured or observed? 2014–2025 reconstruction / 2025–26 publication cycle How current is it? The reconstruction work took place in 2024–2025, covers 2014 to 2025 and was documented in IMF publications of 2025–2026. The record describes method rather than a value and does not describe later method work unless newer documentation is published. What this evidence does not establish The public evidence does not establish the exact formula behind the values in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025, or that CBY-Aden and IMF levels share the same scope. Limits of the measure The reconstruction work is documented; a line-by-line crosswalk to the CBY 2025 annual report is not public. en/evidence/CLM-037/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-037 Evidence record The paths align after normalization; their levels are not equivalent What does this evidence establish? When the remittance series in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 and in the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation are each indexed to 2021 = 100, the two paths are almost identical through 2024: the largest difference in annual growth over 2022–2024 is 0.0032 percentage points. Over 2021–2024 the ratio of the CBY-Aden level to the IMF level is 1.838 in every year. The two indexed paths move almost identically, but this does not show that the raw levels share the same scope. What does it measure? The annual growth paths of the CBY-Aden and IMF remittance series, each indexed to 2021 = 100, compared over 2021–2024. Who or what does it apply to? The remittance series published by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and the IMF series for areas under the internationally recognized government; the exact territorial and conceptual mapping between them remains open When was it measured or observed? Reference years 2021–2024 (indexed comparison), from the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025 and the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation How current is it? The latest year compared is 2024, from the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025 and the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation. It should not be read as describing a later period unless newer comparable editions of both series are published. What this evidence does not establish The raw CBY-Aden and IMF levels are not equivalent, and the stable level ratio of 1.838 over 2021–2024 is not a geographic conversion factor. Limits of the measure When indexed, the two series move almost identically, but no published crosswalk states how CBY-Aden and IMF levels, geography and statistical concepts correspond; a same-year revision remains distinct from change over time. en/evidence/CLM-038/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-038 Evidence record The 2023 valuation change has a precedent and cannot be called the “first ever” What does this evidence establish? Market-rate valuation of foreign-currency accounts has documented precedent in Yemen from 1996, while CBY-Aden separately documents a January-2023 valuation/reporting change affecting current banking series. The two episodes should not be assumed to use identical standards. What does it measure? This record traces how foreign-currency positions have been valued in Yemen's banking statistics, from 1996 IMF metadata to the January 2023 change documented by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); it reports no value. Who or what does it apply to? Accounts denominated in foreign currency and banks' foreign-currency positions, within each source's statistical or reporting scope When was it measured or observed? 1996 historical metadata; 2023 contemporary change; sources reviewed on 10 September 2026 How current is it? The record rests on 1996 IMF metadata and the January 2023 change, with sources reviewed on 10 September 2026. It should not be read as describing later valuation practice unless newer documentation is published. What this evidence does not establish The January 2023 change was not the first market-rate valuation in Yemen, since a precedent is documented from 1996, and the evidence does not show that the historical and contemporary standards are identical. Limits of the measure Historical precedent does not establish continuity or equivalence with the 2023 regime; the exact text of the circular and its legal and statistical history remain unresolved. Who or what does it apply to? Specific to each source or display interface When was it measured or observed? World Bank public data interfaces as reviewed on 10 September 2026, and earlier documented access How current is it? The interfaces were reviewed on 10 September 2026, and what each shows may have changed since. The record should not be read as describing a later state of the interfaces unless they are reviewed again. What this evidence does not establish The difference does not show that data were deleted or withdrawn, or why any correction was made, and one public interface's observations are not a substitute for another's. Limits of the measure What one interface shows does not establish that the underlying data are absent or deleted, or why they were revised. en/evidence/CLM-040/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-040 Evidence record The 2025 external-sector statistics mission produced a 2014–2024 historical series What does this evidence establish? IMF's D4D-II record states that the July 2025 Yemen external-sector statistics mission produced BOP and IIP statistics for 2014–2024. This confirms that the historical series was reconstructed and produced; the exact numerical match with other publications remains unresolved. What does it measure? A documented statistical reconstruction exercise that produced a revised historical external-sector series. Who or what does it apply to? The IMF's analytical framework for external-sector statistics for areas under the internationally recognized government; component scopes and source methods vary When was it measured or observed? Statistics for 2014–2024 produced in July 2025; publication cycle 2025–2026 How current is it? The July 2025 mission produced balance-of-payments and international investment position statistics for 2014–2024; the record documents that production event and holds no later observation. It should not be read as describing later statistical work unless newer documentation is published. What this evidence does not establish The evidence does not show that every row of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 is numerically identical to the IMF mission's output. Limits of the measure The reconstruction work is documented; a line-by-line crosswalk to the CBY 2025 annual report is not public. en/evidence/CLM-041/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-041 Evidence record The published CBY and IMF balance-of-payments components tested do not support a single conversion factor What does this evidence establish? Across the public balance-of-payments components tested for 2021–2024, from the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 and from the IMF series for areas under the internationally recognized government, the evidence does not support a single conversion factor. The remittance ratio is almost constant, but the ratios for imports, grants, the current account and net errors and omissions differ materially, and the IMF documents component-specific sources and transformations. This does not rule out component-specific bridges or a future official crosswalk. What does it measure? Ratios between CBY-Aden and IMF values for each tested balance-of-payments component over 2021–2024, compared to see whether one conversion factor fits all components. Who or what does it apply to? Only the public CBY and IMF balance-of-payments components actually tested; each component retains its source definition, geography and transformation. When was it measured or observed? Overlapping reference years 2021–2024 in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 and the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation How current is it? The test uses the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 and the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation for the overlapping years 2021–2024. It is reassessed if either source publishes a revised series, an official crosswalk or new information on how components are transformed. What this evidence does not establish The constant ratio of 1.838 between the CBY-Aden and IMF remittance series over 2021–2024, and the 33% population share that the IMF used for areas under the internationally recognized government, do not apply to other balance-of-payments components. The test does not show that a conversion is impossible beyond the public components tested. en/evidence/CLM-042/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-042 Evidence record A stable remittance ratio exists; its meaning remains unknown What does this evidence establish? Over 2021–2024, the ratio of the remittance series in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 to the IMF 2025 Article IV series is 1.838 in every year, and the two growth paths are almost identical when indexed to 2021 = 100. The public evidence does not establish what that ratio represents, so it is a numerical regularity with no documented explanation, not a conversion rule. What does it measure? The ratio of the CBY-Aden remittance series to the IMF remittance series in each year from 2021 to 2024. Who or what does it apply to? The CBY-Aden publication scope compared with the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government When was it measured or observed? Overlapping years 2021–2024; IMF reconstruction covering 2014–2025 How current is it? The ratio covers 2021 to 2024, from the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025 and the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation. It should not be read as holding for later years unless newer comparable editions of both series are published. What this evidence does not establish The 1.838 ratio is not a population, geography, informal-share or coverage conversion. Limits of the measure Comparability is component-specific only; differences of sign, scope and method remain material. en/evidence/CLM-043/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-043 Evidence record Before ranking flows, look at the balancing residual What does this evidence establish? In the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025, net errors and omissions are larger than the published remittance line in every year from 2021 to 2025. In 2025 the residual is USD 7.117 billion against USD 3.614 billion for remittances, 1.97 times the remittance line. Net errors and omissions is a balancing residual, not an observed flow or an estimate of hidden remittances. What does it measure? Net errors and omissions in the CBY-Aden balance of payments for 2021–2025, compared in size with the published remittance line. Who or what does it apply to? The balance of payments as each source defines it When was it measured or observed? 2021–2025 How current is it? The latest year in this record is 2025, from the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025. It should not be read as describing a later year unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish Net errors and omissions are not hidden remittances or an observed flow, and no established decomposition shows the residual to be unrecorded capital. Limits of the measure Errors and omissions is a net balancing residual; it cannot identify a missing component or gross offsetting errors. en/evidence/CLM-044/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-044 Evidence record An alternative residual model is not the canonical remittance baseline What does this evidence establish? A balance-of-payments residual model estimates remittances by assigning an assumed residual discrepancy to them. Such an estimate is an alternative model, not a direct observation or the canonical remittance baseline. The estimate considered here rests on material with no publicly accessible original, so, under this resource's publication rule, neither its value nor its producer is reproduced here. What does it measure? An estimate of 2024 remittances produced by a balance-of-payments residual model, kept separate from the adopted remittance baseline. Who or what does it apply to? Yemen as a whole, as an analytical estimate; not an observed official value When was it measured or observed? 2024 estimate How current is it? The estimate refers to 2024. It is a model result rather than an observation and should not be read as describing a later year. What this evidence does not establish A residual-model estimate is not an official or observed national value, and the residual is not a direct observation of informal remittances. Limits of the measure Errors in other balance-of-payments components, and the assumption made about errors and omissions, flow into the remittance residual; informal remittances are not directly observed. en/evidence/CLM-045/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-045 Evidence record A successful cash payment is not yet durable financial use What does this evidence establish? World Bank/G2Px material (May 2024) describes an eight-district digital-payment pilot within Yemen's unconditional cash-transfer programme, reported to have benefited 45,460 recipients, with an emphasis on payments into fully functional accounts and recipient choice. As reported by programme partners, this indicates delivery and exposure to a formal digital service. Yemen evidence can support several links from cash delivery through usability, resilience and local financial relationships, but it does not yet establish persistent post-transfer bank-account or e-wallet use. Beneficiaries, registrations, identities and opened accounts are not measures of durable use. What does it measure? This record sets out a measurement gap between successful delivery of a cash transfer and continued financial use after it; its only figure is the pilot's reported number of recipients. Who or what does it apply to? Local, programme and project populations as each source defines them When was it measured or observed? Evidence published 2023–2026; the pilot material dates from May 2024, and the reference period of the 45,460 figure is not recorded here How current is it? The latest evidence in this record was published in 2026; the pilot material dates from May 2024. The record should not be read as describing later programme reach or use unless newer evidence is published. What this evidence does not establish Cash-transfer beneficiaries, village savings and loan associations (VSLAs), identity targets and opened accounts are not measures of durable financial use. The 45,460 figure is a programme-reported number of recipients, not a count of people who kept using an account. Limits of the measure Evidence exists for several intermediate links; durable use of an account or wallet after the transfer remains unobserved. en/evidence/CLM-046/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-046 Evidence record Pledge, agreement, deposit and disbursement are different stages of support What does this evidence establish? Saudi support is recorded by stage. A pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposited amount, amount made available, budget disbursement, FX-auction use, in-kind support and project cost are not interchangeable, and they are not added into a cumulative total here. What does it measure? This record sets out a distinction and reports no value: a pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposit, amount made available, budget disbursement, use in foreign-exchange auctions, in-kind support and project cost are different stages of Saudi support to Yemen. Who or what does it apply to? Specific to each source or funding or support package When was it measured or observed? 2010–2026 How current is it? The evidence in this record spans 2010 to 2026. It should not be read as describing later support unless newer evidence is published. What this evidence does not establish Adding unlike or overlapping stages does not produce a cumulative total of Saudi support, and no such total is established here. Limits of the measure No single, fully reconciled public ledger of the flows exists; larger packages and their components, and the commitment, deposit, availability, disbursement and use stages, can overlap. en/evidence/CLM-047/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-047 Evidence record A change in an external position is not automatically a transaction What does this evidence establish? Changes in Yemen's external asset or liability positions should be decomposed into transactions, exchange-rate changes, other price changes and other volume changes before they are interpreted as financial flows. The change in international investment position (IIP) stocks between opening and closing dates is not, on its own, a measure of balance-of-payments transactions. What does it measure? This record sets out a method rule for separating balance-of-payments transactions from other changes in Yemen's external asset and liability positions; it reports no value. Who or what does it apply to? As defined by the source concerned When was it measured or observed? No values yet; this record sets out a method rule How current is it? This record sets out a method rule and has no observation date; Yemen's international investment position data are not yet in the public evidence base. What this evidence does not establish The difference between opening and closing international investment position stocks is not, on its own, a measure of balance-of-payments transactions. Limits of the measure The method is documented, but Yemen's international investment position data and the reconciliation table are not yet in the public evidence base. en/evidence/CLM-048/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-048 Evidence record BPM7 updates the standard; it does not rewrite Yemen’s statistical history overnight What does this evidence establish? BPM7 is the updated global external-sector statistical standard, but implementation is a multi-year transition. Yemen's historical series should keep the standard and version under which their sources published them until an explicit conversion or revision is published. What does it measure? This record sets out how Yemen's external-sector series are labelled during the move from the sixth to the seventh edition of the IMF Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6 to BPM7); it reports no value. en/evidence/CLM-049/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-049 Evidence record IMF Staff-Monitored Program (SMP) for Yemen: staff-level agreement of July 2026, subject to Management approval What does this evidence establish? On 16 July 2026, staff of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Yemeni authorities announced staff-level agreement on key policies and reforms that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program (SMP). The IMF stated that the agreement was subject to Management approval and would not result in Board discussion. It is not an IMF financing arrangement. What does it measure? The approval status of a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program (SMP) of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for Yemen, as announced by the IMF on 16 July 2026. Who or what does it apply to? The staff-level policy agreement between IMF staff and the Yemeni authorities, and the status of the proposed Staff-Monitored Program (SMP); not an Executive Board-approved financing arrangement. When was it measured or observed? 16 July 2026; proposed 18-month IMF Staff-Monitored Program at staff-level agreement stage. How current is it? The latest information in this record is the announcement of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) of 16 July 2026, when the agreement was at staff level and subject to IMF Management approval. It should not be read as the programme's status at a later date unless a newer IMF notice is published. What this evidence does not establish The proposed Staff-Monitored Program (SMP) is not an arrangement approved or endorsed by the Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and does not involve IMF financing; the agreement is also not evidence that external-sector statistics have been reconciled. Within the five e-money providers covered by a study of the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS), electronic-money accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019. The same source reports an average 23% dormant/inactive share and notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. Registered accounts therefore cannot be read as active or durable inclusion. What does it measure? The number of electronic-money accounts held with the five providers covered by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) study in December 2019, with the average share of those accounts that the study reports as dormant or inactive in 2019. Who or what does it apply to? Five electronic-money providers/wallets captured by the study When was it measured or observed? Dec-2019; contextual series 2016–2019 How current is it? The account total refers to December 2019, within a study series covering 2016 to 2019. It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The total is not a count of active users or unique people, a national inclusion rate or a 2026 level. Limits of the measure Accounts are not unique people and are not automatically active; the 23% is a source-wide average, not a provider-specific or current rate. en/evidence/CLM-051/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-051 Evidence record Most recorded 2019 e-money value still revolved around cash and account transfers What does this evidence establish? A grouping by CauseWay of Table 8 in the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) study indicates that 57.03% of recorded 2019 e-money transaction value was cash-in or cash-out and 29.97% was movement between bank and electronic accounts; bills and purchases together were 2.41%. The grouping is CauseWay's own, not a headline figure in the source. What does it measure? Shares of the total value of e-money transactions recorded in 2019 by the five providers covered by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) study, grouped by function. Who or what does it apply to? Transactions reported by the source for the five providers covered by the study When was it measured or observed? 2016–2019; derived comparison 2018–2019 How current is it? The values refer to 2019, within a study series covering 2016 to 2019 (the derived comparison covers 2018 and 2019). They should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish It does not establish the number of unique users, the coverage of the merchant ecosystem, household welfare, causal effects or durable inclusion. Limits of the measure The source table reports transaction values by type; it does not count users or merchants, and the grouping used here is this resource's own, not the source's classification. The average share of e-money accounts or users in cities, and the average share of women, in the provider data covered by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) study for 2016–2019. Who or what does it apply to? E-money accounts or users as reported by the source or by providers When was it measured or observed? 2016–2019 How current is it? The averages cover 2016 to 2019. They should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish It does not establish a national gender gap in 2026, a rural access rate or local service availability. Limits of the measure This is not national adult prevalence and not current geography; it is not comparable with Findex without a bridge between their populations and methods, and the 611-user survey has a different sample composition. en/evidence/CLM-054/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-054 Evidence record Borrower, saver and portfolio figures come from different sources and definitions and do not yet form one trend What does this evidence establish? Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 at end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not been verified. The same paper reports what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” in 2023 and a nominal portfolio of about YER44 billion; the verified 2020 anchors are 1.611 million savers/depositors and YER33.379 billion. “Active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure, and both portfolio figures are nominal rials: between December 2020 and December 2023 the average market rate published by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) moved from 792.69 to 1,529.4 rials per US dollar, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen's divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use, so no real or US-dollar change can be derived from them. Because the 2023 primary source document, the exact set of providers covered, saver definition/deduplication and period bridge are not yet available in the evidence base for direct verification, these are separate reference points, each with stated limits, not a trend. Together they do not establish unique people, real credit growth, broader inclusion, improved borrower outcomes or causality. What does it measure? Active microfinance borrowers at end-2015, end-2020 and end-2023, and savers or depositors and nominal loan portfolio at end-2020 and in 2023, from providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD) for 2015 and 2020 and from a 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data for 2023, set side by side as separate figures rather than one series. Who or what does it apply to? Microfinance borrower, saver/depositor and nominal-portfolio measures drawn from provider and reporting groups defined by each source, which are not yet fully harmonized across years. When was it measured or observed? End-2015 and end-2020 (verified primary tables), set beside end-2023 (a secondary figure citing SFD/SMED data). How current is it? The latest figure in this comparison refers to the end of 2023 and comes from a secondary source; it does not describe the market in 2026. The comparison is reassessed if the 2023 primary source and the set of providers it covers become available for direct verification, or if a newer comparable primary observation is added. What this evidence does not establish The figures do not show broader inclusion, real credit deepening, a harmonized trend, improved borrower outcomes, a causal effect, growth in unique people or an unchanged set of providers. en/evidence/CLM-056/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-056 Evidence record The 91% figure is supportable only as a source-attributed share of saver growth—not as a verified 2023 depositor stock share What does this evidence establish? The 2024 Sana’a Center paper on microfinance banks attributes 91% to Al-Kuraimi's share of saver growth; the 2023 provider-level numerator, denominator and calculation have not been reproduced. A 2025 Yemen Review restates 91% as a share of active microfinance depositors. A share of growth and a share of the stock are different measures, so the 2025 stock-share wording is not supported by the evidence available here; it remains a secondary restatement pending primary 2023 provider data or an explicit source correction. What does it measure? The 91% share of growth in microfinance savers that a 2024 policy paper attributes to Al-Kuraimi; the 2023 provider-level numerator, denominator and calculation behind it have not been reproduced. Who or what does it apply to? Two distinct metrics: share of saver growth versus share of depositor/saver stock. The 2023 figure of 91% cannot be moved from one measure to the other without a reproduced numerator and denominator. When was it measured or observed? A statement about 2023 published in 2024, and its restatement in 2025. How current is it? The statement refers to 2023 and was restated in 2025; the evidence base holds no later provider-level figure. Its status changes only if primary 2023 provider data reproduce the measure or the source issues an explicit correction or clarification. What this evidence does not establish It does not establish a verified 2023 stock share, a share of unique clients or a general market share for any provider. Limits of the measure The source's wording concerns a share of growth; the 2023 calculation and the later restatement remain unresolved. en/evidence/CLM-057/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-057 Evidence record June and end-2023 borrower points are not one continuous series What does this evidence establish? The roughly 80,800 active-borrower point cited for June 2023 and the 78,686 end-2023 point come through different source chains. They are kept as separate observations until the provider sets and methods behind them are reconciled, and no June-to-year-end decline is calculated from them. What does it measure? Two counts of active microfinance borrowers in 2023, about 80,800 cited for June and 78,686 for the end of the year, reported through different source chains. Who or what does it apply to? Active-borrower observations for which it has not yet been shown that the June and year-end points cover the same providers and use the same source method. When was it measured or observed? June 2023 and end-2023 active-borrower observations from separate source chains. How current is it? Both observations refer to 2023, the later one to the end of the year; neither describes microfinance after 2023. They remain separate points unless the sources and provider sets are reconciled. What this evidence does not establish The two figures do not establish a decline between June and the end of 2023, monthly values between them, or a continuous series, while the provider sets behind them remain unreconciled. en/evidence/CLM-058/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-058 Evidence record Through 2021, the World Bank reports a broadly flat borrower base while average loan amounts rose What does this evidence establish? World Bank Financial Sector Diagnostics reports that Yemen's active microfinance borrower base remained broadly around 80,000–90,000 through 2021 while average loan amounts rose, with subsector growth appearing to be driven more by larger loans than by net borrower growth. The finding is historical context through 2021, not a 2023/2026 conclusion. What does it measure? The World Bank's account, in its 2024 Yemen Financial Sector Diagnostics, of how the number of active microfinance borrowers and average loan amounts moved through 2021. Who or what does it apply to? Yemen microfinance borrower and average-loan measures summarized in the World Bank Financial Sector Diagnostics, within the source's sector coverage. When was it measured or observed? Historical evidence through 2021. How current is it? The finding covers evidence through 2021 in a source published in 2024. It is not a conclusion about 2023 or 2026, and newer comparable sector evidence would be needed before it could describe the current market. What this evidence does not establish It does not describe 2023 or 2026, it is not a regulatory census of providers, and it does not establish a cause beyond the source's own hedged wording. Limits of the measure Average loan amounts are in rials; how much of the rise is real depends on price and exchange-rate treatment, which is not recorded here. en/evidence/CLM-059/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-059 Evidence record SMEPS programme reach describes the programme, not all MSMEs in Yemen What does this evidence establish? The Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) reports that in 2024 it supported 8,217 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and disbursed USD 22,865,322. For 2021–2024 it reports support to 31,560 MSMEs and a USD 54.7 million programme total whose status (committed or disbursed) is not recorded in the evidence base. The 2021–2024 total may count the same enterprise in more than one year, so it is not a count of unique firms. These are programme results reported by SMEPS itself: they describe programme reach and finance, not national MSME prevalence or financial-sector lending. What does it measure? The number of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) that SMEPS reports supporting, and the programme funds it reports, for 2024 and for 2021–2024. Who or what does it apply to? Micro, small and medium enterprises supported by SMEPS programmes, and the programme portfolio When was it measured or observed? 2024; cumulative 2021–2024 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to 2024, with a cumulative total for 2021–2024. It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish Programme-supported MSMEs are not the national MSME universe, programme disbursement is not financial-sector lending, and programme outputs are not national or causal outcomes. The 2021–2024 total is not a count of unique firms. Limits of the measure Programme figures count the programme's own participants and disbursements; they are not drawn from a national sample of firms. Whether the USD 54.7 million 2021–2024 total is committed or disbursed funding is not recorded in the evidence base. en/evidence/CLM-060/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-060 Evidence record The SMEPS financial-services KPI is a programme result, not a national MSME rate What does this evidence establish? SMEPS's 2024 Annual Report reports that 19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services in 2024, while the 2021–2024 total reported as achieved is 15% against a 40% programme target. The table does not fully specify the metric-specific assessment base or operational definition of 'accessed financial services'. The KPI can therefore be read only within the programme, subject to that limitation; it is not a national MSME access rate. What does it measure? The share of SMEPS-supported micro, small and medium enterprises that SMEPS reports as having accessed financial services, for 2024 and cumulatively for 2021–2024, with the programme target. Who or what does it apply to? SMEPS-supported MSMEs under the programme KPI When was it measured or observed? 2024; cumulative/target 2021–2024 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to 2024; the cumulative result and the programme target cover 2021–2024. It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The percentage is not a national rate of access to financial services for micro, small and medium enterprises, a representative survey estimate or a national rate of unique firms, and it does not show that SMEPS caused access. Limits of the measure The summary KPI table does not fully specify the metric-specific denominator or assessment base, or the operational definition of 'accessed financial services'. This narrows the claim; it does not nullify the source-reported KPI. Original source and verification Open the source record here, or go to the original document where a public link exists. en/evidence/CLM-062/index.html.text: Evidence/CLM-062 Evidence record Formal firms in the 2022 survey: accounts were common, bank finance for working capital was not What does this evidence establish? Among formal firms in the 2022 seven-governorate survey, 58.2% (191 of 328) reported a checking or savings account. Their working capital came mainly from internal sources: on average, 69.12% came from internal funds or retained earnings, 16.66% from money lenders, friends or relatives, 10.15% from advance payments by clients, 1.97% from non-bank financial institutions, 1.31% from supplier credit and 0.56% from banks. In a separate question on the financial intermediaries they use, 73.48% of responding formal firms named an exchange store or money exchanger and 24.39% a commercial bank; firms could name more than one, so these are not market shares. The evidence base does not record the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. Among the 217 informal firms surveyed, 80.18% had no bank account; that sample was drawn from activity and location lists rather than a national register. The formal-firm sample includes micro firms with fewer than five employees, and neither sample represents all Yemeni firms. What does it measure? Firm-level financial behaviour reported by a World Bank custom enterprise survey: account holding, average working-capital source shares, financial intermediaries used, and informal firms' account holding. Who or what does it apply to? Two separate samples in seven selected governorates: 328 formal enterprises (including micro firms with fewer than five employees) and 217 informal enterprises drawn from activity and location lists. Neither sample represents all Yemeni firms. When was it measured or observed? 2022 survey (September 2022); published 2024 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to the 2022 survey (September 2022), published in 2024. It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The evidence base does not record the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. An average working-capital share is not a share of firms, and multiple-response percentages are not market shares. Holding an account does not show that a firm uses bank credit. The formal and informal samples use different frames, so they cannot be added together or compared with the 2013 survey. Firms are not people, so these shares are not comparable with the Findex account-ownership rate. The official rules and guidance of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) on financial consumer protection and complaints, from the August 2023 announcement of its Instructions to its 2024 brochure. Who or what does it apply to? Banks and non-bank financial institutions covered by the consumer-protection framework of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as the brochure describes them When was it measured or observed? 28 August 2023 to 23 March 2024 How current is it? The latest source in this record is the brochure dated 23 March 2024; the Instructions were announced on 28 August 2023. It should not be read as describing the framework at a later date unless newer official material is published or the legal text is extracted. What this evidence does not establish The existence of a complaint and redress framework does not establish that consumers use it, that cases are resolved on time, or that redress outcomes are effective. Who or what does it apply to? The 36 historical Findex measures for Yemen published for 2011 and 2014, and the measures specified for the 2021 wave. When was it measured or observed? 2011 to 2022 How current is it? It compares published values for 2011 and 2014 with the 2021 Findex wave, the latest wave available for Yemen (fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023). It should not be read as describing a later wave unless one is published. en/evidence/FMIIP-BASELINE-2025-01/index.text: Evidence/FMIIP-BASELINE-2025-01 Evidence record FMIIP project baselines for January 2025 count accounts, access points, merchants and agents — not people What does this evidence establish? The results framework of the World Bank-financed Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708) records January 2025 baselines for its own project-defined indicators: 1,062,441 active bank accounts (200,898 of them owned by women), 375,252 active e-wallet accounts, 817 financial access points, 170 merchants accepting electronic payments and 65 agents of licensed financial institutions. These are project baselines that count accounts, access points, merchants and agents — not people. What does it measure? January 2025 baseline values recorded in the results framework of the Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) for indicators the project itself defines; a baseline is the project's starting reference, not an independent measurement of the financial system. Who or what does it apply to? Project-defined indicators of the FMIIP results framework. The definitions and reporting scope behind each baseline are the project's own and are not documented in the evidence base. When was it measured or observed? January 2025 (project baseline) How current is it? The baselines refer to January 2025, the project's starting reference. They should not be read as describing a later date; this record contains no later project result. What this evidence does not establish Accounts are not unique people, and active e-wallet accounts are not subscribers unless a definition shows otherwise. Accounts classified by owner are not a count of women. Merchants are not POS terminals, and agents are not customers. These baselines have not been reconciled with the payment-report totals of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) or with survey measures of account ownership, and dividing them by a population total does not give a share of people. en/evidence/VIS-BORROWING-SOURCES-2014/i.text: Evidence/VIS-BORROWING-SOURCES-2014 Evidence record Borrowing and its sources in 2014 What does this evidence establish? In 2014, 65.9% of adults reported borrowing any money; 51.7% reported borrowing from family or friends, 15.0% from a private informal lender and 0.4% from a financial institution. Each value is a share of all adults; the sources overlap, so they cannot be added up or read as shares of borrowers. What does it measure? Shares of adults aged 15 and over in Yemen who reported borrowing any money, and borrowing from particular sources or for particular purposes, in 2014, as published by the World Bank. Who or what does it apply to? Adults covered by the 2014 Findex data for Yemen; borrowing from any source is shown separately from source or purpose indicators. When was it measured or observed? 2014 How current is it? The values refer to 2014, from the World Bank's 2014 country profile for Yemen. No weighted value from a later Yemen wave is available in this resource for these measures, so they should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish Each source is a separate share of all adults, not of borrowers. The shares overlap, so they do not add up to a total or to 100%, and no 'informal borrowing share' can be derived by subtracting one from another. en/evidence/VIS-DEMAND-VINTAGE-LADDER/in.text: Evidence/VIS-DEMAND-VINTAGE-LADDER Evidence record Latest observation for each people-side financial function What does this evidence establish? The latest weighted evidence differs by financial function: account ownership has a value from the 2021 Findex wave (11.9%, reported for 2022), while the latest weighted values for saving, borrowing and domestic remittances date from 2014 (20.6% of adults saved any money, 65.9% borrowed any money and 18.3% received domestic remittances), and weighted estimates of resilience and of the reasons for not having an account have not yet been calculated for the 2021 wave. What does it measure? The latest observation period available for each people-side financial function (account ownership, saving, borrowing, domestic remittances, resilience and reasons for not having an account), drawn from the Global Findex evidence for Yemen. Who or what does it apply to? The latest period with a supported numeric value for each people-side financial function, with account ownership, saving, borrowing, remittances, resilience and barriers kept separate. When was it measured or observed? 2014 to 2022; no weighted values yet for some measures in the 2021 wave How current is it? The latest observations differ by function: 2022 for account ownership (2021 Findex wave, fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023) and 2014 for saving, borrowing and domestic remittances; resilience and reasons for not having an account have no weighted value yet. None of them describes a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish It is not a composite inclusion score. There is no single latest year for people-side evidence, and a recent date for one function does not make the evidence for another function current. en/evidence/VIS-DOMESTIC-REMITTANCE-PATH.text: Evidence/VIS-DOMESTIC-REMITTANCE-PATH-2014 Evidence record Domestic remittances in 2014 — population reach vs recipient channels What does this evidence establish? In 2014, 18.3% of adults reported receiving domestic remittances. Among those recipients, 31.1% received them through a money transfer operator, 2.0% through a financial institution and 0.0% through a mobile phone. The source gives no channel values for adults who sent remittances; these are unavailable, not zero. What does it measure? The shares of adults aged 15 and over in Yemen who sent or received domestic remittances in 2014 and, among senders and recipients, the channels they used, as published by the World Bank. Who or what does it apply to? All adults in the 2014 Findex data for sending and receiving; for channels, only the adults who sent, or who received, domestic remittances. When was it measured or observed? 2014 How current is it? The values refer to 2014, from the World Bank's 2014 country profile for Yemen. No weighted value from a later Yemen wave is available in this resource for these measures, so they should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish Shares of all adults and channel shares among recipients use different bases and cannot be read on one scale. They do not show how much money flowed through each channel or the composition of remittances in the economy as a whole. en/evidence/VIS-E-MONEY-RULE-STACK/index.text: Evidence/VIS-E-MONEY-RULE-STACK Evidence record Layers of mobile e-money rules What does this evidence establish? The mobile e-money instructions of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) of 9 August 2023 regulate e-money services of non-bank financial institutions under its supervision and set consumer-protection duties, including handling complaints within 10 business days and keeping a complaint register. The amendment of 9 July 2025 permits e-money in US dollars, Saudi riyals and UAE dirhams alongside Yemeni rials, does not allow conversion from rials into foreign currency within its scope, and sets ceilings for individual accounts: YER 1,000,000 per transaction, 2,000,000 per day, 5,000,000 per month and 50,000,000 per year; USD 400, 500, 1,000 and 10,000 or equivalent for foreign-currency accounts; and maximum balances of YER 8,000,000 and USD 1,500 or equivalent. These are legal limits, not observed balances, use or market size, and the evidence does not identify a complete current set of named providers. What does it measure? The permissions, restrictions, consumer-protection duties and transaction and balance ceilings that the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) sets for mobile e-money services in its 2023 instructions and their 2025 amendment. Who or what does it apply to? Mobile e-money accounts regulated under the cited instructions of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) When was it measured or observed? 2023 base rules + 2025 amendment How current is it? The latest instrument in this record is the amendment signed on 9 July 2025, which took effect on issuance; the base instructions date from 9 August 2023. The evidence base holds no consolidated register of later amendments, so the rules should not be read as current beyond that date without checking for a newer amendment. What this evidence does not establish The ceilings are legal limits, not observed use, balances or market size, and the regulated class is not a current list of named providers. en/evidence/VIS-FCP-REDRESS-PATH/index.h.text: Evidence/VIS-FCP-REDRESS-PATH Evidence record If a complaint is not resolved, what happens? What does this evidence establish? A 2024 consumer-protection awareness brochure of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) describes a provider stage of up to 10 business days to settle a complaint, which may be extended by a similar period with the consumer told why, and escalation to CBY-Aden within 14 business days after the settlement period ends. These time limits come from the brochure, not from an extracted legal text of the 2023 Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions. How complaints are actually handled is not measured: the evidence base holds no data on complaint volumes, resolution quality or enforcement. What does it measure? The complaint and escalation steps, and their time limits, described in a consumer-protection brochure of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) dated 23 March 2024. Who or what does it apply to? The complaint path of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for banks and non-bank financial institutions, as described in its 2024 consumer-protection brochure When was it measured or observed? Instructions announced 28 August 2023; brochure dated 23 March 2024; no outcome data How current is it? The latest source is the brochure dated 23 March 2024; the Instructions were announced on 28 August 2023. The evidence base holds no data on complaint outcomes for any date. What this evidence does not establish The existence of a complaint path does not show that complaints are accepted or resolved on time, that redress is adequate or compensation paid, that enforcement is effective, or any outcome for consumers. The time limits come from a 2024 awareness brochure, not from an extracted legal text. en/evidence/VIS-FINDEX-ACCESS-USE/index..text: Evidence/VIS-FINDEX-ACCESS-USE Evidence record Account ownership, account use and digital use: three separate measures What does this evidence establish? In the 2021 Global Findex wave for Yemen (fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023), 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered had an account. Weighted estimates of how many adults used an account, or used one digitally, have not yet been produced for this wave, so ownership is the only level available; owning an account does not show that it is used. What does it measure? Three separate Findex measures for adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered in the 2021 wave: account ownership, account use and digital use, each with its own population base; only account ownership has a published value. Who or what does it apply to? Findex account-ownership, account-use and digital-use indicators, each indicator with its own population and measurement base. When was it measured or observed? 2021 wave / Yemen fieldwork 2022-11 to 2023-01 How current is it? The ownership value refers to the 2021 Findex wave, reported by the World Bank for 2022, with Yemen fieldwork from November 2022 to January 2023; the Global Findex 2025 edition adds no newer Yemen observation. Account-use and digital-use values have not yet been produced. What this evidence does not establish Owning an account does not establish that it is used, and use does not establish digital use. The three measures have different population bases, and it is not established that each group sits inside the previous one, so they are not stages of a single funnel. Raw case percentages from the study documentation are not population estimates. en/evidence/VIS-FINDEX-BARRIERS/index.ht.text: Evidence/VIS-FINDEX-BARRIERS Evidence record Reasons adults give for not having an account What does this evidence establish? Weighted estimates of the reasons that adults without an account give for not having one have not yet been produced for the 2021 wave, so no values are shown. When published, they will apply only to adults without an account and will state the number of respondents, the use of survey weights and how 'don't know' and refused answers are treated; they will not be shares of all adults. What does it measure? The reasons that adults aged 15 and over without an account, in the areas the survey covered, give for not having one, as asked in the Yemen Findex 2021 survey; no weighted values have yet been produced. en/evidence/VIS-FINDEX-GAPS/index.html.text: Evidence/VIS-FINDEX-GAPS Evidence record Account ownership and measured gaps: Global Findex 2021 wave (Yemen fieldwork 2022–23) What does this evidence establish? In the 2021 Global Findex wave for Yemen (fieldwork 7 November 2022 – 9 January 2023; World Bank data year 2022), 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered had an account at a financial institution or with a mobile-money provider. Within the same wave: 5.44% of women and 18.35% of men had an account, a difference of 12.91 percentage points; 6.5% of adults in the poorest 40% and 15.5% in the richest 60% by household income, a difference of about 9.0 percentage points; 6.98% of adults with primary education or less and 19.53% of those with secondary education or more, a difference of 12.55 percentage points; and 5.01% of adults aged 15–24 and 16.11% of those aged 25 and over, a difference of 11.10 percentage points. The survey frame excludes areas the source says represent about 23% of the population. These figures are not a 2026 rate and cannot be mapped to governorates. What does it measure? Account ownership as defined by Global Findex (the share of adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered who report having an account, alone or with someone else, at a bank or another type of financial institution, or who report personally using a mobile-money service in the past 12 months), for all adults and by sex, household income, education and age (2021 Findex wave, fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023). Who or what does it apply to? Adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered (the survey frame excludes areas with about 23% of the population); subgroups as defined within the same wave. When was it measured or observed? World Bank reporting year 2022; Global Findex 2021 study; Yemen fieldwork 2022-11-07 to 2023-01-09 How current is it? These are the latest observations available for Yemen: World Bank Data reports them for 2022, from the Global Findex 2021 study fielded from 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023. The Global Findex 2025 edition adds 2024 observations for many economies but no newer observation for Yemen, so the values do not describe 2024, 2025 or 2026. What this evidence does not establish These are values from one survey wave, not an annual series and not a 2026 rate. They cannot be mapped to governorates, they are not comparable with account counts reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), and the differences between groups do not establish their causes. Limits of the measure The survey frame excludes areas holding about 23% of the population, and more than a quarter of primary sampling units were replaced. No standard errors or confidence intervals are published with these values; the Yemen sample is 1,000 respondents, so subgroup values and the gaps carry sampling uncertainty that is not quantified here. en/evidence/VIS-FINDEX-OBSERVED-WAVES/in.text: Evidence/VIS-FINDEX-OBSERVED-WAVES Evidence record Account ownership — observed waves, not an annual line What does this evidence establish? The World Bank has published three observations of account ownership for Yemen: 3.7% in 2011 (accounts at financial institutions only), 6.4% in 2014 and 11.9% in the 2021 Findex wave, reported for 2022 from fieldwork in November 2022 to January 2023 that excluded areas holding about 23% of the population. The years between these waves were not observed. What does it measure? Account ownership among adults aged 15 and over in Yemen at each observed Global Findex wave (2011, 2014 and 2022), in the areas each survey covered, as published by the World Bank. Who or what does it apply to? Verified Yemen Findex wave points only, each with its scope, period and coverage. When was it measured or observed? 2011 / 2014 / 2022 How current is it? The latest observation is from the 2021 Findex wave, reported by the World Bank for 2022 (Yemen fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023); the Global Findex 2025 edition adds no newer Yemen observation. It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish It does not establish values for the years between waves, an average annual growth rate or the causes of the change, and it is not a 2026 value. There is no Yemen observation for 2017 or 2024. Original source and verification Open the source record here, or go to the original document where a public link exists. en/evidence/VIS-FIRM-CONSTRAINTS/index.h.text: Evidence/VIS-FIRM-CONSTRAINTS Evidence record Finance is not the only constraint surveyed formal firms report, 2022 What does this evidence establish? Among formal firms in the 2022 custom survey of seven governorates, 50% named electricity as a business challenge, 46% fuel shortages, 32% transport or road blockades, 30% tax administration or tax rates, 27% political instability and 22% access to finance; 18% named siege and 17% practices of informal competitors. Firms could name more than one challenge, so the shares add up to more than 100%, and neither the number of firms answering nor the exact question wording is recorded in the evidence base. These results apply to the survey sample in seven governorates and are not a national ranking for all Yemeni firms. What does it measure? The share of surveyed formal firms in seven governorates that named each item as a business challenge, 2022. Who or what does it apply to? Formal enterprises in seven selected governorates covered by the 2022 custom survey When was it measured or observed? 2022 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to the 2022 survey (September 2022). It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The shares describe formal firms in a 2022 custom survey of seven governorates; they are not a national ranking of business constraints for all Yemeni firms. They follow the source's own item wording and are not comparable with the standard Enterprise Survey 'biggest obstacle' indicator. Limits of the measure Firms could name more than one challenge, so the shares add up to more than 100%. Neither the number of firms answering nor the exact question wording is recorded in the evidence base. en/evidence/VIS-FIRM-FINANCE-PATH/index..text: Evidence/VIS-FIRM-FINANCE-PATH Evidence record Loan sources in 18 valid responses from surveyed formal firms, 2022 What does this evidence establish? Of the 328 formal firms surveyed in seven governorates in 2022, 31 reported a line of credit. The question on loan sources has 18 valid responses: 10 name private commercial banks, 5 a non-bank financial institution or microfinance provider, 2 another non-financial institution and 1 a state-owned bank or government agency. The evidence base does not establish whether these 18 responses come from the 31 firms with a line of credit. The counts describe these 18 responses only; they do not represent all surveyed firms, all borrowers or all Yemeni enterprises. What does it measure? Counts of surveyed formal firms in seven governorates reporting a line of credit, and counts of loan sources named in valid responses, 2022. Who or what does it apply to? Formal firms in seven selected governorates: 328 surveyed; 31 report a line of credit; 18 valid loan-source responses When was it measured or observed? 2022 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to the 2022 survey (September 2022). It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The 18 loan-source responses do not represent all surveyed firms, all borrowers or all Yemeni enterprises, and it is not established whether they come from the 31 firms that reported a line of credit. Limits of the measure The loan-source counts rest on a small conditional base of 18 responses, and the survey covers formal firms in seven governorates only. The shares of formal firms rating access to finance as a major or a moderate obstacle, among firms in the survey report's finance-obstacle tabulation (firms that said they did not need a loan are excluded), seven governorates, 2022. Who or what does it apply to? Formal firms in seven selected governorates in the survey report's finance-obstacle tabulation, which excludes firms that said they did not need a loan; the number of firms is not recorded in the evidence base When was it measured or observed? 2022 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to the 2022 survey (September 2022). It should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish The combined 91.84% is not the share of all Yemeni firms, or of all surveyed firms, that face a major or moderate finance obstacle; it applies only to the formal firms in the report's filtered tabulation. Limits of the measure The report's tabulation excludes firms that said they did not need a loan, and the number of firms it covers is not recorded in the evidence base. The survey covers formal firms in seven governorates and is not national. Original source and verification Open the source record here, or go to the original document where a public link exists. en/evidence/VIS-FL-EVIDENCE-LADDER/index.text: Evidence/VIS-FL-EVIDENCE-LADDER Evidence record Financial literacy — activity is not outcome What does this evidence establish? Global Money Week records of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) document financial-literacy activities from March 2023 to March 2025, with selected outputs or completion. Separately, the OECD/INFE 2023 survey, which covered 1,000 respondents in Yemen between 11 March and 1 April 2023, reports scores of 15 out of 100 for financial well-being and 42 out of 100 for financial literacy. No evaluation links the activities to capability or other outcomes, so there is no evidence at the outcome level; taking part in an activity does not by itself establish improved capability or impact. What does it measure? Four levels of evidence on financial literacy in Yemen: Global Money Week programme activity from March 2023 to March 2025, its documented outputs or completion, population capability as measured by the OECD/INFE 2023 survey, and programme outcomes established by evaluation, for which the evidence base holds no evidence. Who or what does it apply to? Three kinds of evidence: programme activity and its documented outputs or completion, population capability measured by survey, and programme outcomes established by evaluation. When was it measured or observed? Activity 2023–2025, and the latest available capability survey (2023) How current is it? The activity records run from March 2023 to March 2025, and the population capability scores come from the OECD/INFE survey fielded in Yemen from 11 March to 1 April 2023. Neither describes financial capability in 2026, and they should not be read as describing a later period unless newer comparable evidence is published. What this evidence does not establish It is not established that the OECD/INFE capability levels, or any change in them, result from Global Money Week. Activities, events, participating bodies and workshops are outputs; they do not establish improved financial capability or a causal impact. en/evidence/VIS-INCLUSION-TRANSMISSION/i.text: Evidence/VIS-INCLUSION-TRANSMISSION Evidence record Financial inclusion is a connected system, not a single score What does this evidence establish? Financial inclusion in Yemen is described here as connected parts: people and capability, firms and income, providers, payment rails, remittance and capital flows, regulation and protection, and enabling conditions and constraints. The documented relationships describe context, dependency or plausible mechanisms where evidence supports them; no relationship carries an evidence-strength rating, and the parts do not form a composite score or show that one part causes another. What does it measure? This record sets out how the parts of Yemen's financial-inclusion system relate to one another; it reports no value. Who or what does it apply to? people, firms, providers, rails, flows, rules, enabling constraints When was it measured or observed? Several periods, varying by domain How current is it? This record states relationships rather than an observation, so it has no single observation date; the evidence behind the relationships comes from different periods and domains. What this evidence does not establish The relationships are not causal claims unless separate evidence supports them; the parts do not form a composite index, and no part is shown to drive another mechanically. en/evidence/VIS-MFI-2014-PANEL/index.htm.text: Evidence/VIS-MFI-2014-PANEL Evidence record Microfinance in 2014 — two comparable quarters, not a long trend What does this evidence establish? For the same nine microfinance providers reporting to the Yemen Microfinance Network (YMN), tables for the first and second quarters of 2014 report active borrowers, voluntary savers and outstanding loan portfolio in nominal rials; one provider's first-quarter figures date from December 2013. The two quarters are comparable only within this group of providers and are not linked to other periods. What does it measure? Active borrowers, voluntary savers and outstanding loan portfolio (nominal Yemeni rials) reported by the same nine microfinance providers in Yemen Microfinance Network (YMN) tables for the first and second quarters of 2014. Who or what does it apply to? The same 2014 reporting panel of nine microfinance providers for borrowers, savers and nominal portfolio. When was it measured or observed? 2014 Q1/Q2 How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to the second quarter of 2014 (end of June 2014). It should not be read as describing a later period. What this evidence does not establish It does not form one continuous national series with the 2012 or 2021 figures. Limits of the measure The nine providers are those reporting to YMN, not a census of the whole sector, and one provider's first-quarter figures date from December 2013.
