en/evidence/VIS-MFI-RUPTURE-LENS/index.h.text: Evidence/VIS-MFI-RUPTURE-LENS Evidence record 2015: a sharp fall in active borrowers within the year What does this evidence establish? For microfinance programmes supported by the Social Fund for Development (SFD), active borrowers fell from 124,917 at 31 March 2015 to 106,825 at 30 September and 93,118 at 31 December. Savers and portfolio were also reported at each date; the year-end portfolio is contradictory within the source (YER 6.741 billion in the table, near YER 9 billion in the text), and neither value is adopted. No values are estimated between the dates, and no cause is estimated. What does it measure? Active borrowers, savers and outstanding loan portfolio (nominal Yemeni rials) reported for SFD-supported microfinance programmes at 31 March, 30 September and 31 December 2015. Who or what does it apply to? Microfinance observations for March, September and December 2015 as each source and reporting population defines them, with the conflicting year-end portfolio values kept visible. When was it measured or observed? 2015 How current is it? The latest observation in this record is dated 31 December 2015. It describes 2015 only and should not be read as describing a later period. What this evidence does not establish It does not estimate a cause of the fall or how large any cause's effect was, gives no values between the three dates, and does not establish which of the two year-end portfolio values, table or narrative, is correct. en/evidence/VIS-MFI-SPINE/index.html.text: Evidence/VIS-MFI-SPINE Evidence record Microfinance observations by date, with gaps and breaks shown What does this evidence establish? Figures reported by microfinance programmes and providers supported by the Social Fund for Development (SFD) exist at dated points from 31 December 2010 to 31 December 2020, not at every year-end. In 2015, three snapshots show active borrowers falling from 124,917 at end-March to 93,118 at end-December; the 2018 portfolio value is not published here because its verification is incomplete; 2019 has only a first-quarter observation; February 2021 figures are available only through a Yemen Microfinance Network (YMN) document that cites SFD; and no primary observation has been located for 2022 or 2024. The end-2023 figure comes from a secondary source whose provider set has not been verified and is not combined with these observations. There is no continuous annual series. What does it measure? Active borrowers, savers and outstanding loan portfolio (nominal Yemeni rials) reported by SFD-supported microfinance programmes and providers at each dated observation from 2010 to 2024, with years that have no usable observation marked as gaps. Who or what does it apply to? Microfinance programme observations and reporting populations as each source and date defines them, with changes in reporting scope kept visible. When was it measured or observed? Dated observations between 2010 and 2024 How current is it? The latest SFD observation in this record is dated 31 December 2020. February 2021 figures exist only through a secondary document that cites SFD, and no primary observation has been located for 2022 or 2024, so the record should not be read as describing microfinance after 2020. What this evidence does not establish It gives no values between observed dates, a quarter-end figure does not stand in for a missing year-end, and withheld or contradictory portfolio values are not settled figures. Each observation keeps its own reporting coverage and evidence state, so the points do not form one continuous or national series. en/evidence/VIS-OECD-FCP-TIMELINE/index..text: Evidence/VIS-OECD-FCP-TIMELINE Evidence record Financial consumer protection: which steps from framework to outcome are evidenced? What does this evidence establish? The Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) announced Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions on 28 August 2023 and issued a consumer-protection awareness brochure on 23 March 2024, which describes a complaint and escalation path. The OECD's 2026 review of Yemen's financial sector provides context and recommendations. Apart from the brochure's own account of a dedicated consumer-protection department, the evidence base holds no evidence on implementation, complaint handling, enforcement or consumer outcomes; a framework or guidance document is not evidence that protection works in practice. What does it measure? The stages of financial consumer protection in Yemen — framework, stated purpose, awareness activity, implementation, complaints and redress, enforcement and consumer outcomes — and the evidence recorded for each. Who or what does it apply to? Official instruments and guidance of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), with context attributed to the OECD, keeping the framework separate from implementation and outcomes When was it measured or observed? 2023 to 2024 (official sources), with OECD context from 2026; later stages have no evidence How current is it? The latest official source in this record dates from 23 March 2024, and the OECD analysis from 2026. The evidence base holds no evidence on implementation, enforcement or consumer outcomes for any date. What this evidence does not establish The existence of an instrument does not by itself establish a complaint path, implementation or effective protection, and OECD analysis or other secondary material does not raise the evidence to that level. en/evidence/VIS-PAYMENT-ANATOMY/index.ht.text: Evidence/VIS-PAYMENT-ANATOMY Evidence record What does the payment system actually count? What does this evidence establish? The first-half 2025 payment report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) counts cards, ATMs, POS terminals, POS transactions, e-wallets, e-wallet subscribers and accounts. Each uses its own unit: accounts and subscribers are not necessarily unique people, transactions are events, and terminals are equipment. They cannot be combined into a people-level inclusion rate, because no documented method exists for matching and deduplicating them. What does it measure? Counts of payment-system items — cards, ATMs, POS terminals, POS transactions, e-wallets, e-wallet subscribers and accounts — reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for the first half of 2025, each in its own unit. Who or what does it apply to? Cards, ATMs, POS terminals, transactions, e-wallets, subscribers and accounts within the payment-system reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), first half of 2025; each has its own unit. When was it measured or observed? 2025 H1 How current is it? The counts refer to the first half of 2025. They should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable payment report is published. What this evidence does not establish Cards, accounts, subscribers, transactions and terminals are not people, and they cannot be combined into a single digital-inclusion score. The first-half 2025 counts are not comparable with the third-quarter 2024 payments bulletin until the reporting scope and definitions of the two publications are reconciled. en/evidence/VIS-PAYMENT-RAILS/index.html.text: Evidence/VIS-PAYMENT-RAILS Evidence record How the payment architecture is changing What does this evidence establish? The recorded payment-reform steps from June 2024 to August 2026 sit at separate stages. Rules: a decision of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) requiring exchange companies and money-transfer agents to execute new domestic cash transfers through the unified money-transfer network (26 June 2024), and the mobile e-money amendment (9 July 2025). Project: the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP), approved on 17 June 2025 and started in July 2025, with components supporting the development of a Fast Payment System (FPS) and the establishment of a Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS). Decisions and institutions: a CBY-Aden board decision on what it calls a mandatory national QR standard (29 March 2026), unified-network integration work (17 June 2026), restructuring of the Unified Money Network company (27 July 2026) and the founding assembly of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC) on 3 August 2026. The FMIIP baseline for January 2025 records FPS and RTGS as not yet operational, with no participating institutions, and no later operational state is recorded. The only information on use is a January 2026 CBY-Aden statement about activity on the unified network, which is CBY-Aden's own statement, not an independent measurement. What does it measure? Dated payment-reform steps — rules, project components, decisions, integration work and new institutions — recorded between June 2024 and August 2026, each at the furthest stage its evidence supports. Who or what does it apply to? Payment-reform rules, projects, decisions and institutions documented by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), the World Bank and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), with rules, projects, integration, institutions, operation and use kept separate When was it measured or observed? 2024–2026 How current is it? The latest step in this record is the founding of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC), whose founding assembly met on 3 August 2026 and whose board first met on 4 August 2026. The record should not be read as describing a later stage unless newer official evidence is published. What this evidence does not establish A rule, project component, integration decision or new institution is not evidence of operation, adoption, transaction activity or a financial-inclusion outcome. The Fast Payment System (FPS) and the Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS) are not shown to be operating: the baseline of the Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) for January 2025 records both as not yet operational, and no later operational state is recorded. en/evidence/VIS-POS-TERMINALS/index.html.text: Evidence/VIS-POS-TERMINALS Evidence record Reported POS terminals, monthly What does this evidence establish? POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026, within CBY-Aden's reporting scope. Between December 2025 (1,357) and January 2026 (1,473), the raw totals imply growth of 8.55%, while the January source graphic displays +11%; both the reported totals and the publisher's displayed percentage are shown, and the mismatch is recorded as a discrepancy within the source. Terminal counts are devices, not merchants, unique users or an inclusion outcome. What does it measure? The monthly number of point-of-sale (POS) terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) within its reporting scope, March 2025 to January 2026. Who or what does it apply to? POS terminals within the payment-system reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); how far that scope covers each area of Yemen is not established. When was it measured or observed? Mar-2025–Jan-2026 monthly How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to January 2026; the series runs monthly from March 2025. January 2026 was the latest monthly POS release on the payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) when checked on 26 September 2026. The figures should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable release is published. What this evidence does not establish Growth in terminal numbers does not show merchant adoption, active use of POS services, growth in unique users or an inclusion outcome. The +11% displayed in the January 2026 release and the 8.55% change derived from the raw totals are not arithmetically consistent. The totals fall within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and are not shown to cover all of Yemen. Limits of the measure From July 2025 the monthly releases take the form of a one-page infographic; continuity of the reporting scope across that change has not been verified. en/evidence/VIS-POS-TRANSACTIONS/index.h.text: Evidence/VIS-POS-TRANSACTIONS Evidence record Reported POS transactions, monthly What does this evidence establish? POS transactions reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 8,015 in March 2025 to 24,026 in January 2026, within CBY-Aden's reporting scope, but not steadily: the monthly high was 27,187 in July 2025. Between December 2025 (21,099) and January 2026 (24,026), the raw totals imply growth of 13.87%, while the January source graphic displays +4.9%; both are shown, and the mismatch is recorded as a discrepancy within the source. Transactions are events, not unique users or merchants, so the series does not measure how many people or businesses used POS services. What does it measure? The monthly number of POS transactions reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) within its reporting scope, March 2025 to January 2026. Who or what does it apply to? POS transactions within the payment-system reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); how far that scope covers each area of Yemen is not established. When was it measured or observed? Mar-2025–Jan-2026 monthly How current is it? The latest observation in this record refers to January 2026; the series runs monthly from March 2025. January 2026 was the latest monthly POS release on the payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) when checked on 26 September 2026. The figures should not be read as describing a later period unless a newer comparable release is published. What this evidence does not establish Transactions are events, not unique users or merchants, so the series does not show how many people or businesses used POS services. The monthly values are shown as published, without smoothing or interpolation, and the +4.9% displayed in the January 2026 release and the 13.87% change derived from the raw totals are not arithmetically consistent. The totals fall within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and are not shown to cover all of Yemen. Limits of the measure From July 2025 the monthly releases take the form of a one-page infographic; continuity of the reporting scope across that change has not been verified. en/evidence/VIS-PROVIDER-OBSERVABILITY/i.text: Evidence/VIS-PROVIDER-OBSERVABILITY Evidence record What do we actually know about each provider class? What does this evidence establish? For each provider class the evidence separates the issuing authority, the dated list or count, dated status decisions and evidence of operation. Banks: the licensed-bank list of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names the licensed banks, some of them classified as microfinance banks by name; bank status decisions are not reviewed here. Exchange and remittance providers: the official 2026 roster lists exchange companies, individual exchange establishments and remittance agents, and selected CBY-Aden decisions of 2026 suspend the licences of named entities or close their premises. E-wallets: CBY-Aden publications give e-wallet counts for 2024 and 2025 whose definitions have not been reconciled, and a June 2024 circular names wallets, entities or services as unlicensed; the evidence base holds no current named list of licensed wallets. Non-bank microfinance institutions: the evidence base holds only network membership pages, not a licensing list. Payment-system operators: the evidence base holds no named list. In every class, a list or licence establishes a dated formal status, not that each listed entity or location is operating. What does it measure? For each class of financial-service provider, the issuing authority, the dated list or count, dated status decisions and any evidence of operation, 2024–2026. Who or what does it apply to? Banks, exchange and remittance providers, e-wallets, non-bank microfinance institutions and payment-system operators, as recorded by the issuing authority or source for each class When was it measured or observed? Dated lists and decisions, 2024–2026 How current is it? Each class is dated separately, from the June 2024 circular to decisions dated up to 24 September 2026 and the bank list as checked on 7 September 2026; no class should be read as describing a date later than its own evidence. What this evidence does not establish A list or licence does not show that a provider is operating or reaching customers; a list of unlicensed names is not a register of licensed providers; a decision about named entities does not make a complete list of providers; and the dimensions do not add up to an overall confidence score. en/evidence/VIS-PROVIDER-TIME/index.html.text: Evidence/VIS-PROVIDER-TIME Evidence record Provider status over time: the 2026 roster and dated decisions What does this evidence establish? The official 2026 exchange and remittance roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. Selected decisions of the CBY-Aden Governor dated January to September 2026 suspend or withdraw the licences of named entities or close their premises; they are kept separate from the roster and matched to it entity by entity, because the roster's issue date is not stated. Listing or licensing is not evidence of current operation. What does it measure? The 2026 exchange and remittance roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), counted by class, alongside selected CBY-Aden decisions of 2026 that change the licence status of named entities. Who or what does it apply to? Provider classes and named entities as defined by the cited authority sources; annual roster inclusion does not establish current operation. When was it measured or observed? The official 2026 roster (issue date not stated) and decisions dated January to September 2026. How current is it? The roster is the official 2026 roster, whose issue date is not stated; the latest decision covered is Decision No. 18 of 24 September 2026. A decision changes the status only of the entities it names; it does not redefine the whole roster or show that entities it does not name are operating. What this evidence does not establish The 2026 roster can be counted by class, but the counts are not a verified census of providers operating now. The 2026 decisions are matched to named entities one by one, without assuming whether the roster already reflects them, because the roster does not state its issue date; the complete named set of wallet and payment-service providers is not established. en/evidence/VIS-REMITTANCE-COST/index.ht.text: Evidence/VIS-REMITTANCE-COST Evidence record Quoted cost of sending US$200 and US$500 to Yemen from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, 2025 Q3 What does this evidence establish? In 2025 Q3, the average quoted cost of sending US$200 from Saudi Arabia to Yemen was 2.70% of the amount sent, and 1.26% for US$500; from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) the averages were 7.53% and 5.62% respectively. These are averages of quotes for formal products listed by the World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide database in two corridors; they are not a national Yemen remittance-cost average and do not cover all providers or informal channels. What does it measure? The total cost of sending US$200 or US$500 from Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates to Yemen, as a percentage of the amount sent, averaged over quotes for formal products in 2025 Q3. Who or what does it apply to? Formal remittance products listed by the World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide database for the Saudi Arabia–Yemen and United Arab Emirates–Yemen corridors, by send amount, 2025 Q3 When was it measured or observed? 2025 Q3 How current is it? The averages refer to the third quarter of 2025. As checked on 26 September 2026, both corridor pages still showed the third quarter of 2025 as the latest quarter. What this evidence does not establish These averages cover two corridors, two send amounts and formal products listed by Remittance Prices Worldwide; they are not a national average cost of remittances to Yemen and do not represent all providers, all remittances or informal channels. Limits of the measure Each average is specific to its send amount and can vary by provider, payment instrument, receiving method, fee and exchange-rate margin; the number of providers and quotes behind it is not recorded in the evidence base. en/evidence/VIS-REMITTANCE-MACRO/index.h.text: Evidence/VIS-REMITTANCE-MACRO Evidence record Remittances — IMF-reported history, estimate and projections What does this evidence establish? For external-sector remittances, the IMF's 2025 Article IV staff report gives 2018–2024 as reported history based on staff calculations, including US$1,861.7 million in 2024. A later supplement to the same consultation gives US$1,977 million as the 2025 estimate and projections rising from US$2,159 million in 2026 to US$3,110 million in 2030. The two documents were published at different times, so the two parts are not joined into one continuous series. The series covers the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government, not the whole of Yemen. Estimates and projections are not observations, and the series is not a measure of informal hawala volume. What does it measure? Annual external-sector remittances, in US$ million, in the IMF series for 2018–2030, with each year labelled as reported history (2018–2024), estimate (2025) or projection (2026–2030). Who or what does it apply to? IMF external-sector remittance series on the IMF’s analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government; each year labelled as reported history, estimate or projection, with its source document When was it measured or observed? 2018–2030 How current is it? Reported history runs to 2024 (IMF staff report, staff calculations); 2025 is an estimate and 2026–2030 are projections from a later supplement. Estimates and projections are not observations, so the 2025–2030 values are not current evidence, and the 2024 value should not be read as a current level unless a newer comparable observation is published. What this evidence does not establish Estimates and projections are not observations, and a forecast revision is not an economic change. The two IMF documents do not form one continuous series. The series is not a measure of informal hawala volume, and its level, which covers areas under the internationally recognized government, is not a figure for the whole of Yemen. Financial access points as defined in the results framework of the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708) When was it measured or observed? Baseline January 2025; target June 2030; no result recorded How current is it? The baseline refers to January 2025 and the target to June 2030; no observed result is recorded for any later date. Adding different types of access point does not give a valid total without a documented classification and deduplication rule. The June 2030 target of 1,021 access points has meaning only against the January 2025 baseline of 817 under the same project definition. en/evidence/compare/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Compare evidence without forcing unlike measures onto one scale Select 2–4 records. Compare definition, period, population or calculation base, geography, unit and method before comparing values. A mismatch is a reason to qualify the comparison, not to hide it; when definitions or populations do not match, “not comparable” is a valid result. Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. 01 Analysis Three measures that cannot be combined Three kinds of figure are often set side by side. 11.9% is the share of adults (15+) in the survey's covered areas who had an account in the 2021 Global Findex wave, with fieldwork in 2022–2023. About 3.3 million is what a 2024 secondary source calls “active savers” in microfinance in 2023 — a count that has not been deduplicated into unique people. And 1,062,441 active bank accounts and 375,252 active e-wallet accounts are the FMIIP project's baselines for January 2025 — accounts, not people. These figures measure different things, for different populations and dates, from different kinds of evidence. They cannot be added, subtracted, ranked or converted into one another, and no population total is used here to turn the counts into shares. For these figures, “not comparable” is the correct result. First ask whether the records can be compared at all; then look at the numbers. Can these records actually be compared? The comparison table sets the selected records side by side on definition, period, population or calculation base, source scope and method, and on geography and unit where these are recorded. Terms such as accounts, active accounts, subscribers, beneficiaries, merchants and POS terminals may sound related but are not interchangeable. Material mismatches remain visible and prevent a false common scale or combined result. en/evidence/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Inspect the evidence behind the answer Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. 01 How to search, inspect and compare the records Use the Evidence hub to find a claim, indicator, visual or source-backed record, then inspect the definition, group covered, calculation base, period, geography, method, limitations, source and evidence date. Compare records when similar labels may hide different units or populations. Disagreement, series breaks and missing evidence remain visible rather than being averaged or filled in. The hub is an index for verification; detailed evidence lives in the linked records and comparison view. ⌕ Compare evidence Start here: selected evidence records The official 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted; whether providers operate now is a separate question The official 2026 roster of exchange and remittance providers issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These are roster entries counted by the roster's own classes: the three class totals are not a count of unique providers, nor a verified count of providers operating now. Because the roster does not state its issue date, CBY-Aden's 2026 decisions (dated January to September 2026) suspending or withdrawing the licences of named entities, or closing their premises, are matched with the roster entity by entity, because a decision may or may not already be reflected in it. Does not establish: Adding the three classes does not give a count of unique providers, because no rule for identifying the same entity across classes has been applied. Inclusion in the annual roster is not proof of current operation, branch activity or service availability, including for entities named in 2026 enforcement decisions. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-009 Evidence freshness differs by domain The evidence here is not equally current across domains: several payments/regulatory observations are from 2025–2026, while key representative people-side evidence is older. Does not establish: Older evidence is not invalid because of its age, and recent administrative evidence does not measure current financial inclusion across the population. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-014 Enforcement decisions are events, not a market census Governor's decisions of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) dated January to September 2026 record licence withdrawals, suspensions and closures for specific exchange and remittance providers. This record covers selected CBY-Aden Governor's decisions of 2026 concerning exchange and remittance providers (Nos. 1–6, 9–11, 13–15, 17 and 18); other decision numbers are not included and their subjects are not assessed. The official 2026 roster can be counted by class, but these decisions are matched with it entity by entity and are not subtracted from it to produce a count of providers operating now. Does not establish: The 2026 annual roster can be counted by class, but it is not a census of operating providers. Subtracting suspension, withdrawal and closure decisions from the roster does not give a current count of operating providers: the roster does not state its issue date, so each decision is matched to named entities one by one, without assuming whether the roster already reflects it. A provider not named in these decisions is not thereby shown to be active or compliant. The record does not cover 2026 decision numbers other than those listed, and it does not assess their subjects. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-019 Raw case shares are not population estimates World Bank variable pages expose raw sample case counts and percentages for the Yemen Findex file, but explicitly warn that those figures cannot be interpreted as summary statistics of the population of interest. Does not establish: The raw, unweighted case percentages shown on the World Bank variable pages are not estimates for Yemen's adult population and are not reported in this resource. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-024 There is no single latest year for all people-side evidence The people-side evidence here does not have one latest year: account ownership has a latest verified Yemen aggregate in 2022, while weighted public evidence currently available here for account use, saving, borrowing and domestic-remittance behaviour is centered on 2014; latest-wave resilience and barrier values remain unpublished until the required weighted computation is complete. Historical results stay separate from any newer estimate until that computation and its verification are complete. Does not establish: The 2014 behaviour values do not describe current behaviour, and raw case percentages from the 2021 wave are not a substitute for weighted population estimates. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-031 A public interface is not the same thing as the underlying dataset World Bank public remittance interfaces do not expose Yemen history uniformly. One interface, reviewed on 10 September 2026, showed an older span of years, while other World Bank interfaces and earlier documented retrievals contained later observations. The difference reflects what each interface displays and how its data can be traced; it is not evidence that later underlying data are absent. Does not establish: The difference does not show that data were deleted or withdrawn, or why any correction was made, and one public interface's observations are not a substitute for another's. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-039 IMF Staff-Monitored Program (SMP) for Yemen: staff-level agreement of July 2026, subject to Management approval On 16 July 2026, staff of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Yemeni authorities announced staff-level agreement on key policies and reforms that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program (SMP). The IMF stated that the agreement was subject to Management approval and would not result in Board discussion. It is not an IMF financing arrangement. Does not establish: The proposed Staff-Monitored Program (SMP) is not an arrangement approved or endorsed by the Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and does not involve IMF financing; the agreement is also not evidence that external-sector statistics have been reconciled. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-049 June and end-2023 borrower points are not one continuous series The roughly 80,800 active-borrower point cited for June 2023 and the 78,686 end-2023 point come through different source chains. They are kept as separate observations until the provider sets and methods behind them are reconciled, and no June-to-year-end decline is calculated from them. Does not establish: The two figures do not establish a decline between June and the end of 2023, monthly values between them, or a continuous series, while the provider sets behind them remain unreconciled. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-057 The SMEPS financial-services KPI is a programme result, not a national MSME rate SMEPS's 2024 Annual Report reports that 19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services in 2024, while the 2021–2024 total reported as achieved is 15% against a 40% programme target. The table does not fully specify the metric-specific assessment base or operational definition of 'accessed financial services'. The KPI can therefore be read only within the programme, subject to that limitation; it is not a national MSME access rate. Does not establish: The percentage is not a national rate of access to financial services for micro, small and medium enterprises, a representative survey estimate or a national rate of unique firms, and it does not show that SMEPS caused access. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-060 Formal firms in the 2022 survey: accounts were common, bank finance for working capital was not Among formal firms in the 2022 seven-governorate survey, 58.2% (191 of 328) reported a checking or savings account. Their working capital came mainly from internal sources: on average, 69.12% came from internal funds or retained earnings, 16.66% from money lenders, friends or relatives, 10.15% from advance payments by clients, 1.97% from non-bank financial institutions, 1.31% from supplier credit and 0.56% from banks. In a separate question on the financial intermediaries they use, 73.48% of responding formal firms named an exchange store or money exchanger and 24.39% a commercial bank; firms could name more than one, so these are not market shares. The evidence base does not record the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. Among the 217 informal firms surveyed, 80.18% had no bank account; that sample was drawn from activity and location lists rather than a national register. The formal-firm sample includes micro firms with fewer than five employees, and neither sample represents all Yemeni firms. Does not establish: The evidence base does not record the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. An average working-capital share is not a share of firms, and multiple-response percentages are not market shares. Holding an account does not show that a firm uses bank credit. The formal and informal samples use different frames, so they cannot be added together or compared with the 2013 survey. Firms are not people, so these shares are not comparable with the Findex account-ownership rate. Open evidence record → Reference CLM-062 Where is the evidence current — and where is it old? Evidence dates differ by domain: several payments and regulatory observations date from 2025–2026, while key representative evidence about people is older. Each item is placed by its observation or publication date and by its evidence type: representative survey, administrative record, regulatory material, secondary evidence or unresolved gap. Newer administrative data are not automatically a current population outcome, and older evidence is not automatically invalid. Old evidence is not automatically invalid; recent administrative/regulatory evidence is not a current population outcome. Open evidence record → Reference VIS-EVIDENCE-FRESHNESS What may explain the number — without pretending to prove it? This summary starts from one quantitative measure and links it only to contextual mechanisms, policy propositions, research priorities or needs for verification against the original source, where an explicit, documented relationship exists. The links help interpret the number; they do not estimate prevalence, effect size or causality. The links do not establish causation, prevalence or a sentiment score unless separate evidence does. Open evidence record → Reference VIS-MECHANISM-METRIC-BRIDGE Consumer protection and complaint path: official rules and guidance Evidence on the consumer-protection and complaint path of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden): the announcement of the 2023 Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions (28 August 2023), whose legal text has not been extracted here, and 2024 awareness material and a brochure describing the complaint and escalation steps. Actual complaint handling and redress outcomes are separate questions on which the evidence base holds no evidence. The existence of a complaint and redress framework does not establish that consumers use it, that cases are resolved on time, or that redress outcomes are effective. Open evidence record → Reference DS-FCP-ARCH Qualitative evidence register A structured register of 20 reconciled qualitative evidence items used to interpret mechanisms, institutional conditions and source-specific narratives without turning them into population prevalence or causal estimates. Qualitative evidence can support mechanisms and context, but it does not by itself establish population prevalence, quantified effect size or causality. Open evidence record → Reference DS-QUAL-EVIDENCE OECD: institutional fragility and weak formal access (qualitative interpretation) The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) links fragmented institutions, supervisory gaps and weak formal access to financial-sector fragility and low trust. The evidence is contextual interpretation, not measured prevalence or a causal effect estimate. It cannot establish prevalence, a quantified level of trust or a causal effect size. Open evidence record → Reference QUAL-001 How many respondents answered each Findex question Weighted estimates for the 2021 wave have not yet been produced, so no values are shown. When they are published, each will be accompanied by the number of respondents who gave a valid answer, the number of missing or invalid answers, and a note where a question was asked only of a sub-group; these counts describe the sample and are not population estimates. Raw case percentages are not population prevalence rates, and indicators are not ranked by them. Open evidence record → Reference VIS-FINDEX-SAMPLE-SUPPORT Latest observation for each people-side financial function The latest weighted evidence differs by financial function: account ownership has a value from the 2021 Findex wave (11.9%, reported for 2022), while the latest weighted values for saving, borrowing and domestic remittances date from 2014 (20.6% of adults saved any money, 65.9% borrowed any money and 18.3% received domestic remittances), and weighted estimates of resilience and of the reasons for not having an account have not yet been calculated for the 2021 wave. It is not a composite inclusion score. There is no single latest year for people-side evidence, and a recent date for one function does not make the evidence for another function current. Open evidence record → Reference VIS-DEMAND-VINTAGE-LADDER Published historical Findex results for Yemen Weighted Findex values for Yemen from the 2011 and 2014 waves, one value per measure and wave, each with its population base, missing values and publication status, so older measures stay interpretable without being presented as current. Historical weighted values hold for their stated wave and base, but they do not establish current 2026 behaviour and do not describe later years unless newer comparable evidence is published. Open evidence record → Reference DS-FINDEX-PUBLIC-HISTORY How recent the people-side evidence is, by financial function Shows, for ten financial functions, the period that each function's evidence refers to, so that the people-side answer does not imply one common latest year. The currentness map does not make older evidence current, and a function with no newer numeric observation remains an evidence gap rather than zero or an interpolated value. Open evidence record → Reference DS-DEMAND-VINTAGE-LENS What kind of evidence is this? Evidence in this resource falls into distinct types: weighted population measures, administrative records, perception studies, official secondary analysis, recommendations, and the stage a reform or programme has reached. Each type supports different conclusions; the types are not a ranking of truth or a numeric confidence score. One type of evidence does not stand in for another: a perception is not a population outcome, a recommendation is not implementation, a project milestone is not usage, and an account or transaction is not a unique person. An evidence type is not a probability or certainty score, and the order in which types are presented does not rank them. en/explore/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Start with the question, not the dataset. The question determines what evidence is relevant — and what cannot yet be answered. Start with the decision or uncertainty you need to resolve, then follow the answer to the evidence, its limits and its source. Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. 01 What it means Every question should make six things clear What do we know now? How strong is the evidence? Who or what does it apply to? What does it not establish? What do we still not know? What new evidence could change the answer? Evidence is not combined merely because it concerns the same topic. 02 What this does not establish A related number is not automatically an answer Two values can concern the same topic and still answer different questions because their populations, definitions, periods or source coverage differ. Evidence is linked only when that relationship can be defended; similarity of topic does not make values comparable or establish causality. 03 What we still do not know If the evidence is not enough When the evidence is insufficient, an unknown stays unknown. The gap becomes a measurement question rather than an undocumented estimate. Missing evidence is not zero and does not justify estimation. Questions that lead into the evidence Find the question closest to your decision Every answer keeps its period, population or calculation base, limits and source in view. Understand the wider picture 2 What is changing in Yemen's financial-inclusion system — and what does it mean for people and firms? A connected view showing different measurement dates and the links that remain unmeasured. Are reforms and payment infrastructure turning into access, use, quality and outcomes? A stage-by-stage chain from rule to result. People, use and flows 4 Who is being left behind — and where are the measured gaps? Population measures, same-wave disparities and what the evidence cannot explain. Is digital finance becoming durable financial use — or do the available data still mainly measure infrastructure and transactions? Infrastructure, registration, activity and durable-use evidence kept separate. What do remittances and other money flows tell us about households’ connection to the financial system? Successive releases of national flow data, channels, costs and evidence on household use. Where can people and firms actually reach financial services — and where is the map still blank? Observed access evidence and the requirements for a defensible national access map. Firms, institutions and providers 3 For firms, how serious a constraint is finance — and how does it compare with other constraints? How often finance is named among other constraints, how severe the finance obstacle is for a defined group of firms, the credit path and programme evidence. How are borrower reach, savers/depositors, nominal portfolio and provider structure changing in microfinance? Borrower reach, savers/depositors, nominal portfolio and provider structure remain separate measures rather than one inclusion measure. Which providers are evidenced, under whose authority, and what do we actually know about their status? Authority, listing/licensing and dated status events without inferring operation. Verify and decide what to measure 2 Which missing evidence would materially change financial-inclusion decisions? Decision-linked evidence gaps, the minimum evidence needed and where it may come from. How can I check the evidence behind a claim, see why sources disagree and reproduce a result? Evidence records, field-by-field comparison, how derived figures are calculated, and how to cite them. Go deeper The system is changing. What has reached people? Yemen’s rules, institutions and payment infrastructure have moved faster than its representative evidence about people. The gap between the two is not an answer to guess; it is the next thing to measure. Evidence period: Global Findex fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023 · POS counts March 2025 – January 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 Open this ReadingAll Evidence Readings What the evidence cannot yet answer A current people-side inclusion baseline The Global Findex 2025 edition contains 2024 observations for many economies, but Yemen's latest representative account-ownership observation remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, for 2022 (from the Yemen Findex 2021 study fielded in 2022–2023). Major payment-system and reform changes are more recent. The latest published people-level values for receiving domestic remittances, and through which channels, are from 2014; the 2021-wave microdata contain these questions, but weighted estimates have not yet been produced. Evidence needed: New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency. Open this measurement priority Financial inclusion across population groups: measure disparities before explaining them Within the same survey wave, account ownership differs by 12.91 percentage points between women (5.44%) and men (18.35%), and by about 9.0 percentage points between adults in the poorest 40% (6.5%) and the richest 60% (15.5%) by household income. Comparable current differences by age group and displacement status are not established in the evidence base, and the contribution of identity, device, income, geography, trust and household constraints to any measured disparity is not established. Evidence needed: Representative or clearly bounded disaggregated quantitative evidence to measure subgroup outcomes, with linked mechanism variables and qualitative or stronger causal designs where explanation is required. Open this measurement priority A current MSME finance demand/use baseline A 2022 survey of formal firms in seven governorates and programme evidence from the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) can each be used within its own scope; neither supplies a current representative national MSME finance baseline. Evidence needed: A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome. Open this measurement priority A register of active financial access points Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points. Evidence needed: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated. Open this measurement priority Consumer experience and redress outcomes Official material specifies complaint and escalation architecture, including source-defined time windows; actual complaint volumes, resolution times and outcomes are not documented in the available evidence. Evidence needed: Complaint and redress data from providers and the regulator, plus consumer-side evidence on experience, including fees, disclosure and trust. Open this measurement priority

en/finance/index.html.text: Explore / How are borrower reach, savers/depositors, nominal portfolio and provider structure changing in microfinance? Finance: borrower, saver and balance figures measure different things Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active microfinance borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020; a 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023, for a set of providers that has not yet been verified. Saver, portfolio and bank balance-sheet figures use different definitions, provider coverage and valuation bases, so this resource keeps them separate and does not read them as one trend or as deeper inclusion. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What the finance evidence does not establish Savers or depositors are not necessarily unique people. Nominal portfolio growth is not real credit deepening. A listed microfinance bank is not proof of operation or outreach. A restatement of the same year's figures is not an economic boom. Historical or secondary borrower figures are not a current national inclusion rate, and these separate data points do not establish improved borrower outcomes or causality. What remains unresolved This resource still lacks a fully harmonized current institution-level series that reconciles provider coverage, borrower and saver definitions, deduplication, currency and valuation basis, nominal versus real values, and comparable reporting periods. The underlying 2023 SFD/SMED primary source behind several secondary figures has been identified but is not yet available for direct verification. Microfinance portfolio figures are also not expressed here as a share of bank credit: twelve microfinance banks appear on the same CBY-Aden bank list, so the two stocks may overlap, and they differ in valuation basis, date and institutional coverage. 01 Analysis Microfinance history is informative, but not a continuous annual series The historical record contains exact quarterly and year-end observations, years for which only references are available, and years with no usable observation. In 2015, primary SFD evidence shows active borrowers declining from 124,917 at end-March to 106,825 at end-September and 93,118 at end-December, alongside a declining reported portfolio. This resource keeps those observed points and gaps as they are; it does not interpolate the missing months or estimate a causal conflict effect. 02 Analysis Borrowers, savers and nominal portfolio do not form one harmonized trend Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not yet been verified. That paper also reports what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” and a nominal portfolio of about YER 44 billion in 2023. The verified 2020 figures are 1.611 million savers/depositors and YER 33.379 billion; “active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure. Both portfolio figures are nominal rials. Between December 2020 and December 2023 the average market rate published by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) moved from 792.69 to 1,529.4 rials per US dollar, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen's divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use. No real or US-dollar change can be derived from the two figures. With the 2023 primary source document, provider coverage, saver definition and the link between the two periods also unresolved, these values are separate data points, not a trend. Another view of the evidence Borrowers, savers and loan portfolio: separate dated anchors, not one series Text description of this view Analytical question: What does the available microfinance evidence show about borrowers, savers and portfolio size over time? What the evidence shows: Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified tables record 93,118 active borrowers and 509,590 savers at end-2015, and 88,445 borrowers and 1.611 million savers/depositors at end-2020. The loan portfolio is YER 6.741 billion at end-2015 in the provider table (the source narrative gives a figure near YER 9 billion) and YER 33.379 billion at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper by the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, citing SFD/SMED loan-portfolio data, reports 78,686 borrowers, what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” and a nominal portfolio of about YER 44 billion for end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not been verified. “Active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen’s divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use. The figures are therefore separate dated anchors: they do not show a trend or a divergence, and they do not establish unique people, real credit deepening or a US-dollar change. Scope and time: end-2015, end-2020 and end-2023 (secondary source), plus a contextual finding through 2021 · Microfinance institutions and banks as covered by each source (providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development for 2015 and 2020); the set of providers covered in 2023 and the deduplication of savers are unresolved What not to conclude: The anchors are not a harmonized trend or evidence of divergence. They do not show growth in unique people, real credit deepening, broader inclusion, better borrower outcomes or a causal effect of the conflict. 03 Analysis Who provides microfinance: what the lists and panels show Of the 26 banks on the list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, 12 are identified by the source label as microfinance banks; appearing on the list establishes listing, not operation or outreach. Historical microfinance figures come from provider reporting panels whose membership changes — the 2014 panel, for example, covers nine providers — so provider counts and totals from different periods are not one continuous series. 04 Evidence A published balance-sheet jump can partly be a valuation change The same 2022 consolidated banking positions are published at materially higher levels from the 2023 annual report onward, alongside a documented January-2023 shift to market-exchange-rate valuation of foreign-currency positions. The published difference does not by itself establish growth in assets, deposits or credit because the restatement changes the comparison base. 05 System context Finance sits between funding, providers and real economic use Institutional finance connects funding and liquidity to providers, credit products, firms and households. But each link has a different measure: capital available to an institution is not credit disbursed; portfolio is not borrowers; borrowers are not unique households; and larger loans are not necessarily wider outreach. This resource links Finance to Firms, Providers and external flows while preserving those boundaries. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. System context Balance-sheet capacity is visible; a complete current financial-soundness diagnosis is not The compiled monetary series provide balance-sheet context on bank deposits, credit to the private sector, bank reserves, capital and reserves, loans and advances, and foreign-currency deposits across their available reporting periods. These measures help describe intermediation capacity and structure, but they are not a complete current financial-soundness assessment: solvency, asset quality or current system-wide soundness cannot be inferred from balance-sheet aggregates alone. The current evidence base does not yet contain a harmonized, publication-ready set of non-performing-loan, capital-adequacy and liquidity ratios with common definitions and vintages. Analysis External support passes through stages and forms that cannot simply be added together A pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposit, amount made available, budget disbursement, FX-auction use, in-kind support and project cost are different stages or forms of support. They may describe the same support pathway at different stages or overlapping components. This resource therefore does not manufacture a cumulative finance total by adding unlike amounts. System context The financial system changed through shocks, constraints and policy responses — not one continuous trend The documented chronology traces several distinct breaks: reserve and import-finance pressure by 2015–16; the 2016 central-bank split; rapid growth of currency outside banks by 2017; Saudi reserve support in 2018 and 2023; the 2019 split in cash circulation and payments; the oil-export shock after 2022; FX auctions and external support in 2023–24; banking-liquidity stress and administrative FX/import measures in 2025; and later payment-infrastructure investment. Each event keeps its territorial and institutional scope; where money is involved, agreement, deposit, availability, disbursement and downstream use are kept apart and never added together; and revisions to remittance figures for the same year are kept separate from actual economic change. These events help explain the environment in which finance operates, but their sequence does not prove that any one event caused a financial-inclusion outcome. System context An evidence-based chronology of the financial system The dated events below help explain the conditions under which finance operates: funding and liquidity pressures, exchange-rate conditions, intermediation and payment infrastructure. Each event opens a record with its source and limitations. The chronology is context, not a causal model of financial inclusion. Demand-side evidence Holding a product and owning an account are related — not interchangeable Product-holding and mobile-access figures attributed to the OECD's 2026 financial-sector review have not yet been verified against the review's own text, and they are not shown here. Any such measures would in any case use questions and constructs different from the Global Findex account-ownership measure and would remain separate evidence rather than a harmonised series. Product holding, account ownership, device access and financial-service use must not be averaged or treated as interchangeable. Dated events in Yemen's financial system Each event keeps its date, its source and what it does not establish. The order of events does not show that one caused another. 2014–2015 The conflict that escalated from late 2014 disrupted output, public finance, external inflows and monetary conditions; by late 2015 official foreign reserves had fallen below US$2 billion, about two months of imports. Relevance to financial inclusion: This conditions banks, import finance, cash demand and service continuity. Does not establish: It does not quantify population financial inclusion in 2015 or attribute later inclusion outcomes to one shock. Sources: Yemen's Economic Outlook, Spring 2016 · Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) February 2016 With reserves under pressure, the Central Bank of Yemen stopped supporting imports at the official exchange rate except for wheat and rice. Relevance to financial inclusion: Import-finance constraints affect liquidity, prices, firms and trade-settlement channels, but are not themselves an inclusion measure. Does not establish: It does not show which households or firms lost financial-service access. Sources: Yemen's Economic Outlook, Spring 2016 September 2016 A 2016 decision relocated the Central Bank of Yemen from Sana'a to Aden, leaving two central-bank authorities operating under the divided political and territorial order. Relevance to financial inclusion: Provider status, payment interoperability, cash conditions and formal financial access can diverge by territory. Does not establish: Institutional fragmentation does not by itself prove that a specific provider or service stopped operating in a specific location. Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): appraisal document (project approved 17 June 2025) 2017–2018 World Bank monitoring estimated that currency outside banks rose from YER810.9 billion in 2014 to YER1,673 billion by end-2017, alongside large issuance of new banknotes, and expected rapid money-supply growth in 2018. Relevance to financial inclusion: It provides context for cash dependence and pressure on formal intermediation. Does not establish: Currency outside banks is not equal to household cash holdings, exclusion, or the number of unbanked people. Sources: Yemen Economic Monitoring Brief, Fall 2018 January–March 2018 Saudi Arabia issued a directive for, and then signed an agreement to deliver, a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen, with the stated aim of supporting the financial and economic position and the riyal. Relevance to financial inclusion: Stabilization and import-finance support can affect firms, prices and banking liquidity indirectly. Does not establish: The signed amount is not identical to later FX sales and is not an inclusion outcome. Sources: Saudi directive and agreement on a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (January–March 2018) December 2019 Tighter enforcement in Sana'a of the ban on newer rial banknotes contributed to a payments crisis and widened dual exchange rates between old and new notes across the divided monetary areas. Relevance to financial inclusion: A nominally available transfer or payment channel may have different usability and cost by territory. Does not establish: It does not quantify unique users switching to digital finance or prove durable digital adoption. Sources: Yemen Monthly Economic Update, December 2019 Early 2020 World Bank monitoring reported that the bulk of the 2018 Saudi US$2 billion deposit had been exhausted by end-January 2020 and highlighted multiple exchange-rate regimes and remittance risks from the COVID-19 shock. Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittances matter as both household flows and part of broader FX/payment conditions. Does not establish: A stated risk to remittances is not an observed decline unless separately measured. Sources: Yemen's Economic Update, April 2020 October 2022–January 2023 Attacks on oil export facilities in October 2022 were followed by the suspension of oil exports from January 2023, sharply reducing a major source of government and foreign-exchange revenue in areas under the internationally recognized government. Relevance to financial inclusion: Bank liquidity, FX availability, firm finance and payment conditions need to be read against this external-revenue break. Does not establish: The oil-export shock does not itself quantify access to financial services or household adoption. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) 21 February 2023 Saudi Arabia signed a US$1 billion deposit agreement with the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and stated that the amount was fully deposited in the bank's account. Relevance to financial inclusion: The link to inclusion is indirect through macro stability, banking and import-finance conditions. Does not establish: The US$0.775 billion later made available and any use of it in FX auctions are part of the same US$1 billion, not additional support. Sources: Agreement on a US$1 billion Saudi deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (21 February 2023) 2023–2024 The IMF reports US$1.2 billion in Saudi budget support over 2023–24 and a US$1 billion deposit at the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), of which US$0.775 billion had been made available; CBY-Aden auctioned US$1.05 billion for import financing during 2023–24. Relevance to financial inclusion: These flows condition formal banking and firm activity but are not direct inclusion outcomes. Does not establish: The US$1.05 billion of FX auctions is downstream use of support already counted, not a separate donor inflow. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) · Agreement on a US$1 billion Saudi deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (21 February 2023) 2022–2024 In the IMF’s macroeconomic framework for areas under the internationally recognized government, the current-account deficit improved from about 40.5% of GDP in 2022 to an average of about 14.5% in 2023–24, reflecting import compression, strong remittances and bilateral grants despite the halt in oil exports. Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittances, imports and FX conditions interact, but the aggregate balance does not reveal who used formal services. Does not establish: The deficit improvement is not proof of stronger household welfare, financial inclusion or productive investment. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) March–June 2024 A new 100-rial coin in Sana'a in March 2024 was followed by an April CBY-Aden directive for banks headquartered in Sana'a to relocate to Aden and further June measures affecting unlicensed entities, wallets, payment services and remittance networks. Relevance to financial inclusion: The same provider name can carry different regulatory and operational meanings by territory. Does not establish: A directive or prohibition does not prove actual compliance, closure, relocation or user access at every location. Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): appraisal document (project approved 17 June 2025) By 30 May 2024 World Bank/G2Px reported that Yemen's Unconditional Cash Transfer programme had piloted digital payments in eight districts, reaching 45,460 recipients, with the pilot emphasizing payments into fully functional accounts and recipient choice. Relevance to financial inclusion: This is direct Yemen evidence that a social transfer can create formal account exposure. Durable inclusion still requires follow-up on activation, repeat transactions, merchant use, saving, cash-out, cost and user experience. Does not establish: The 45,460 recipients are not evidence of 45,460 persistent active users, a national inclusion rate, or sustained post-transfer digital use. Sources: Digitalizing Government-to-Person (G2P) Payments in Yemen: unconditional cash transfer (UCT) pilot (2024) 2024 value as revised between CBY-Aden annual reports The 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gives remittances for 2024 of USD 6,245 million; its 2025 annual report restates the same year at USD 3,422.16 million, a downward revision of about 45.2%. Relevance to financial inclusion: Any analysis of remittance trends must disclose changes between report editions and in method before drawing behavioural conclusions. Does not establish: A revised 2024 level is not evidence that remittances collapsed by 45.2% during 2024. Sources: Annual Report 2024 · Annual Report 2025 2022–April 2025 In the IMF's banking data for areas under the internationally recognized government, the liquid-assets to short-term-liabilities ratio fell from 148 in 2022 to 69 in April 2025, while the capital-to-assets ratio fell from about 5 to about 2.5. Relevance to financial inclusion: Provider resilience and usable service capacity are system conditions for inclusion. Does not establish: Prudential ratios do not show how many unique people gained or lost access. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) 17 June 2025–2030 project period The World Bank approved a US$20 million IDA grant for the Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (P180708) on 17 June 2025. The project is active, implemented by UNDP, closes on 30 June 2030, and the latest publicly disclosed Implementation Status and Results Report (ISR) identified for this resource is report no. 2, dated 8 April 2026. Relevance to financial inclusion: The project can create payment-system capacity and targeted access/usage mechanisms, while population adoption and inclusion effects require later evidence. Does not establish: The US$20 million commitment, an implementation report, a system go-live or a 2030 target is not evidence that users have already adopted services or that inclusion outcomes have been achieved. Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): project record and results framework (2025–2030) · Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP): implementation overview (2025–2030) · Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP): Implementation Status and Results Report, sequence 2 (8 April 2026) July 2025 onward The internationally recognized government established the National Committee for the Regulation and Financing of Imports to prioritize FX for essential imports, improve import transparency and channel FX through the formal banking sector. Relevance to financial inclusion: This may change incentives and flows through banks and exchangers, which should be measured. Does not establish: Creation of the committee does not prove improved access, lower costs or successful formalization. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) Mid-July–early August 2025 The IMF reports the rial, in markets in areas under the internationally recognized government, strengthening from about YER2,900 to about YER1,600 per US dollar from mid-July to early August 2025 after a package of FX and market measures. Relevance to financial inclusion: Exchange-rate conditions affect prices, remittance conversion, firm costs and channel incentives. Does not establish: The appreciation does not by itself prove durable macro stability or improved financial inclusion. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) September 2025 The IMF reports operational foreign-exchange reserves of about US$350 million in September 2025, covering roughly one month of imports. Relevance to financial inclusion: Reserve scarcity affects import finance, bank liquidity and prices. Does not establish: Import-cover reserves do not measure household financial resilience or account use. Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) 1 March 2026 The Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen signed an agreement with Yemen's Ministry of Finance to begin depositing SAR1.3 billion in economic support for operating expenses and salaries. Relevance to financial inclusion: It can affect public cash flow, salaries, demand and macro conditions. Does not establish: The SAR1.3 billion agreement is not shown to be the same flow as IMF-reported USD commitments or disbursements; no source-level crosswalk establishes that. An agreement to deposit is not evidence that a deposit or a disbursement has taken place. Sources: Agreement between the Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen (SDRPY) and Yemen's Ministry of Finance on SAR1.3 billion in economic support (1 March 2026) 4 June 2026 The World Bank Group endorsed a Country Partnership Framework for Yemen for FY2026–FY2030 and approved four new operations totaling US$285 million. The framework focuses on nutrition, electricity, agribusiness, mariculture and fisheries, with women’s participation and private-sector development as cross-cutting enablers. Relevance to financial inclusion: This context helps interpret firm finance, payment infrastructure and participation constraints as connected parts of a wider economic system. Does not establish: Endorsement of a strategy or approval of operations does not prove improved financial access, service use, jobs, implementation quality or inclusion outcomes. Sources: Republic of Yemen: Country Partnership Framework for FY2026–FY2030 30 June 2026 The World Bank approved a US$100 million IDA grant for the Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project in Yemen. The project is expected to reach 1.8 million people, support around 55,000 individuals through Village Savings and Loan Associations, and support more than 675,000 people in obtaining national identity cards and birth certificates; these are design features and targets of the project, not achieved results. Relevance to financial inclusion: Identity documentation and savings-group participation are potentially important enabling steps that should be measured separately from account ownership, active use and service quality. Does not establish: Project targets, beneficiary counts, identity-document support and VSLA participation do not establish national prevalence, active bank or wallet use, or persistence after programme support ends. Sources: Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project, Yemen (approved 30 June 2026) 16 July 2026 IMF staff and the Yemeni authorities reached a staff-level agreement on policies that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program. The agreement is subject to IMF Management approval, and the IMF press release on the mission states that it will not result in an Executive Board discussion; priorities include fiscal and monetary management, reserve rebuilding, and financial-sector and electricity reforms. Relevance to financial inclusion: Financial-sector reform commitments matter for intermediation, resilience and oversight, while inclusion effects require later evidence on provider behaviour, access, use, cost, quality and protection. Does not establish: A staff-level agreement does not establish IMF financing, Executive Board approval, completed reforms, improved bank soundness or improved financial inclusion. Sources: Yemen: staff-level agreement on a proposed Staff-Monitored Program (16 July 2026) Current analytical rule The chronology treats remittances, international support, FX auctions, import compression, reserve changes, bank liquidity, regulatory actions and payment infrastructure as related but non-interchangeable kinds of evidence. Relevance to financial inclusion: This is the bridge from macro-financial chronology to inclusion decisions: capacity, access, use, quality and outcomes remain separate states. Does not establish: Chronological proximity never substitutes for causal identification. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading When the baseline moves Yemen’s banking series shows why a large published jump must be separated from a change in measurement before it becomes an economic story. Evidence Reading What exactly do we mean by microfinance growth? Yemen’s microfinance record does not move on one axis. Borrower counts, saver or depositor measures, nominal portfolios and institutional form are not the same measure, and they do not yet form one harmonised growth series. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. For firms, how serious a constraint is finance — and how does it compare with other constraints? What measurement would change the decision? A current MSME finance demand/use baseline A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome. This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer. Open this measurement priority Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type. This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups.
