en/firms/index.html.text: Explore / For firms, how serious a constraint is finance — and how does it compare with other constraints? Firms: how much finance matters depends on the question and the firms asked In a 2022 survey of formal firms in seven governorates, 22% named access to finance as a business challenge, against 50% for electricity and 46% for fuel shortages. Among firms in the report’s finance-obstacle tabulation, which excludes firms that said they did not need a loan, 91.84% rated financing obstacles as major or moderate. These answers, the credit paths of the few firms with a line of credit and what a programme reports for the firms it supported address different questions and cannot be merged into one national percentage. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What these figures do not establish The 22% general-business challenge measure and the 91.84% finance-severity measure use different questions and bases, so they are not two estimates of the same national rate. The 18 valid loan-source responses describe only that small conditional group. Results reported by the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) describe the firms the programme supported; they are not national MSME prevalence and do not establish that the programme caused the results. 01 Analysis Finance in the context of other business constraints Among formal firms in the seven-governorate 2022 survey, the shares naming each item as a business challenge were: electricity 50%, fuel shortages 46%, transport or road blockades 32%, tax administration or tax rates 30%, political instability 27%, access to finance 22%, siege 18% and practices of informal competitors 17%. Respondents could name more than one challenge, so the shares add up to more than 100%, and neither the exact question wording nor the base for this question is recorded in the evidence base; small differences between adjacent items should not be read as a fixed ranking. These results answer “what was cited as a general challenge in this survey?” — not “what is the national ranking of constraints for all Yemeni firms?” Another view of the evidence Finance is not the only constraint surveyed formal firms report, 2022 Text description of this view Analytical question: How often did surveyed formal firms name access to finance, compared with other business challenges? What the evidence shows: Among formal firms in the 2022 custom survey of seven governorates, 50% named electricity as a business challenge, 46% fuel shortages, 32% transport or road blockades, 30% tax administration or tax rates, 27% political instability and 22% access to finance; 18% named siege and 17% practices of informal competitors. Firms could name more than one challenge, so the shares add up to more than 100%, and neither the number of firms answering nor the exact question wording is recorded in the evidence base. These results apply to the survey sample in seven governorates and are not a national ranking for all Yemeni firms. Scope and time: 2022 · Formal enterprises in seven selected governorates covered by the 2022 custom survey What not to conclude: The shares describe formal firms in a 2022 custom survey of seven governorates; they are not a national ranking of business constraints for all Yemeni firms. They follow the source's own item wording and are not comparable with the standard Enterprise Survey 'biggest obstacle' indicator. Open evidence record → 02 Analysis A different question produces a much larger finance number Among the firms in the report's finance-obstacle tabulation, which excludes firms that said they did not need a loan, 68.71% rated financing obstacles as major and 23.13% as moderate — 91.84% combined. This is a result for that filtered group, not the share of all Yemeni firms facing a major or moderate finance obstacle. 03 Analysis Lines of credit are rare in this sample, and their source is known for only 18 firms Within the formal-firm sample, 31 of 328 firms reported a line of credit from financial or non-financial institutions, and only 18 gave a valid response to the loan-source question. The source mix can therefore be described only for those 18 responses — not for all surveyed firms, all borrowers or all Yemeni enterprises. 04 Evidence Formal firms in this sample: most held a bank account, but banks financed almost none of their working capital Among formal firms in the 2022 seven-governorate survey, 58.2% (191 of 328) reported a checking or savings account. Their working capital came mainly from internal sources: on average, 69.12% came from internal funds or retained earnings, 16.66% from money lenders, friends or relatives, 10.15% from advance payments by clients, 1.97% from non-bank financial institutions, 1.31% from supplier credit and 0.56% from banks. In a separate question on the financial intermediaries they use, 73.48% of responding formal firms named an exchange store or money exchanger and 24.39% a commercial bank; firms could name more than one, so these are not market shares. The evidence base does not hold the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. Among the 217 informal firms surveyed, 80.18% had no bank account; that sample was drawn from activity and location lists rather than a national register. The formal-firm sample includes micro firms with fewer than five employees, and neither sample represents all Yemeni firms. 05 What it means What this means The finance problem does not begin and end with whether a loan exists. The full journey includes the need for finance, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and what happened to the firm afterwards. Current evidence does not cover that entire journey nationally. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. Evidence Programme reach is useful evidence about the programme itself The Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) reports that in 2024 it supported 8,217 MSMEs and disbursed USD 22,865,322, and that across 2021–2024 its support reached 31,560 MSMEs with a programme total of USD 54.7 million; the evidence base does not specify whether this total is funding committed or funding disbursed. The 2021–2024 total is not established as a count of unique firms. These are programme-delivery measures for the firms the programme supported; they are not a count of Yemen’s MSME population, a measure of financial-sector lending, or proof of causal impact. Evidence A programme result is not a national rate SMEPS’s 2024 Annual Report states that 19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services in 2024, and gives 15% for 2021–2024 against a programme target of 40%. The report does not fully specify the calculation base or the operational definition of “accessed financial services”. The KPI can therefore be read only for the firms the programme supported, with that limitation visible: it is not a national MSME access rate, and the 40% remains a target, not an observed result. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading How can 22% and 91.84% both be right? A 2022 survey of formal firms in seven selected governorates can tell us that finance was named less often than electricity or fuel, and also that most firms in a narrower group rated finance a major or moderate obstacle. The numbers do not contradict each other. They answer different questions. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. How are borrower reach, savers/depositors, nominal portfolio and provider structure changing in microfinance? What measurement would change the decision? A current MSME finance demand/use baseline A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome. This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer. Open this measurement priority Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type. This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups. Open this measurement priority Verify it yourself Open the evidence record behind each answer, or go to the sources or the methodology. en/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Financial inclusion in Yemen is not one number. Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence is a bilingual public evidence resource that helps users understand, compare and verify evidence on financial inclusion in Yemen. It helps decision-making by making clear what the evidence establishes, what it does not, when and to whom it applies, and where it comes from. It does not make decisions for users or simulate policy outcomes. The evidence spans people, firms, providers, payments, money flows, rules and infrastructure, measured at different times and under different definitions. Start with the question you need to answer. Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. Common starting questions Start from the problem you need to resolve View all 11 questions → Who is being left behind — and where are the measured gaps? Population measures, same-wave disparities and what the evidence cannot explain. Are reforms and payment infrastructure turning into access, use, quality and outcomes? A stage-by-stage chain from rule to result. For firms, how serious a constraint is finance — and how does it compare with other constraints? How often finance is named among other constraints, how severe the finance obstacle is for a defined group of firms, the credit path and programme evidence. How can I check the evidence behind a claim, see why sources disagree and reproduce a result? Evidence records, field-by-field comparison, how derived figures are calculated, and how to cite them. Evidence signals Three figures, three different things measured The latest representative population measure is the World Bank’s Global Findex 2021 survey of Yemen (fieldwork November 2022 to January 2023; World Bank data year 2022): 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account at a financial institution or with a mobile-money provider. Areas holding about 23% of the population were not surveyed. In the same survey, 18.35% of men and 5.44% of women had an account, a gap of 12.91 percentage points. Separately, POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026, within CBY-Aden’s reporting scope. These are different measures: people, a disparity within one survey, and infrastructure. None substitutes for another. Evidence records behind these figures (4) Latest representative account-ownership measure available A measured gender gap in account ownership POS infrastructure expanded Financial inclusion is a connected system, not a single score What this does not establish What should not be inferred? More infrastructure does not by itself prove that more people are using financial services. A licensed institution is not proof that every listed location is operating. Access does not prove use; use does not prove service quality or impact; and the number of accounts is not the number of people. Analysis Different evidence describes different moments. Population surveys, administrative payment data, provider-status decisions, programme reports and macroeconomic series are updated on different schedules. Each conclusion therefore carries the period it actually covers. “Latest” means latest for that question or measure, not latest for Yemen as a whole. System context From rule to result, every link needs evidence. A reform, new payment rail or programme can matter for inclusion through a chain that runs from a rule or investment to implementation, operation, reachable access, actual use, service quality and protection, and finally outcome. The evidence stops at the furthest stage it actually supports; it does not cross an unmeasured link. Across the wider picture, people and capability, firms and income, providers, payment rails, remittance and capital flows, regulation and consumer protection, and enabling conditions and constraints are related but not interchangeable. Those links show context, dependency or plausible mechanisms where evidence supports them; they are not causal arrows or a composite score. Another view of the evidence Financial inclusion is a connected system, not a single score Text description of this view Analytical question: How do the parts of Yemen’s financial-inclusion system connect? What the evidence shows: Financial inclusion in Yemen is described here as connected parts: people and capability, firms and income, providers, payment rails, remittance and capital flows, regulation and protection, and enabling conditions and constraints. The documented relationships describe context, dependency or plausible mechanisms where evidence supports them; no relationship carries an evidence-strength rating, and the parts do not form a composite score or show that one part causes another. Scope and time: Several periods, varying by domain · people, firms, providers, rails, flows, rules, enabling constraints What not to conclude: The relationships are not causal claims unless separate evidence supports them; the parts do not form a composite index, and no part is shown to drive another mechanically. Open evidence record → What we still do not know The gaps the evidence cannot yet close The evidence available here cannot yet support a reliable national map of operating financial access points, a current population inclusion rate, or a causal explanation for any measured gap. Those are visible knowledge gaps, not values to be filled in. Verify the evidence Challenge the answer Open the evidence record to see the definition, population covered, calculation base, period, geography, method, source, derivation, limitations and what would change it. Where credible figures disagree, compare those fields before comparing the values. Featured Reading The system is changing. What has reached people? Yemen’s rules, institutions and payment infrastructure have moved faster than its representative evidence about people. The gap between the two is not an answer to guess; it is the next thing to measure. Evidence period: Global Findex fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023 · POS counts March 2025 – January 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 Open this ReadingAll Evidence Readings 01 Evidence Readings Evidence-led essays, each traceable to the records behind it. 02 Measurement Agenda What remains unknown and what measurement would strengthen the decision. 03 Data & sources Find the original sources behind the evidence, with their titles, publishers and links.

en/measurement/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Missing evidence matters when it could change a decision. This agenda links evidence gaps to specific decision questions. It does not rank national priorities or use a hidden score. Each item states the decision affected, what evidence is missing, the feasibility and sensitivity constraints, and what would become knowable if that evidence existed. Priority labels describe sequencing within this resource; they are not government, funding or policy rankings. Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. 01 What it means How to read the agenda A measurement item is an evidence-to-decision record, not a recommendation to government or a wish list. It identifies the pages and decisions affected, the evidence currently missing, feasibility and sensitivity constraints, the basis for its position in this resource’s evidence agenda, and what would change if the evidence became available. 02 Evidence Stable references for citation Each priority has a stable reference, such as MA-001, so that it can be cited, linked and corrected without depending on a title that may change. 03 Analysis Priority labels describe evidence sequencing This resource does not compress decision importance, feasibility, evidence quality and sensitivity into one opaque score. P0/P1 indicate how directly a missing measure blocks questions covered by this resource and how it depends on other evidence. They are not national policy priorities, funding rankings or judgements about the importance of the underlying population or issue. 04 System context Why measurement is part of this resource Measurement connects the rest of this resource. A new round of a population survey can update People and test whether infrastructure changes reached users. A verified access-point register can connect Providers to Access. Post-reform use and complaints data can connect Reforms and Payments to service quality. A firm-finance journey can connect business constraints to actual applications, approvals, terms and outcomes. 05 What this does not establish What a measurement priority does not establish A P0/P1 label does not mean the unmeasured phenomenon is large, worsening or absent. It describes only how the evidence gap affects the questions covered by this resource. A measurement gap is not a zero, and an unmeasured outcome is not evidence that a reform failed. 06 What we still do not know What remains uncertain about the agenda itself Feasibility, sensitivity and cost can change when a specific measurement is designed with the institution that would collect or hold the data. Those implementation facts cannot be assumed in advance and would need to be confirmed before any commissioning decision. 07 Measurement update How the agenda changes When a measurement is completed, the new evidence is assessed against the decision it was meant to improve. If the question becomes answerable, the gap closes or narrows; if a new incompatibility or uncertainty appears, the item is revised while keeping the same reference so its history remains traceable. 08 Verify the evidence Verify each gap Open any measurement item to see what is known now, what evidence is still missing, which pages and decisions are affected, how feasible the measurement appears, what sensitivity constraints apply, how its priority label was assigned, and which evidence records revealed the gap. 09 Measurement agenda Measurements that would change decisions Each agenda priority sets out the current evidence, the missing evidence, what the decision would gain, the proposed method, feasibility, sensitivity or data-responsibility constraints, the priority rationale and what would change if the evidence became available. Priority: P0 · People A current people-side inclusion baseline Current evidence: The Global Findex 2025 edition contains 2024 observations for many economies, but Yemen's latest representative account-ownership observation remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, for 2022 (from the Yemen Findex 2021 study fielded in 2022–2023). Major payment-system and reform changes are more recent. The latest published people-level values for receiving domestic remittances, and through which channels, are from 2014; the 2021-wave microdata contain these questions, but weighted estimates have not yet been produced. Missing evidence: New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency. Decision it would strengthen: A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population. Reference MA-001 This gap is examined in: The system is changing. What has reached people? More about this priority Measurement guardrail The latest representative people-side measure predates the current reform and infrastructure changes. A new measurement must document its population, geographic coverage, fieldwork period and survey weights, and keep core concepts comparable with the previous wave. Feasibility MEDIUM — requires a representative demand-side survey or approved weighted microdata collection. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because multiple current policy/product questions depend on population outcomes while newer evidence is largely administrative, institutional or programme-based. What the measurement would change This resource could update the people-side baseline, assess change by comparable dimensions, and stop relying on an older population wave for current decisions. Priority: P0 · Payments / People Active and repeat digital use Current evidence: Administrative data show registrations, infrastructure and transactions, while historical evidence also records dormancy and one-time or imposed use; unique repeat users are not measured consistently. Missing evidence: Provider/rail administrative data with deduplication rules and/or demand-side active-use measures. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use. Reference MA-002 This gap is examined in: When does digital growth become durable use? More about this priority Measurement guardrail Registered accounts, subscribers, terminals or transaction totals cannot stand in for unique active people. Frequency, recency, value and duration of use should be tracked where feasible. Feasibility MEDIUM — possible through provider/rail data if definitions and deduplication rules are agreed; may need demand-side validation. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because digital infrastructure and transaction evidence are expanding while unique repeat use remains unresolved. What the measurement would change Separates registration and transaction volume from sustained user adoption. Priority: P0 · People / Equity Financial inclusion across population groups: measure disparities before explaining them Current evidence: Within the same survey wave, account ownership differs by 12.91 percentage points between women (5.44%) and men (18.35%), and by about 9.0 percentage points between adults in the poorest 40% (6.5%) and the richest 60% (15.5%) by household income. Comparable current differences by age group and displacement status are not established in the evidence base, and the contribution of identity, device, income, geography, trust and household constraints to any measured disparity is not established. Missing evidence: Representative or clearly bounded disaggregated quantitative evidence to measure subgroup outcomes, with linked mechanism variables and qualitative or stronger causal designs where explanation is required. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show which subgroup differences are actually measured and would allow plausible mechanisms to be tested without treating untested explanations as causes. Reference MA-003 This gap is examined in: The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open. More about this priority Measurement guardrail Do not turn an unmeasured subgroup into a measured gap. Measuring a disparity and explaining it are separate evidence products; causal mechanisms require a design capable of testing them. Feasibility MEDIUM — survey modules and bounded qualitative work are feasible, but causal attribution needs stronger designs. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because material disparities by sex and by household income are measured within one survey wave, while current age- and displacement-disaggregated evidence and causal explanations remain incomplete; without new measurement, unmeasured subgroup gaps and their causes would remain speculative. What the measurement would change Keeps apart what needs different evidence: whether a disparity is measured, what is associated with it, and what design could test a causal mechanism or intervention. Priority: P0 · Firms / MSME A current MSME finance demand/use baseline Current evidence: A 2022 survey of formal firms in seven governorates and programme evidence from the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) can each be used within its own scope; neither supplies a current representative national MSME finance baseline. Missing evidence: A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer. Reference MA-004 This gap is examined in: How can 22% and 91.84% both be right? More about this priority Measurement guardrail The 2013 and 2022 surveys use incompatible sampling frames; do not build a trend between them unless comparability is established variable by variable. SMEPS's own 2024 report adds a programme KPI (19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services), but this does not replace a current representative MSME demand/use baseline, and the base on which this KPI is calculated is not yet clearly documented. Feasibility MEDIUM — requires a representative firm/MSME survey and/or validated administrative-firm linkage. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because the current 2022 seven-governorate survey and SMEPS programme evidence answer different bounded questions and cannot supply a national baseline. What the measurement would change This resource could quantify attrition from finance need through application, approval/rejection, amount/terms, use and repayment pressure nationally. Priority: P0 · Providers / Geography A register of active financial access points Current evidence: Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points. Missing evidence: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted. Reference MA-005 This gap is examined in: When the unit changes, the story changes More about this priority Measurement guardrail Listed/licensed address is not necessarily active access; modelled accessibility must remain distinct from observed service use. Feasibility MEDIUM-HIGH if regulator/providers can supply point-level status and location under a shared governance rule. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because access decisions and atlas design are blocked by the difference between institutional lists and verified operating presence. What the measurement would change Would allow a defensible access atlas and an analysis of coverage and travel distance, without treating missingness as zero. Priority: P0 · Consumer protection / Quality Consumer experience and redress outcomes Current evidence: Official material specifies complaint and escalation architecture, including source-defined time windows; actual complaint volumes, resolution times and outcomes are not documented in the available evidence. Missing evidence: Complaint and redress data from providers and the regulator, plus consumer-side evidence on experience, including fees, disclosure and trust. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would allow redress performance and service quality to be assessed rather than inferred from the existence of rules. Reference MA-006 More about this priority Measurement guardrail Rules and complaint architecture do not establish service quality or successful remedy. Feasibility MEDIUM — regulator/provider administrative data plus consumer-side evidence. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because the rules/process are documented but performance cannot be inferred from existence. What the measurement would change Allows service-quality and redress performance to be assessed rather than assumed. Priority: P1 · Identity / Digital access Digital onboarding and identity journeys Current evidence: KYC and e-money rules are documented, but this resource lacks journey-level evidence on attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost. Missing evidence: Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points. Reference MA-007 More about this priority Measurement guardrail Do not infer exclusion from the existence of KYC rules; measure where and why people fail or abandon the journey. Feasibility MEDIUM — provider journey logs or structured user research. Why this is a priority P1 within this evidence agenda because rules are known but journey frictions remain unmeasured; important once higher-order baseline/use gaps are addressed. What the measurement would change Turns a generic KYC/exclusion debate into identifiable journey failure points. Priority: P1 · Credit infrastructure / MSME Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use Current evidence: Legal texts, project documents and institutional records can establish that credit infrastructure exists or is being developed; lender participation, inquiry use and borrower reach are not yet documented as one complete evidence chain. Missing evidence: Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups. Reference MA-008 More about this priority Measurement guardrail Establishment or legal authority does not prove operational coverage or lender use. Feasibility MEDIUM — administrative data likely exist but require institutional access and compatible definitions. Why this is a priority P1 within this evidence agenda because legal/institutional existence is known but use in lending decisions remains open. What the measurement would change Shows whether infrastructure reaches actual credit decisions rather than only institutional establishment. Priority: P0 · Social protection / Payments Persistence of financial use after cash transfers Current evidence: Programme evidence can establish delivery, beneficiary reach, successful payout and exposure to an account or wallet; sustained use after the transfer remains unmeasured. Missing evidence: Longitudinal programme or provider cohort data, or repeated beneficiary follow-up, with privacy-safe linkage from transfer receipt to account or wallet activation, repeat use, merchant use, saving and cash-out. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether transfer-related financial exposure becomes persistent use and which observed conditions are associated with repeat use. Reference MA-009 This gap is examined in: The payment arrived. What happened next? More about this priority Measurement guardrail Enrollment, successful payout or account opening are not durable financial use. Feasibility MEDIUM — cohort linkage or repeated beneficiary follow-up, depending on programme/provider data access. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because successful delivery and account exposure do not answer whether use persists after the programme transaction. What the measurement would change Distinguishes one-off programme/payment exposure from sustained financial use. Priority: P0 · Reforms / Payments / Quality Reform transmission and service quality Current evidence: Recent evidence documents rules, institutions, projects, procurement and selected infrastructure activity, but the chain to access, use, quality and outcomes is incomplete. Missing evidence: Reform-specific operational and user-side evidence tied to the same implementation timeline, from go-live through coverage, reliability, cost and outcome. Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the furthest evidenced state of each reform and the next unmeasured result without treating missing evidence as failure. Reference MA-010 This gap is examined in: When does a payment reform become financial inclusion? More about this priority Measurement guardrail Every transition from infrastructure to outcome requires its own indicator; missing downstream evidence is not failure. Feasibility MEDIUM — depends on access to the institutions implementing each reform and on indicator definitions. Why this is a priority P0 within this evidence agenda because rules, institutions and projects are current while downstream results remain unevenly measured. What the measurement would change Allows this resource to say how far a reform has progressed in evidence terms without equating milestones with outcomes. Evidence records that revealed these gaps The official 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted; whether providers operate now is a separate question The official 2026 roster of exchange and remittance providers issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These are roster entries counted by the roster's own classes: the three class totals are not a count of unique providers, nor a verified count of providers operating now. Because the roster does not state its issue date, CBY-Aden's 2026 decisions (dated January to September 2026) suspending or withdrawing the licences of named entities, or closing their premises, are matched with the roster entity by entity, because a decision may or may not already be reflected in it. Does not establish: Adding the three classes does not give a count of unique providers, because no rule for identifying the same entity across classes has been applied. Inclusion in the annual roster is not proof of current operation, branch activity or service availability, including for entities named in 2026 enforcement decisions. Open evidence record → What we still do not know The evidence gaps recorded in this resource as of the edition of this resource dated 26 September 2026 are of these types: a missing period, a missing calculation base, a missing primary file, a map layer that cannot yet be built, and an unresolved source scope. A gap can close when new evidence arrives; a blank or missing observation is not zero and is not evidence of absence. A gap is not zero, and it is not evidence of absence or failure. Open evidence record → What we still do not know Text description of this view Analytical question: Which missing evidence is blocking an answer or decision? What the evidence shows: The evidence gaps recorded in this resource as of the edition of this resource dated 26 September 2026 are of these types: a missing period, a missing calculation base, a missing primary file, a map layer that cannot yet be built, and an unresolved source scope. A gap can close when new evidence arrives; a blank or missing observation is not zero and is not evidence of absence. Scope and time: As of the edition of this resource dated 26 September 2026 · Documented gaps that block an answer: missing periods, unavailable sources, missing calculation bases and primary files not yet available What not to conclude: A gap is not zero, and it is not evidence of absence or failure. en/methodology/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Preserve the meaning of the evidence before comparing the numbers. Every published figure has been checked against the source it is attributed to. A figure that could not be verified is withheld, and a figure known only from a secondary source is labelled as secondary. Each figure keeps its unit, population, period and geography; derived figures can be recomputed from recorded inputs; and material corrections are recorded. The method exists to prevent one common failure: treating different people, accounts, providers, periods, geographies and programme records as if they measured the same thing. Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. 01 Evidence Start with what is being measured People, accounts, active accounts, savers, borrowers, providers, service points, terminals, transactions, balances, programme beneficiaries and reform milestones are different analytical objects. The method never assumes that one can stand in for another. 02 What it means Evidence from several dates can be valid at once Population surveys, administrative records, provider rosters, regulations, project milestones and programme results update at different times. This resource preserves observation or fieldwork dates separately from release dates so a newer publication is not mistaken for a newer measurement. 03 What it means What the evidence covers — and what it does not Coverage differs by topic. A few topics have current observations: the formal status of providers under CBY-Aden lists, bank credit and other monetary statistics, and remittance prices in two corridors. Most people-side topics rest on the latest representative survey wave (fieldwork 2022–23) or on 2014 values, and several — frequency of use, financial resilience, digital capability, affordability and differences by age — are defined in the 2021 survey data but not yet estimated. Payments, regulation and consumer protection are evidenced mainly through administrative and regulatory records, which show systems and rules rather than use or outcomes. This resource has no current Yemen evidence on service reliability, the geography of operating access points, inclusion by displacement or disability status, digital fraud, insurance or pensions. Gaps are shown as gaps: they are not filled with other countries' figures, and each is linked to a measurement priority. 04 Analysis How evidence is accepted, and in what role A source enters the evidence base when its original link and date can be recorded and its content can be checked against the source itself; its publisher, issuer and reuse terms are recorded when they have been confirmed. A source's role is recorded for each use rather than once for the source: the same report can be primary factual evidence for one record and context for another. The roles are primary factual evidence, a dated status event, Yemen analytical literature, a global method reference and context. The kind of document — a law, decision, survey, dataset or report — is recorded separately, and no numerical quality score is assigned. Primary evidence and status events support public figures directly. A figure known only from a secondary source appears only when it is attributed and labelled as secondary. Analytical literature is attributed to its authors, and global references inform method without standing in for Yemen evidence. A figure that cannot be verified against its stated source is withheld. 05 System context Measuring in a divided, conflict-affected setting Four features of Yemen change how evidence is read. Central-bank authority has been divided since 2016, so official lists, decisions and statistics carry the scope of the authority that issued them. Rial values can differ between monetary areas, so a nominal figure is read with its valuation basis where the source records it. Survey coverage is incomplete: the latest Findex wave excluded areas holding about 23% of the population and replaced more than a quarter of its sampling units. And programme data describe programme populations. None of this explains a result by itself: conflict is context for interpretation, not a cause the evidence has established. 06 Analysis Uncertainty is stated, not manufactured Survey estimates carry sampling and coverage uncertainty. Where a source publishes a confidence interval or standard error, it is reported with the estimate. Where it does not, no interval, standard error or significance test is added unless it can be reproduced from the survey's own weights and design. A derived value, such as the difference between two percentages, keeps the precision of its inputs, with no added decimal places, and small differences between estimates are not read as a ranking. 07 Analysis Derived evidence must be reproducible When this resource calculates a gap, share, ratio, revision or other derived measure, it records the inputs and method needed to reproduce the calculation. A derivation cannot create coverage, comparability or causal meaning that the inputs did not contain. 08 System context Comparison is conditional on compatibility Before values share a scale, this resource checks definition, period, geography, population or base, unit, source coverage and method. A material mismatch stays visible and can block a common scale. The purpose is not to prevent comparison; it is to prevent a false one. 09 Evidence How an item’s evidence state affects what you see An item’s evidence state — for example observed, derived, historical, conflicting, superseded or corrected — determines how it is described and whether it appears in search and Compare. An item whose state is unclear is not presented as reusable evidence until the state is resolved. 10 What this does not establish What the method does not claim Traceability is not certainty. A primary source can still be old; a recent administrative record may not measure people; a representative survey may not support governorate estimates; a correct calculation may still use a narrow base. The method preserves those limits rather than turning them into one confidence score. 11 Verify the evidence Correction is part of the evidence trail When a source is revised or an error is found, the public evidence record is corrected without losing its stable identity. New or conflicting evidence is checked against the original source before it changes a public record. If it materially changes the interpretation, the current record states what changed and why; if the conflict cannot be resolved, the uncertainty remains visible. Superseded evidence remains traceable when public retention is appropriate. 12 Verify the evidence Challenge the answer From a public answer, open the evidence record and inspect the original source (its link or version), unit, population or calculation base, geography, period, method and reuse rights and publication status. Compare it with other evidence only when definitions permit. An unresolved source conflict stays visible rather than being averaged, harmonized or silently repaired. If something is wrong or incomplete, use the correction channel and cite the stable evidence ID. 13 Measurement framework Composite scores follow survey-round-specific rules Composite financial-literacy measures combine several constructs and follow scoring rules specific to the survey round that produced them. Reproducing a score therefore requires the definitions, question set and calculation rules for that round; carrying scoring rules across editions can change what the measure represents. A financial-literacy score is not an access rate. Related evidence records Accounts and transactions are not unique people Administrative accounts, e-wallet subscribers and payment transactions are not equivalent to unique people measured by Findex. Does not establish: Dividing administrative counts by population does not produce a share of people unless a documented unique-person method exists; no such share is established here. Open evidence record → Evidence freshness differs by domain The evidence here is not equally current across domains: several payments/regulatory observations are from 2025–2026, while key representative people-side evidence is older. Does not establish: Older evidence is not invalid because of its age, and recent administrative evidence does not measure current financial inclusion across the population. Open evidence record → Latest monthly POS release listed by CBY-Aden: January 2026 (page checked 26 September 2026) The payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists monthly POS releases from March 2025 to January 2026. When the page was checked on 26 September 2026, January 2026 was the latest release listed; no later month is inferred. Does not establish: It does not show that POS activity stopped after January 2026; it identifies only the latest monthly release listed on the payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) when checked on 26 September 2026. Open evidence record → Informative history without a continuous annual series The historical microfinance evidence is informative but does not form a continuous annual series. This resource keeps the exact quarterly and year-end points, anomalies, years known only through a reference in another source, and years with no data, rather than filling the gaps. Does not establish: A year with no observation does not indicate zero microfinance activity, and the observations do not establish a trend across the missing years. Open evidence record → What the Yemen Findex 2021 study contains The Yemen Global Findex 2021 study file has 1,000 respondents and 113 variables; Yemen fieldwork ran from 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023 and all population estimates require survey weights. Does not establish: Raw case percentages in the study documentation are not population estimates. Open evidence record → Raw case shares are not population estimates World Bank variable pages expose raw sample case counts and percentages for the Yemen Findex file, but explicitly warn that those figures cannot be interpreted as summary statistics of the population of interest. Does not establish: The raw, unweighted case percentages shown on the World Bank variable pages are not estimates for Yemen's adult population and are not reported in this resource. Open evidence record → Geographic coverage limits of the latest Findex wave The latest Yemen Findex wave excludes Al Baydaa, Al Jawf, Mareb, Sadah, Socotra and several districts elsewhere; the source states excluded areas represent approximately 23% of the population, and over one-fourth of primary sampling units were replaced during fieldwork. Does not establish: The wave does not cover all of Yemen, and its results cannot be used to map financial inclusion by governorate. Open evidence record → Demand-side measures defined; custom estimates not yet published A 32-metric demand-side panel has been specified across access, barriers, digital use, saving, borrowing, resilience, remittances, income flows, financial worry and connectivity. Custom weighted estimates are not published yet because they require authorized respondent-level data, correct survey weights and successful reproduction of the official benchmark values. Does not establish: The 32 specified measures are planned, not measured: none is yet a published indicator, because the weighted estimates have not been reproduced and checked against official benchmarks. Open evidence record → A smoother published path is a methods question, not a conclusion In the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025, the published remittance series rises with unusually similar annual growth rates across overlapping years. That pattern is useful for method scrutiny, but it does not establish smoothing, interpolation or low real-world volatility. Does not establish: The pattern does not establish smoothing, interpolation or low real-world volatility. Open evidence record → A reconstruction programme is documented; the exact CBY formula is not IMF documents a 2024–2025 external-sector statistical reconstruction effort with CBY-Aden, including a demographic-behavioural personal-transfer model where informal-channel data were limited. This establishes method context, not the exact formula or scope used for every remittance value in the CBY-Aden Annual Report 2025. Does not establish: The public evidence does not establish the exact formula behind the values in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025, or that CBY-Aden and IMF levels share the same scope. Open evidence record → The 2023 valuation change has a precedent and cannot be called the “first ever” Market-rate valuation of foreign-currency accounts has documented precedent in Yemen from 1996, while CBY-Aden separately documents a January-2023 valuation/reporting change affecting current banking series. The two episodes should not be assumed to use identical standards. Does not establish: The January 2023 change was not the first market-rate valuation in Yemen, since a precedent is documented from 1996, and the evidence does not show that the historical and contemporary standards are identical. Open evidence record → A public interface is not the same thing as the underlying dataset World Bank public remittance interfaces do not expose Yemen history uniformly. One interface, reviewed on 10 September 2026, showed an older span of years, while other World Bank interfaces and earlier documented retrievals contained later observations. The difference reflects what each interface displays and how its data can be traced; it is not evidence that later underlying data are absent. Does not establish: The difference does not show that data were deleted or withdrawn, or why any correction was made, and one public interface's observations are not a substitute for another's. Open evidence record → A stable remittance ratio exists; its meaning remains unknown Over 2021–2024, the ratio of the remittance series in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 to the IMF 2025 Article IV series is 1.838 in every year, and the two growth paths are almost identical when indexed to 2021 = 100. The public evidence does not establish what that ratio represents, so it is a numerical regularity with no documented explanation, not a conversion rule. Does not establish: The 1.838 ratio is not a population, geography, informal-share or coverage conversion. Open evidence record → A change in an external position is not automatically a transaction Changes in Yemen's external asset or liability positions should be decomposed into transactions, exchange-rate changes, other price changes and other volume changes before they are interpreted as financial flows. The change in international investment position (IIP) stocks between opening and closing dates is not, on its own, a measure of balance-of-payments transactions. Does not establish: The difference between opening and closing international investment position stocks is not, on its own, a measure of balance-of-payments transactions. Open evidence record → BPM7 updates the standard; it does not rewrite Yemen’s statistical history overnight BPM7 is the updated global external-sector statistical standard, but implementation is a multi-year transition. Yemen's historical series should keep the standard and version under which their sources published them until an explicit conversion or revision is published. Does not establish: The release of BPM7 does not mean that Yemen's historical data have been restated under it, or that Yemeni sources have already adopted it. Open evidence record → How many respondents answered each Findex question Weighted estimates for the 2021 wave have not yet been produced, so no values are shown. When they are published, each will be accompanied by the number of respondents who gave a valid answer, the number of missing or invalid answers, and a note where a question was asked only of a sub-group; these counts describe the sample and are not population estimates. Raw case percentages are not population prevalence rates, and indicators are not ranked by them. Open evidence record → Which historical Findex measures can be compared with the latest wave A comparability map linking 36 historical Findex measures to the measures specified for the latest wave, while separating publishable historical values from latest-wave measures whose required computation is not yet complete. A crosswalk identifies conceptual comparability; it does not make every historical and latest-wave metric numerically interchangeable, and latest-wave values remain unavailable until the required computation and quality checks are complete. Open evidence record → Continue from here Choose the next path that matches what you need to do. Evidence→Data & sources→Corrections→

en/payments/index.html.text: Explore / Is digital finance becoming durable financial use — or do the available data still mainly measure infrastructure and transactions? Payments: POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 to 1,473 between March 2025 and January 2026; how many people use them is not measured Administrative payment data can show devices, accounts, transactions and values at high frequency. They are useful signals about the payment system, but each counts a different object, and none can be turned into a number of people or an inclusion outcome without a documented method. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What payment growth does not establish More terminals do not prove more unique users. More transactions do not reveal how many people used the service. Nominal transaction value does not show real purchasing-power growth. Accounts, wallet subscribers and registrations are not necessarily active people. A rule, project or new institution is not observed adoption. And successful cash delivery or opening an account is not proof of durable post-transfer use. What is still missing to measure use This resource still lacks a comparable, privacy-safe measure of unique and repeat payment users across providers and rails, with frequency, recency, transaction purpose, failed/abandoned attempts and clear active-use definitions. It also lacks the downstream usage series needed to measure adoption after major payment-rail milestones. The FMIIP results framework itself keeps operational state, participating institutions, use cases, merchant acceptance, active accounts, customer transaction costs and electronic-payment beneficiaries as separate measures; project targets remain targets until they are observed. 01 Analysis POS: three different signals Within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), reported POS terminals rose from 561 to 1,473 between March 2025 and January 2026, transaction counts from 8,015 to 24,026 (after a high of 27,187 in July 2025) and nominal transaction value from YER 320 million to YER 1.262 billion. This page keeps these three measures separate. A terminal is infrastructure, a transaction is an event and transaction value is a nominal monetary amount; none equals a person. 02 What it means Before comparing payment numbers, ask what each one counts Cards, accounts, e-wallet subscribers, POS terminals and transactions count different things. Accounts or subscribers may contain duplication or inactivity; terminals are infrastructure; transactions are events. A people-level inclusion rate requires a documented unique-person method rather than a division of administrative totals by population. Another view of the evidence What does the payment system actually count? Text description of this view Analytical question: What does each administrative payment metric actually count? What the evidence shows: The first-half 2025 payment report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) counts cards, ATMs, POS terminals, POS transactions, e-wallets, e-wallet subscribers and accounts. Each uses its own unit: accounts and subscribers are not necessarily unique people, transactions are events, and terminals are equipment. They cannot be combined into a people-level inclusion rate, because no documented method exists for matching and deduplicating them. Scope and time: 2025 H1 · Cards, ATMs, POS terminals, transactions, e-wallets, subscribers and accounts within the payment-system reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), first half of 2025; each has its own unit. What not to conclude: Cards, accounts, subscribers, transactions and terminals are not people, and they cannot be combined into a single digital-inclusion score. The first-half 2025 counts are not comparable with the third-quarter 2024 payments bulletin until the reporting scope and definitions of the two publications are reconciled. Open evidence record → 03 Evidence E-wallet subscribers: figures from two reports that do not form one series The CBY-Aden payments report for the third quarter of 2024 gives e-wallet subscriber counts of 414,631 for Q1, 507,585 for Q2 and 581,075 for Q3. The first-half 2025 infographic reports 2,102,484 subscribers. The two publications' subscriber definitions and reporting scope have not been reconciled, so the 2025 figure is not joined to the 2024 quarters and the difference is not read as growth. A subscriber count is not a count of unique people or of active users, and neither publication measures how many adults use a wallet. 04 System context What FPS and RTGS mean — and what they do not yet prove The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) separates three payment-infrastructure jobs. The Fast Payment System (FPS) is the project’s fast electronic-payment component, which the project supports in areas under the internationally recognized government. The Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS), to be managed by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) alongside an upgrade of its core banking system, is the settlement backbone the project links to large-value payments between financial institutions. A third component supports access and use through access-point mapping, capacity building for financial institutions and payment service providers, merchant onboarding in underserved areas and outreach. Separately, CBY-Aden records from 2026 show a board decision on what the source calls a national QR standard and e-wallet interconnection, unified-network integration work, and the establishment and governance of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC). These records show what architecture and institutions are being built; they do not by themselves establish go-live, reliability, transaction coverage, active use or inclusion outcomes. 05 Analysis Historical e-money evidence shows why registration cannot be read as durable use Within a study of five e-money providers by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS), e-money accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019, while the same source reports an average 23% dormant/inactive share and notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. CauseWay’s reproducible grouping of the source’s 2019 transaction-value table indicates 57.03% cash-in/cash-out, 29.97% movement between bank and electronic accounts, and 2.41% for bills and purchases together. These are historical patterns within the study’s providers, not current national prevalence. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. Evidence January 2026 was the latest monthly POS release on the CBY-Aden payments page as checked on 26 September 2026 The payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 26 September 2026, publishes monthly POS releases from March 2025 through January 2026. This resource therefore stops the monthly series at January 2026. That does not mean activity stopped; it means no later monthly release had been published on that page when it was checked. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading When does digital growth become durable use? Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it. Evidence Reading When does a payment reform become financial inclusion? A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. Who is being left behind — and where are the measured gaps? Are reforms and payment infrastructure turning into access, use, quality and outcomes? What measurement would change the decision? Active and repeat digital use Provider/rail administrative data with deduplication rules and/or demand-side active-use measures. This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use. Open this measurement priority Digital onboarding and identity journeys Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost. This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points. en/people/index.html.text: Explore / Who is being left behind — and where are the measured gaps? People: one population, evidence from different dates The latest representative survey available, the Global Findex 2021 wave (Yemen fieldwork November 2022 to January 2023), found that 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account: 5.44% of women and 18.35% of men. That establishes a low level of account ownership and measured gaps between groups for that wave. It is not a 2026 rate, it does not explain the gaps, and it cannot be combined with other measures of access, use, resilience or geography into one “latest” number. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What this evidence does not establish The 11.9% measure is not a 2026 rate and cannot be mapped by governorate from this wave. The 12.91-point gender difference and the 9.0-point income difference do not establish their causes. Administrative counts of accounts, wallets, savers, transactions or devices cannot substitute for a weighted people-level measure. The evidence base does not include confidence intervals for these subgroup values, and none are calculated here, so small differences between subgroups should not be over-read. The latest wave does not cover all geography The latest Yemen Findex wave excludes Al Baydaa, Al Jawf, Mareb, Sadah, Socotra and several districts elsewhere; the source states that excluded areas represent approximately 23% of the population and that over one-fourth of primary sampling units were replaced during fieldwork. The Yemen sample has 1,000 respondents, interviewed between 7 November 2022 and 9 January 2023, and population estimates require the survey weights. 01 Evidence The latest representative account-ownership measure available Global Findex 2021 reports 11.9% account ownership for Yemen; the Yemen fieldwork was carried out in 2022–23. The value is a survey measure for that wave and fieldwork period, not a 2026 population rate. 02 Evidence Measured gaps by sex and income — not yet explanations In the same wave, 5.44% of women and 18.35% of men have an account — a difference of 12.91 percentage points. Adults in the richest 60% by household income (15.5%) and in the poorest 40% (6.5%) differ by about 9.0 percentage points. Among adults with primary education or less, 6.98% have an account; the matching figure for adults with more education is not in the evidence base, so no education gap is stated. Because each comparison is within one survey wave, the disparities can be described; their causes cannot be established from these differences alone, and they are not 2026 estimates. Another view of the evidence Account ownership and measured gaps: Global Findex 2021 wave (Yemen fieldwork 2022–23) Text description of this view Analytical question: What does the latest representative evidence say about account ownership and measured gaps? What the evidence shows: In the 2021 Global Findex wave for Yemen (fieldwork 7 November 2022 – 9 January 2023; World Bank data year 2022), 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered had an account at a financial institution or with a mobile-money provider. Within the same wave: 5.44% of women and 18.35% of men had an account, a difference of 12.91 percentage points; 6.5% of adults in the poorest 40% and 15.5% in the richest 60% by household income, a difference of about 9.0 percentage points; 6.98% of adults with primary education or less and 19.53% of those with secondary education or more, a difference of 12.55 percentage points; and 5.01% of adults aged 15–24 and 16.11% of those aged 25 and over, a difference of 11.10 percentage points. The survey frame excludes areas the source says represent about 23% of the population. These figures are not a 2026 rate and cannot be mapped to governorates. Scope and time: World Bank reporting year 2022; Global Findex 2021 study; Yemen fieldwork 2022-11-07 to 2023-01-09 · Adults aged 15 and over in the areas the survey covered (the survey frame excludes areas with about 23% of the population); subgroups as defined within the same wave. What not to conclude: These are values from one survey wave, not an annual series and not a 2026 rate. They cannot be mapped to governorates, they are not comparable with account counts reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), and the differences between groups do not establish their causes. Open evidence record → 03 What it means How to read these figures Population survey figures measure people under the survey design and weights. They cannot be replaced by counts of bank accounts, wallets, savers, transactions or payment devices. Those count different things. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. Analysis Do not turn three observations into an annual trend Official World Bank evidence gives three survey observations: a 2011 comparator of 3.7% for accounts at a financial institution, a 2014 account headline of 6.4%, and 11.9% in the latest verified wave (Global Findex 2021, with Yemen fieldwork in 2022–23). The years between them are not observed, and the concepts are not assumed to be identical across waves, so this resource does not interpolate an annual trend. Analysis Saving and borrowing tell a different — older — story In the 2014 World Bank weighted country profile, 65.9% of adults reported borrowing any money, including 51.7% from family or friends, 15.0% from a private informal lender and 0.4% from a financial institution. Separately, 20.6% reported saving any money, including 0.9% at a financial institution and 4.5% through a savings club or a person outside the family. The categories are not additive, and each percentage applies to the all-adult base used by that question. Analysis Receipt is not the same as financial use In the 2014 World Bank weighted country profile, 18.3% of adults reported receiving domestic remittances. Among recipients, 31.1% received them through a money-transfer operator, 2.0% through a financial institution and 0.0% through a mobile phone. The base changes from all adults to remittance recipients, so the channel percentages cannot be read on the same base as the 18.3% receipt rate. System context Activity is not a capability outcome Global Money Week records of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) show programme activity during 2023–2025. Activity, documented output or completion, population-level capability measurement and evaluated programme outcome are four different levels of evidence: taking part in an activity does not by itself establish improved capability or impact, and programme effectiveness cannot be claimed without evaluation evidence that has a baseline and an endline. Population capability measures, such as the OECD/INFE scores, are a different kind of evidence, and this resource does not attribute them to these activities. Other people-side evidence (2023) Financial inclusion is not only account ownership Account ownership is one dimension of financial inclusion; financial capability and financial well-being are others. In the OECD/INFE 2023 International Survey of Adult Financial Literacy, Yemen scored 42 out of 100 on overall financial literacy and 15 out of 100 on financial well-being. The Yemen survey covered 1,000 respondents interviewed by telephone and face to face between 11 March and 1 April 2023, and the report notes that the data were collected within a technical-assistance or regional project. The report does not establish whether the Yemen sample covers all areas or is nationally representative. These scores sit alongside — not replace or combine with — the Global Findex account-ownership measure, and neither is a percentage of people who are financially included. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading The system is changing. What has reached people? Yemen’s rules, institutions and payment infrastructure have moved faster than its representative evidence about people. The gap between the two is not an answer to guess; it is the next thing to measure. Evidence Reading The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open. The latest Findex observation shows a large gap between women’s and men’s account ownership inside a system where few adults of either sex have an account. The evidence tells us where the disparity is. It does not yet tell us which barriers produce it. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. Is digital finance becoming durable financial use — or do the available data still mainly measure infrastructure and transactions? What do remittances and other money flows tell us about households’ connection to the financial system? What measurement would change the decision? A current people-side inclusion baseline New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency. A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population. Open this measurement priority Active and repeat digital use Provider/rail administrative data with deduplication rules and/or demand-side active-use measures. This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use. Open this measurement priority Verify it yourself Open the evidence record behind each answer, or go to the sources or the methodology.
