en/providers/index.html.text: Explore / Which providers are evidenced, under whose authority, and what do we actually know about their status? Providers: official lists show formal status on a date; operation needs other evidence The list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks, and its 2026 exchange and remittance roster lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These sources show who holds which formal status under that authority on a stated date. Operation, activity, reach and service quality require additional evidence. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What provider evidence does not establish Listing or licensing is not operation. A provider count is not a branch or service-point count. A dated negative or enforcement event is not a permanent status. A named set of providers covered by the evidence does not establish activity, market share, client reach, service quality or inclusion outcomes without additional evidence. What we still do not know well enough The 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted by source category, but this resource still lacks a fully reconciled view of current operation across all provider classes. The main open questions are entity deduplication across categories, reconciliation of the 2026 enforcement decisions (dated January–September 2026) with the roster, wallet-universe comparability, dated operating status and verified service geography. 01 Scope Whose list is this? The provider lists and status decisions on this page come from instruments issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); the bank list was checked on 7 September 2026. Since 2016 central-bank authority has been divided, and some banks on that list have addresses in Sana'a and Taiz in the source. Status under any other authority is not established here; this defines the scope of the evidence and is not a judgement about either authority. Absence from a CBY-Aden list does not show that a provider is unlicensed elsewhere, and presence on it does not show that a provider can operate across all of Yemen. 02 Evidence Banks: a dated formal roster, not an operating census The list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks; 12 of them are classified as microfinance banks on the basis of their names in the source. These are facts about formal listing and classification. They do not establish whether every institution is operating, which branches are active, what products are available, market share, payment-rail participation or underserved-client reach. Another view of the evidence What do we actually know about each provider class? Text description of this view Analytical question: What can official evidence establish about each provider class at the dates shown? What the evidence shows: For each provider class the evidence separates the issuing authority, the dated list or count, dated status decisions and evidence of operation. Banks: the licensed-bank list of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names the licensed banks, some of them classified as microfinance banks by name; bank status decisions are not reviewed here. Exchange and remittance providers: the official 2026 roster lists exchange companies, individual exchange establishments and remittance agents, and selected CBY-Aden decisions of 2026 suspend the licences of named entities or close their premises. E-wallets: CBY-Aden publications give e-wallet counts for 2024 and 2025 whose definitions have not been reconciled, and a June 2024 circular names wallets, entities or services as unlicensed; the evidence base holds no current named list of licensed wallets. Non-bank microfinance institutions: the evidence base holds only network membership pages, not a licensing list. Payment-system operators: the evidence base holds no named list. In every class, a list or licence establishes a dated formal status, not that each listed entity or location is operating. Scope and time: Dated lists and decisions, 2024–2026 · Banks, exchange and remittance providers, e-wallets, non-bank microfinance institutions and payment-system operators, as recorded by the issuing authority or source for each class What not to conclude: A list or licence does not show that a provider is operating or reaching customers; a list of unlicensed names is not a register of licensed providers; a decision about named entities does not make a complete list of providers; and the dimensions do not add up to an overall confidence score. Open evidence record → 03 Analysis Exchange and remittance: the 2026 roster is countable; operation remains a separate question The official 2026 roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These are three source-defined categories, not a deduplicated total of unique firms. The 2026 suspension, withdrawal or closure decisions are separate status evidence: they are dated January–September 2026, some were issued before the roster and some after it, and the roster’s own issue date is not stated. They have to be reconciled entity by entity before any count of providers operating on a given date is stated. 04 Analysis Status events update an entity; they do not create the market denominator Licence withdrawal, suspension and other enforcement decisions in 2026 are dated events for named entities and belong on each provider's status history. Because the annual roster and the 2026 decisions refer to different dates and require entity-level matching, this resource does not mechanically subtract the decisions from the 2026 roster to produce a count of operating providers. Silence about another provider is not evidence that it is active or compliant. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. Analysis Wallet counts are not yet one clean provider trend Official material from the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) reports different wallet counts at different dates and in different contexts: 7 in 2024 Q3, 9 in 2025 H1 and 8 licensed e-wallets in a September 2025 statement. This resource does not plot the sequence 7, 9, 8 as entry and exit because the definitions and the sets of wallets each source covers have not been reconciled. A June 2024 circular separately named 12 wallets, entities or services as unlicensed on that source date; that negative list cannot be carried forward as a 2026 status or used to infer the full list of licensed wallets. System context Where providers sit in the wider system Provider authority and status sit upstream of access and use. A provider may be legally present but have limited operating geography; a payment or finance product may exist without evidence of active use; and an enforcement event may change formal status without telling us what happened to customer access. This resource therefore links provider status to Access, Payments, Finance and Reforms without collapsing those questions. System structure Money exchangers are part of the financial system, not a footnote Historical evidence shows that money-exchange businesses have long formed a substantial part of Yemen’s financial-service landscape. That earlier evidence helps explain why exchange and remittance providers matter to the system, but it does not establish the complete set of providers operating in 2026, their operating status, branch activity or geographic reach. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading What exactly do we mean by microfinance growth? Yemen’s microfinance record does not move on one axis. Borrower counts, saver or depositor measures, nominal portfolios and institutional form are not the same measure, and they do not yet form one harmonised growth series. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. Where can people and firms actually reach financial services — and where is the map still blank? What measurement would change the decision? A register of active financial access points An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated. This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted. Open this measurement priority Digital onboarding and identity journeys Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost. This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points. Open this measurement priority Verify it yourself Open the evidence record behind each answer, or go to the sources or the methodology. en/readings/after-transfer-persistence/i.text: Evidence Readings/The payment arrived. What happened next? Evidence Reading The payment arrived. What happened next? Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments. Evidence period World Bank and G2Px material, May 2024 · reference period of the recipient figure not recorded Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: A delivered payment, a recipient count or an opened account is not durable active use unless follow-up shows continued use, and immediate cash-out is not by itself evidence of failure. A transfer can succeed before a financial relationship begins. The intended recipient can be identified, the payment authorised and the funds delivered; the recipient can reach them; an account can be opened and made usable; and a programme can extend a new delivery channel into places where distributing cash is hard. Those are real results, and they should be measured and credited as such. Financial inclusion asks a different question: what happens after the money arrives? World Bank and G2Px material from May 2024 describes a digital-payment pilot in eight districts within Yemen’s unconditional cash-transfer programme, reported by programme partners to have benefited 45,460 recipients. The pilot emphasised payment into fully functional accounts and recipient choice. That goes beyond a change in disbursement technology. A fully functional account can, by design, receive money, hold value and make payments; and choice matters because a system built around recipients should not treat them as passive receivers of a programme payment. But possibility is not persistence. The available Yemen evidence does not yet tell us whether recipients used those accounts between transfers, kept balances in them, received other money, paid merchants or bills, made transfers of their own, switched providers, or kept using the account after the programme payments that prompted it weakened or ended. That is the missing observation. Successful delivery is only one step Text description of this view Analytical question: Where does evidence stop between a cash transfer and sustained financial use? What the evidence shows: World Bank G2Px (government-to-person payments) material documents a digital-payment pilot within Yemen's unconditional cash-transfer programme that reached 45,460 recipients in eight districts, paying into fully functional accounts with recipient choice; this establishes delivery and exposure to a formal digital service. The evidence base holds no longitudinal follow-up, so it does not show whether recipients kept using the account or e-wallet afterwards, and the persistence link stays open. Delivering a payment is not lasting financial use: beneficiaries, registrations, identities and opened e-wallets or accounts are not durable active use without follow-up. Scope and time: Programme-specific dates; persistence period currently unmeasured · Programme beneficiaries and programme/provider activity states; not automatically unique active financial users What not to conclude: Without follow-up, beneficiaries, registrations, identities and opened e-wallets or accounts are not durable active use. Programme-specific dates; persistence period currently unmeasuredProgramme beneficiaries and programme/provider activity states; not automatically unique active financial users Delivery and inclusion are different results A digital cash-transfer programme may improve delivery even if recipients later withdraw most or all of each transfer in cash. Immediate cash-out can be rational: local merchants may prefer cash, acceptance networks may be thin, liquidity may be uncertain, and fees, distance, reliability, trust or familiarity may make cash the better instrument for immediate needs. Cash-out should not automatically be labelled failure, and account opening should not automatically be labelled inclusion. It is more useful to report three families of results separately: Delivery: was the right payment made to the right person, safely, accurately and on time? Access to a usable account: did the recipient obtain a genuinely functional account, on terms they could understand, with a meaningful choice? Persistent use: did the account keep a role in the recipient’s financial life between or after programme payments? Each can improve while another remains unmeasured. The period between payments may tell us most A payment-day metric tells us whether the programme worked on payment day. Persistence runs on another clock. Useful questions include: Was the account still active a month, three months, six months and a year later? Was it used between transfer cycles? Did money from outside the programme enter the account? Was some value kept rather than withdrawn at once? Did the recipient pay a merchant or a bill from it, or start a transfer? Was it used after the programme payments ended? Did the recipient stay with the provider, switch or stop? What happened when a transaction failed or a complaint was made? What did using the account cost in money, time and travel? The aim is not to expect every cash-transfer recipient to become a frequent user of digital finance. It is to find out whether the new channel created an option of lasting value, and for whom. Choice matters only if it can be exercised The pilot’s emphasis on recipient choice is analytically important. Whether an account can become more than a payment channel depends on design features such as a real choice of provider, a fully functional account, reachable access points, clear terms and the ability to use the account beyond the programme payment. But choice written into a programme design is not necessarily choice experienced by recipients. Exercising it needs viable providers or channels, understandable fees, usable access points, control of credentials, reliable service and a practical ability to switch. So the measurement question is not only whether choice was offered, but whether recipients could exercise it without risking their access to the payment. Where the evidence stops The current evidence does not establish that Yemen’s pilot produced persistent use. It does not establish that cashing out was irrational or undesirable, or that paying transfers digitally automatically improves household resilience, women’s agency or financial health. And it does not establish that the pilot failed simply because those later outcomes have not been measured. The 45,460 figure counts recipients reported by the programme, not people who kept using an account. The pilot material provides evidence of movement toward digital delivery and describes recipients being given usable accounts. Whether that became a durable financial relationship is a separate empirical question. What would change this reading? A longitudinal follow-up of recipients, linked where appropriate and safely possible to administrative payment data. At minimum it would distinguish payment success, account activation, the timing of cash-out, activity between transfers, activity a month, three months, six months and a year later, balances kept, deposits from outside the programme, payments and transfers the recipient starts, switching provider, dormancy, complaints, failed or reversed transactions, fees, the cost in travel and time, control of the account, and use after the transfers end. It should then ask recipients why they used, returned, switched or stopped. If the account disappears from the recipient’s financial life between one payment and the next, did digitisation change the delivery channel, or did it change the financial relationship? Trace the evidence Each statement this Reading relies on is backed by an Evidence Record. Follow a record to its original sources before reusing a figure. Every figure in this Reading traces through the records below to a named source. Where a record also rests on material with no public link to its original document, that material is not listed and no figure from it is shown. Return to the question Are reforms and payment infrastructure turning into access, use, quality and outcomes? A successful cash payment is not yet durable financial use Reference CLM-045 Digitalizing Government-to-Person (G2P) Payments in Yemen: unconditional cash transfer (UCT) pilot (2024) Also draws on material that has no public link to its original document; that material is not listed or linked. Sources SRC-WB-G2PX-YEM-UCT-2024-001 Digitalizing Government-to-Person (G2P) Payments in Yemen: unconditional cash transfer (UCT) pilot (2024) World Bank (G2Px) · Event or programme page Source record Copy source reference This source record does not establish permission to republish the original file, table or chart. Check source-specific terms before redistribution. Related readings When does digital growth become durable use?Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it. When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced. All Evidence Readings

en/readings/banking-jump-measurement-bas.text: Evidence Readings/When the baseline moves Evidence Reading When the baseline moves Yemen’s banking series shows why a large published jump must be separated from a change in measurement before it becomes an economic story. Evidence period Positions at end-2022 as published in the 2022 annual report and restated from 2023 · valuation change of January 2023 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: A same-year restatement does not show a credit, deposit or asset boom or a change in solvency, and the evidence does not yet divide the jump between valuation and economic movement. A number can rise because the economy changed. It can also rise because the way an existing position is valued, classified or reported changed. Yemen’s banking data require the two to be kept apart. The same 2022 consolidated positions of commercial and Islamic banks are published at materially higher levels in the annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) from 2023 onward than in the 2022 report. The change comes alongside a documented January 2023 shift to valuing foreign-currency positions at the market exchange rate. The point is not that the later values are wrong. It is that a comparison across the break does not start from a single, unchanged statistical base. A growth rate calculated across a method break can partly measure the method. Restated end-2022 bank positions after a change in valuation basis Text description of this view Analytical question: How much of the same-period banking jump is restatement rather than economic movement? What the evidence shows: The same end-2022 consolidated balance-sheet positions of commercial and Islamic banks are published at materially higher levels in the annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) from 2023 onward than in its 2022 report, alongside a documented January 2023 shift to valuing foreign-currency positions at the market exchange rate. The change of valuation basis can account for part of the difference, so the published jump does not by itself establish economic change of the same size: a same-year restatement does not show a boom in credit, deposits or assets, or a change in solvency. Nor does it mean the restated values are wrong or that every later movement is accounting only. Scope and time: 2022 positions as published before/after the 2023 method break · Same reference-period banking positions across publication vintages What not to conclude: A same-year restatement of banking positions does not show an economic boom, credit expansion, deposit surge or change in solvency. 2022 positions as published before/after the 2023 method breakSame reference-period banking positions across publication vintages The break runs across more than one line The restatement shows up across several balance-sheet positions, not in one isolated indicator. That matters, because a simultaneous change in deposits, credit, assets or foreign-currency positions can otherwise be read as an equally large shift in financial intermediation. The current evidence does not support that reading. The valuation note documents a change in treatment. It does not provide a line-by-line bridge showing how much of each restated balance comes from valuation, classification, coverage or economic movement, so that decomposition remains open. History rules out an easy “first-ever” story Market-rate valuation of foreign-currency accounts has documented precedent in Yemen from 1996. That does not prove the 1996 and 2023 arrangements were identical, but it does mean January 2023 should not be described as the first time Yemen used market-rate valuation. The defensible statement is narrower: the current banking series contains a documented valuation or reporting break from January 2023, and that break changes how comparisons around it should be read. What remains usable A method break does not make the banking series unusable; it changes the rule for comparing it. Where possible, compare observations within one statistical vintage and under the same reported treatment. Where a value for the same period is restated, keep both vintages visible until the bridge between them is understood. Even within a consistent vintage, nominal balance-sheet growth does not by itself establish: real credit growth; more borrowers; wider access; better allocation of credit; stronger bank soundness; or greater financial inclusion. Those are separate questions, each with its own evidence. Where the evidence stops The evidence does not yet include a verified line-by-line reconciliation of the old and new 2022 bases. For that reason this Reading publishes no headline percentage for the size of the restatement and does not treat the difference as a measured economic gain. That restraint is part of the result. What would change this reading? The exact January 2023 circular, together with a reconciliation table showing, for each affected balance-sheet line: the legacy value; the restated value; the valuation treatment; any change in classification or in the reporting population; and the part, if any, attributable to underlying economic movement. Until that bridge exists, the safe rule is simple. Show the break. Keep the vintage. Do not calculate growth through a changed base as if the base had never moved. en/readings/define-what-you-count/index..text: Evidence Readings/When the unit changes, the story changes Evidence Reading When the unit changes, the story changes People, accounts, subscribers, terminals and transactions all describe parts of Yemen’s financial system. They are not interchangeable measures of financial inclusion, and a target or a trend is only as sound as the unit it keeps. Evidence period Global Findex fieldwork 2022–2023 · POS counts March 2025 – January 2026 · project baseline January 2025, target 2030 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: Accounts, active accounts, subscribers, wallets, terminals and transactions cannot be converted into unique people, and a target cannot be compared with a result whose unit, population or activity definition differs. Financial-inclusion figures can all move in the same direction and still tell us different things. Adults with an account, accounts on a provider’s books, registered wallet subscribers, active accounts, transactions, POS terminals, programme beneficiaries: each can be useful. The problem begins when one quietly takes the place of another. Yemen’s representative Findex evidence measures people. Administrative systems count accounts and other financial products, infrastructure and activity. Programmes count the firms or beneficiaries they support. These measures can describe one financial system without measuring one outcome. One system, different things being counted Text description of this view Analytical question: Are people, accounts, wallets, terminals and transactions being kept as different measurement objects? What the evidence shows: Inclusion evidence for Yemen counts different things in different systems. A population survey counts people: the Global Findex 2021 study for Yemen has 1,000 respondents, and its population estimates require the survey weights. Administrative reports count accounts, e-wallet subscribers, terminals and transactions; programmes count participants, outputs and targets. The Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) target of 1,021 access points by 2030, against a January 2025 baseline of 817 under the project's own definition, cannot be added to or compared with counts of ATMs, POS terminals or agents until the project's taxonomy and deduplication rules are documented. A baseline or target changes meaning when the counted object changes: accounts, e-wallets, subscribers, terminals and transactions are not unique people unless a documented method converts them. Scope and time: Current evidence available here; dates vary by item · Each lane retains its own survey or administrative universe What not to conclude: Accounts, e-wallets, subscribers, terminals and transactions are not counts of unique people, and this resource holds no documented method that converts them. Current evidence available here; dates vary by itemEach lane retains its own survey or administrative universe Start with the noun “11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account” (Global Findex, fieldwork 2022–2023) and “POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 to 1,473 between March 2025 and January 2026” are both legitimate observations. The first is about people, estimated from a weighted survey. The second is about pieces of infrastructure counted in an administrative system. One terminal can serve many people, and one person can use many terminals. A person can hold several accounts; an account can generate many transactions; a registered subscriber may be inactive. The noun is part of the metric. Change the noun and the story can change without anything changing in reality. The denominator still matters Even when the counted object is people, the denominator cannot disappear. The Yemen Findex study has 1,000 respondents, but population estimates require the survey weights and design. The respondents are the observations from which the estimate is made, not the denominator of Yemen’s adult population, and raw case percentages are not population estimates. The survey frame also excludes areas holding about 23% of the population. Programme measures are legitimate within their own universe The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project sets a 2030 target of 1,021 access points against a January 2025 baseline of 817, under the project’s own definition. That is legitimate project-monitoring evidence. It is not a count of people. Nor can it be added to, or compared directly with, counts of ATMs, POS terminals or agents unless the project’s access-point definitions and de-duplication rules are documented, and in the evidence base they are not. A bounded measure is not weak because its universe is narrow; it becomes misleading when that universe disappears from view. When targets drift A baseline may measure adults with an account. Monitoring may later report registered accounts; a dashboard may highlight active wallets; a performance report may celebrate transactions; and the final narrative may call the result greater inclusion. Every number in that chain can be correct while the chain itself is wrong. That is metric drift. Before accepting any baseline, target or claim of progress, ask: What exactly is being counted? Among whom does the number apply? What makes the unit active, or included? Are the baseline and the result measured under the same definition? What does the measure still not tell us? What would change this reading? A metric crosswalk for Yemen’s main inclusion measures, recording for each one what is counted, whether units are unique, the universe, the denominator, the activity rule, the period, the source, any link to unique people or firms, and whether it measures access, registration, active use, frequency, quality or outcome. Where a bridge is missing, the gap should be visible rather than filled by assumption. The practical rule: Do not compare two numbers until you can complete this sentence for both: “This counts ___ among ___ under the rule ___ during ___.” If the blanks differ materially, the first question is not how much the number changed. It is whether there is a comparison at all. Trace the evidence Each statement this Reading relies on is backed by an Evidence Record. Follow a record to its original sources before reusing a figure. en/readings/digital-workaround-not-yet-d.text: Evidence Readings/When does digital growth become durable use? Evidence Reading When does digital growth become durable use? Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it. Evidence period Provider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: Registrations, accounts, one-time use, transaction growth and infrastructure expansion do not prove unique, repeat, voluntary or durable financial use. By December 2019, the five e-money providers covered by a study of the Institute of Banking Studies had 807,919 electronic-money accounts. The same study reports an average dormant or inactive share of 23%, and notes that some accounts were used only once, or because circumstances required it. This is not a paradox. The number of accounts establishes scale within the source universe. Dormancy and one-off use show why scale alone does not establish durable financial use. Account growth is not the same as durable digital use Text description of this view Analytical question: What did historical e-money growth actually establish about use? What the evidence shows: In the historical study by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) of five electronic-money providers, accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019, with an average dormant or inactive share of 23%; the source notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. A CauseWay grouping of the study's 2019 transaction values puts 57.03% in cash-in and cash-out, 29.97% in movements between bank and electronic accounts, and 2.41% in bills and purchases combined; the grouping is CauseWay's, not a source headline. Account registrations and digital activity do not, on their own, establish voluntary and sustained use: registered accounts are not unique active people, and the 2016–2019 pattern cannot be extended to national prevalence in 2026. Scope and time: 2016–2019, with account level at Dec-2019 · Five electronic-money providers in the historical study by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS); transaction-value categories limited to those in the source What not to conclude: Registered accounts are not unique active people, and the historical five-provider pattern does not show national prevalence in 2026. 2016–2019, with account level at Dec-2019Five electronic-money providers in the historical study by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS); transaction-value categories limited to those in the source An account can exist without becoming a relationship Registration does not tell us whether an account was used once or repeatedly, whether use was voluntary or triggered by a payment someone else made, whether value stayed in the account, whether the user paid or saved with it, or whether the service became preferable to cash for any purpose. What the money moved for CauseWay’s grouping of a 2019 transaction table in the same study indicates that 57.03% of recorded e-money transaction value was cash-in or cash-out and 29.97% was movement between bank and electronic accounts; bills and purchases together were 2.41%. The grouping is CauseWay’s, not a headline in the source. Cash-in and cash-out are not failed digital finance. Where moving value safely or easily is hard, that function has real economic use. But a system dominated by entry to and exit from cash tells us something different from repeated merchant, bill, saving or other digital use. Useful before durable The evidence supports neither extreme: that every new account proves inclusion, or that episodic use proves digital finance failed. A service can solve a real problem once and still not become a persistent financial relationship. The historical provider evidence also reports strong urban concentration and a low share of women within its own universe. These are not 2026 national estimates. Their present value is to show what current measurement must test: who uses digital finance, not merely how many accounts exist. What would change this reading? Current data on unique active users, recency and frequency of use, what accounts are used for, value retained in the account, merchant and bill payments, dormancy, failed transactions, cost, complaints and provider-side behaviour, combined with demand-side questions on why people open an account, use it, return to it or stop. The measures that matter are registration, activity, recency, frequency, function, choice or trigger, quality and persistence, and they should not be read as an automatic ladder. Scale tells us how large the digital system became. Return use tells us whether it entered financial life. Trace the evidence Each statement this Reading relies on is backed by an Evidence Record. What happened next?Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments. When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced. All Evidence Readings

en/readings/finance-constraint-different.text: Evidence Readings/How can 22% and 91.84% both be right? Evidence Reading How can 22% and 91.84% both be right? A 2022 survey of formal firms in seven selected governorates can tell us that finance was named less often than electricity or fuel, and also that most firms in a narrower group rated finance a major or moderate obstacle. The numbers do not contradict each other. They answer different questions. Evidence period World Bank custom enterprise survey, September 2022, seven governorates · SMEPS programme report for 2024 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: The 22% general-business-challenge share and the 91.84% finance-severity result do not share a question or denominator, and the seven-governorate survey does not describe all Yemeni firms. Among formal firms in a 2022 custom survey covering seven selected governorates, 22% named access to finance as a business challenge. In the same question, 50% named electricity, 46% fuel shortages, 32% transport or road blockades, 30% tax administration or tax rates and 27% political instability. Firms could name more than one challenge. Read alone, 22% makes finance look secondary. A separate tabulation in the same survey report excludes firms that said they did not need a loan. Among the firms that remain, 68.71% rate access to finance a major obstacle and 23.13% a moderate one: 91.84% together. Both figures can be right. The denominator is not a footnote to the result. It is part of the result. Three finance questions, three different bases Text description of this view Analytical question: Why do the firm-finance percentages differ without actually contradicting one another? What the evidence shows: These figures answer three different questions on three different bases. In a 2022 survey of formal firms in seven governorates, 22% of firms named access to finance as a general business challenge. Among firms in the report's finance-obstacle table, which excludes firms that said they did not need a loan, 91.84% rated finance a major or moderate obstacle. The Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) reports that 19% of the micro, small and medium enterprises it supported “accessed financial services” in 2024, and 15% over 2021–2024. The figures do not contradict each other; they are not estimates for the same population, a single national rate or a causal programme effect. Scope and time: 2022 survey; 2024 and 2021–24 programme reporting · Formal firms in seven governorates (2022 survey); the subset in the report's finance-obstacle table; micro, small and medium enterprises supported by the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) What not to conclude: The figures of 22%, 91.84%, 19% and 15% are not estimates for the same population, and none is a causal programme effect. 2022 survey; 2024 and 2021–24 programme reportingFormal firms in seven governorates (2022 survey); the subset in the report's finance-obstacle table; micro, small and medium enterprises supported by the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) Two questions, two groups of firms The 22% is comparative. It places finance among electricity, fuel, transport, taxation and instability, following the survey’s own item wording; it is not the standard Enterprise Survey “biggest obstacle” indicator, and it does not rank constraints by their causal effect. A loan does not make electricity reliable, and a guarantee does not reopen a road. Finance belongs inside the business environment, not above it. The 91.84% describes severity within a narrower, finance-relevant group. It does not mean that 91.84% of Yemeni firms, or even of the surveyed firms, face a major or moderate finance obstacle: the group changed before the percentage was calculated, and the number of firms in that tabulation is not recorded in the evidence base. How firms actually fund themselves The survey covered 328 formal firms. Of these, 31 reported a line of credit, and the question on loan sources has 18 valid responses; the evidence base does not show whether those 18 come from the 31. Counts this small can describe the responses. They cannot support national market-share claims. Working capital adds another layer. On average, formal firms reported financing working capital as follows: 69.12% from internal funds or retained earnings, 16.66% from money lenders, friends or relatives, 10.15% from advance payments by clients, 1.97% from non-bank financial institutions, 1.31% from supplier credit and 0.56% from banks. These are average shares, not shares of firms. The mix does not prove that every non-bank source hides unmet demand for bank credit, but it does show that formal bank finance plays a very small observed role in this survey’s working-capital mix. Constraints can be complements Electricity and finance do not need to compete for first place. Finance can help a firm invest in resilience, inventory, equipment or energy; but if operating conditions destroy expected returns, available finance may remain unattractive. The interaction between them is the important economic question. Programme evidence adds another universe. SMEPS reports that 19% of the MSMEs it supported accessed financial services in 2024, and 15% over 2021–2024 against a 40% programme target. That is useful programme evidence, not a national MSME rate. Why it matters in Yemen Two misreadings are tempting. One says 22% means finance is not a serious issue. The other says 91.84% means nearly all Yemeni firms are severely finance-constrained. Neither is supported. A stronger reading is that finance appears serious for an important subset of firms, while firms also face severe non-financial constraints and rely heavily on internal or non-bank sources. That changes the intervention question: for which firms, for what productive purpose, on what terms, and alongside which other constraints would additional finance unlock investment or resilience? Where the evidence stops The survey covers formal firms in seven selected governorates, not all Yemeni firms. Its finance questions use different denominators, the loan-source table rests on 18 valid responses, and SMEPS reports on its own programme universe. None of this supports a current national rate of MSME access to finance, or a causal effect. What would change this reading? A current, representative measure of the firm-finance journey — need, demand, application or discouragement, approval, terms, source, use and outcome — linked to firm size, sector, formality, ownership, the owner’s sex where statistically supportable, geography and the other operating constraints firms face. If firms can face severe financing constraints while facing even more immediate problems, and many fund operations without banks, what exactly should a successful firm-finance intervention be trying to unlock? en/readings/from-rail-to-result-missing-.text: Evidence Readings/When does a payment reform become financial inclusion? Evidence Reading When does a payment reform become financial inclusion? A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced. Evidence period POS counts March 2025 – January 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 · project results framework January 2025 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: Regulation, infrastructure, a new institution or go-live does not by itself show access, use, quality or outcomes, and missing downstream evidence does not mean a reform failed. Yemen’s payment system has changed. Official records document new rules, institutional steps, integration work, expanding reported infrastructure and transaction activity. POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026 within its reporting scope. Between June and August 2026, its records also document further institution-building: integration work on the unified domestic money-transfer network, and the founding of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company. These are material developments, and they do not all prove the same thing. A completed milestone tells us where implementation has reached. It does not tell us what changed downstream. The missing links from payment infrastructure to inclusion results Text description of this view Analytical question: Which link in the reform-to-outcome chain is actually evidenced? What the evidence shows: The evidence reaches the first steps of the chain only. Rules and programmes are documented: a decision of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) of 26 June 2024 requiring new domestic cash transfers to go through the unified transfer network, with stated exceptions; the Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP), which started in July 2025 with components to support a Fast Payment System in areas under the internationally recognized government, a real-time gross settlement system with an upgrade of CBY-Aden core banking, and an access-point database; and a CBY-Aden board decision of 29 March 2026 on a mandatory national QR standard, linking of e-wallets and CBY-Aden's participation as a main shareholder in the Fast Payment System operator company. Institutional steps followed in June–August 2026: unified-network integration work, the restructuring of the Unified Money Network company, and the founding assembly and first board meeting of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC). The evidence also holds POS figures for January 2026 within CBY-Aden's reporting scope (1,473 terminals; 24,026 transactions) and an attributed CBY-Aden statement on unified-network activity from January 2026. Nothing here measures access by people, use, service quality or outcomes: those steps are open, which means not yet measured, not failed. Scope and time: Dates vary by reform/rail; exact event/observation dates travel with nodes · Each state retains its own administrative, provider, user or population universe What not to conclude: A rule, procurement, installation, institutional event or go-live does not by itself show access, use, quality or outcome; an open step has not yet been measured and does not mean the reform failed. Dates vary by reform/rail; exact event/observation dates travel with nodesEach state retains its own administrative, provider, user or population universe A reform passes through stages that need different evidence A payment reform can be followed along a chain: rule or funding → implementation or institution → operation → reachable access → actual use → quality and protection → outcome Each link asks for different evidence. A legal instrument can establish that a rule exists. An institutional decision can establish that a company, a governance arrangement or an integration step was created. A technical launch can establish that a service became operational. Infrastructure counts can establish that acceptance devices or service points were reported, and transactions can establish activity. None of these, by itself, establishes population reach, repeated use, affordability, reliability, consumer protection or a financial outcome. The links can also move out of step. The Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company is an institution that has been established, not a system in operation, and the results framework of the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project recorded the fast payment system and the real-time gross settlement system as not yet operational in January 2025, with no later operational state recorded here. Infrastructure and transactions answer their own questions The rise in POS terminals is meaningful, but a terminal count is not a count of people. It does not tell us how many terminals were routinely working, how many unique merchants used them, how many unique customers paid through them, how reliable the service was, or whether the expansion changed financial behaviour. Its inability to answer those questions is not a failure of the series; it answers a different one. A recorded transaction brings us closer to use: it proves that activity occurred inside the reporting system. It does not tell us how many unique people used the service, whether they came back, what the transaction cost, whether it succeeded at the first attempt, what happened when it failed, whether complaints were resolved, or whether the service changed convenience, safety, resilience or productive activity. Missing evidence is not evidence of failure The distinction works in both directions. It is wrong to call a new rail or regulation “financial inclusion” simply because it exists, and equally wrong to call a reform a failure because its downstream effects have not yet been measured. The accurate statement is narrower: the evidence has reached a particular stage, and the next stage remains open. That is a conclusion about the evidence, not a judgement on the reform. For each major reform or system change, monitoring should identify the furthest stage that is actually evidenced and then ask for the next missing link. A rule may be in place while implementation remains open; an institution may exist while operation remains open; operation may be proven while reach remains open; reach may be proven while repeated use remains open; use may be proven while reliability, cost or redress remain open; and service quality may be proven while household or firm outcomes remain open. Why it matters in Yemen The evidence is not updated at the same pace. Regulation, institution-building and administrative payment data can move faster than representative evidence about people. Fragmented authority, infrastructure constraints and differences in reporting coverage make it especially risky to turn one operational signal into a national outcome, so the public record needs to keep the chain visible rather than compress it into a single word. What would change this reading? For each major reform or rail, a connected set of measures covering operational status and coverage; participating institutions; reachable access; unique active users; recency and frequency of use; transaction success, failure, reversal and delay; the cost customers actually pay; complaints and redress; repeated use; and the outcome the reform is ultimately expected to affect. The data need not live in one system, but their definitions must connect without pretending that unlike measures are equivalent. Measure forward from the last proven state, not backward from the outcome you hope to claim. Trace the evidence Each statement this Reading relies on is backed by an Evidence Record. en/readings/gender-gap-measured-causes-o.text: Evidence Readings/The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open. Evidence Reading The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open. The latest Findex observation shows a large gap between women’s and men’s account ownership inside a system where few adults of either sex have an account. The evidence tells us where the disparity is. It does not yet tell us which barriers produce it. Evidence period Global Findex, Yemen fieldwork 7 November 2022 – 9 January 2023 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: The measured gap does not establish its causes, the causal contribution of any proposed mechanism, or the size of the gap in 2026; a plausible mechanism is not an established causal explanation. In the latest Global Findex wave for Yemen, 18.35% of men and 5.44% of women aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account, a gap of 12.91 percentage points. This is a valid comparison within one survey wave. It is a measured disparity, and it is not, by itself, an explanation. The gap also sits inside a low-access system. Overall account ownership in the same wave is 11.9%, and men’s measured level is low too. The sharper question is therefore: Why does an already low-access financial system reach women so much less than men? That moves attention away from “fixing women” and towards the conditions under which access is produced. A measured gap, mechanisms still to test Text description of this view Analytical question: What is measured about the gender gap, and what remains hypothesis? What the evidence shows: In the Global Findex 2021 wave for Yemen (fieldwork 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023), 5.44% of women and 18.35% of men aged 15 and over in the survey's coverage had an account, a difference of 12.91 percentage points; the survey excluded areas holding about 23% of the population. Possible mechanisms such as identity, mobile-phone access, income, distance and trust are hypotheses still to be tested, not measured causes. The wave is not a 2026 estimate and not a map of differences by governorate. Scope and time: 2021 wave; Yemen fieldwork 2022–23 · Adults in the Findex survey coverage; same-wave male/female comparison What not to conclude: The measured same-wave gap does not establish its causes, its size in 2026 or differences between governorates. 2021 wave; Yemen fieldwork 2022–23Adults in the Findex survey coverage; same-wave male/female comparison The mechanism is still open Plausible mechanisms include income, employment, identity documents, phone ownership and control, distance, mobility, trust, household decision-making, provider practice and product design. For Yemen these are hypotheses to test, not findings; the current evidence does not divide the 12.91-point gap among them. The same survey records a gap of about 9.0 percentage points between adults in the poorest 40% of households by income (6.5%) and those in the richest 60% (15.5%). That does not explain the gender gap. It shows why one-dimensional explanations are risky. Measure the journey, not only the endpoint Account ownership is one point on a longer path. Better measurement would ask whether a woman can open an account, whether she controls the device and the account, whether she uses it and returns to it, what it costs her, whether it works, whether she can obtain redress, whether she decides how it is used, and whether it improves something she values. Provider data can follow the same path from the other side: applications, approvals, rejections, active use, dormancy, balances, credit, complaints, fraud, resolution and exit, each with a visible denominator. What would change this reading? A current representative survey design for Yemen that combines up-to-date sex-disaggregated measures of access, use, quality and protection; the variables that could explain the gap, collected in the same survey; comparisons among different groups of women; and provider-side customer funnels. The gap tells us where to investigate. It does not tell us which intervention to choose. If we can measure the gap but cannot yet locate where women are being lost — at access, activation, use, persistence or quality — how can we know that an intervention is aimed at the right problem? en/readings/microfinance-structural-dive.text: Evidence Readings/What exactly do we mean by microfinance growth? Evidence Reading What exactly do we mean by microfinance growth? Yemen’s microfinance record does not move on one axis. Borrower counts, saver or depositor measures, nominal portfolios and institutional form are not the same measure, and they do not yet form one harmonised growth series. Evidence period Borrower, saver and portfolio observations for end-2015, end-2020 and 2023 · licensed-bank list checked on 7 September 2026 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: Changes in saver or depositor counts, nominal portfolio or provider structure do not, on their own, establish broader inclusion, real credit deepening, market dominance, growth in unique people or improved borrower outcomes, and the borrower, saver and portfolio observations do not form one harmonised trend. “Microfinance growth” sounds like one result. The evidence describes several. Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper citing SFD data reports 78,686 active borrowers at end-2023, but the set of providers behind that later point has not been verified against the earlier primary series. The observations are informative. They are not yet one continuous trend. Borrowers, savers and portfolio: separate anchors, not one trend Text description of this view Analytical question: Is microfinance change coming from broader borrower reach or from other dimensions? What the evidence shows: Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020; a 2024 Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023, for a set of providers not yet verified. “Active savers” (2023) and “savers/depositors” (2020) have not been shown to be the same measure, the rial valuation of the portfolio figures is not recorded, and incompatible 2023 observations are not joined into one series. These anchors are not comparable enough to show a direction for borrowers, savers or portfolio, and they do not establish growth in unique people, broader inclusion, real credit deepening, better borrower outcomes or any cause. Scope and time: 2015, 2020 and bounded 2023 anchors · Source-specific microfinance institution/provider sets covered by the sources; saver/depositor definitions not fully harmonized What not to conclude: Separate nominal and administrative anchors do not show growth in unique people, real credit deepening, better borrower outcomes or any cause. 2015, 2020 and bounded 2023 anchorsSource-specific microfinance institution/provider sets covered by the sources; saver/depositor definitions not fully harmonized Borrowers are one dimension The borrower record shows that the number of active borrowers can move differently from the financial volume that providers carry. The World Bank’s Financial Sector Diagnostics describe an active borrower base that stayed broadly around 80,000–90,000 through 2021 while average loan amounts rose. That supports a bounded historical reading: financial volume can expand without a comparable expansion in the number of active borrowers. It does not tell us why. Loan size, client mix, provider composition, inflation, currency conditions and reporting coverage may all matter, and the current evidence does not separate their effects. Savers and depositors are another The verified 2020 record shows about 1.611 million savers or depositors. The same 2024 paper reports what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” in 2023. The two labels are not assumed to describe the same measure: the provider universe, the definition of an active saver and the de-duplication rule have not been harmonised across the evidence. The later figure therefore remains a bounded secondary observation. It is not 3.3 million unique people, and it is not a national savings rate. Nominal portfolio is a third The verified 2020 record shows an outstanding portfolio of about YER 33.379 billion; the 2024 paper reports a nominal portfolio of about YER 44 billion for 2023. A larger nominal portfolio does not, on its own, establish deeper real credit. The evidence base holds no common price or exchange-rate treatment that would turn these nominal rials into one real series across Yemen’s divided monetary conditions, and it does not record which rial valuation each figure uses. The portfolio can be described as larger in nominal reported terms where the source supports it. It should not be presented as measured real financial deepening. Institutional form is a fourth Institutional form matters too. The licensed-bank list of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden, as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks, 12 of which this resource classifies as microfinance banks from their names. A listing or licence establishes an institutional status. It does not establish current operation, geographic reach, client mix or outreach, so institutional change can matter without answering the inclusion question. A share of growth is not a share of the stock A 2024 Sana’a Center paper attributes about 91% of saver growth over the period it analyses to Al-Kuraimi. That is a statement about the source of an increase. It is not, in this evidence base, a verified 2023 share of the total saver stock, and a later restatement that treats it as one is not used here. The case shows why the unit and the calculation base must travel with the number. What would change this reading? The defensible answer to “is microfinance growing?” is a set of separate questions rather than one sector growth rate. Did active borrowers increase? Did saver or depositor relationships expand under a stable definition? Did the nominal portfolio grow, and did average loan exposure change? Did provider structure change? Did any of this reach more unique people or firms, and did service quality or borrower outcomes improve? Different answers can coexist. Answering them needs a reconciled provider-level panel with stable definitions for unique active borrowers, unique active depositors or savers, balances and outstanding exposure, loan size, portfolio quality, geography, provider type, operating status, and complaints and customer outcomes, together with explicit rules for provider coverage, de-duplication, and prices or exchange rates when nominal values are compared over time. If borrower counts, saver relationships, nominal portfolios and institutional form move differently, what exactly should we mean when we say microfinance is growing in Yemen? en/readings/reforms-newer-than-people-ev.text: Evidence Readings/The system is changing. What has reached people? Evidence Reading The system is changing. What has reached people? Yemen’s rules, institutions and payment infrastructure have moved faster than its representative evidence about people. The gap between the two is not an answer to guess; it is the next thing to measure. Evidence period Global Findex fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023 · POS counts March 2025 – January 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: Recent infrastructure, regulatory and programme events are not measures of people’s access, use, service quality or outcomes, and the older Findex observation is not a 2026 population rate. The latest representative observation of account ownership in Yemen remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, from Global Findex fieldwork conducted between 7 November 2022 and 9 January 2023. The financial system around that observation has kept moving. Rules changed, reported payment infrastructure expanded, institutional arrangements evolved and programmes advanced. All of that matters, and none of it, by itself, tells us Yemen’s current population-level inclusion rate. The newest evidence is not always the evidence closest to the outcome. The founding assembly of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company in August 2026 is current evidence of institution-building. A January 2026 count of POS terminals is current evidence of reported acceptance infrastructure. Neither is a 2026 population estimate. Different dates: newer infrastructure and reforms, older evidence on people Text description of this view Analytical question: How should newer reform and infrastructure evidence be read beside older population evidence? What the evidence shows: The latest representative measure of account ownership in Yemen is 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over, from the Global Findex 2021 wave (fieldwork 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023; the survey excluded areas holding about 23% of the population). Payment-infrastructure data are newer: POS terminals reported within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026. Institutional and reform events are newer still, from the World Bank's approval of the Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) on 17 June 2025 to the first board meeting of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC) on 4 August 2026. The evidence base holds no representative people-side measure after that fieldwork, so whether people's access, use or outcomes changed after these events is an open question; the difference in timing does not show that they improved. Scope and time: 2022–23 people fieldwork beside 2025–26 system events · Separate survey, administrative, institutional and programme universes What not to conclude: Newer infrastructure and reform events do not show current access, use or outcomes for people, and the 2022–23 survey value is not a 2026 rate. 2022–23 people fieldwork beside 2025–26 system eventsSeparate survey, administrative, institutional and programme universes Four clocks, four questions Findex answers a question administrative systems cannot: what share of people in the survey population report owning an account as Findex defines it? Its limits travel with the number. It is a weighted survey, not a census; its frame excludes areas holding about 23% of the population; more than a quarter of its primary sampling units were replaced during fieldwork; it cannot be mapped by governorate; and it is not a 2026 rate. Rules and institutional records can establish that an instruction was issued, an institution was founded or a governance step occurred. They do not establish effective implementation, customer experience, active use or outcomes. The infrastructure clock moves fastest. POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026 within its reporting scope. That is meaningful administrative evidence, but it does not tell us how many terminals were routinely working, how many unique merchants or customers used them, how reliable or costly the service was, or whether use was repeated. That the count cannot answer those questions is not a failure; it was not designed to. Programme baselines and targets are valuable management evidence. But a baseline is not a result, a target is not an achievement, and a programme-defined unit is not national prevalence. There is no single date called “current” The better question is not “what is the latest number?” but “latest evidence of what?” Currentness is specific to the question. A newer administrative source can sit beside an older representative survey without contradiction, because they answer different questions. Whether change has reached people is itself a set of measurement questions: access, active use, quality, protection, persistence and outcomes. These are not automatic stages that follow from one another. What would change this reading? A new representative measurement of people that keeps comparability on account ownership and adds: active and repeated digital use; saving and borrowing; the purposes of payments; barriers to opening an account; affordability and reliability; fraud and redress; receipt and use of remittances; gaps by gender and income; geography and displacement, where statistically supportable; persistence after programme participation or a transfer. Read alongside sharper administrative data on unique users, frequency, reliability, cost and complaints, it would not force survey and administrative data into one number. It would build the bridge between what changed in the system and what changed for people. Trace the evidence Each statement this Reading relies on is backed by an Evidence Record. en/readings/same-year-different-number/i.text: Evidence Readings/Same year, different number Evidence Reading Same year, different number Successive annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden give very different remittance values for 2024. A revision of this size is a measurement event to be explained before it can be read as an economic story. Evidence period Reference years 2021–2024 · CBY-Aden annual reports 2024 and 2025 · IMF Article IV consultation 2025 Last reviewed 26 September 2026 What not to conclude: No single series is the correct level; no single scale factor — such as the roughly constant ratio of 1.838 between the CBY-Aden and IMF remittance series, or the 33% population share the IMF used for areas administered from Aden — is a universal conversion; net errors and omissions are not hidden remittances; and a residual-model estimate is not a baseline. Two annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) give markedly different remittance values for the same reference year. The 2024 report put remittances in 2024 at USD 6.245 billion; the 2025 report restated 2024 at about USD 3.42 billion. The gap is large, but it does not show that remittances collapsed. Both values describe 2024. Before the difference can be read as economic movement, the change in statistical vintage, scope or method has to be understood. Same year, two published values Text description of this view Analytical question: How should the same reference year be read across publication vintages? What the evidence shows: The 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) published remittances of US$6,245 million for 2024; the 2025 annual report restated 2024 at US$3,422.16 million. This is a restatement of the same year, not a fall between years. Indexed to 2021 = 100, the CBY-Aden 2025-report path and the IMF 2025 Article IV staff-report path both reach about 118 in 2024. The two indexed paths are almost identical: the annual-growth gap over 2022–2024 is at most about 0.0032 percentage points, and the CBY-Aden level stays about 1.838 times the IMF level over 2021–2024. They cannot be read as two independent confirmations of the trend, and their raw levels are not equivalent. Scope and time: Reference year 2024 in two publication vintages; indexed paths 2021–2024 · Remittances as defined by each source: annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for 2024 and 2025; IMF 2025 Article IV staff report, on the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government What not to conclude: A same-year restatement is not a fall between years. The raw levels of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and IMF series are not equivalent, and their near-identical indexed paths cannot be read as two independent confirmations of the trend. Reference year 2024 in two publication vintages; indexed paths 2021–2024Remittances as defined by each source: annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for 2024 and 2025; IMF 2025 Article IV staff report, on the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government Two publications, one reference year Revisions are normal in economic statistics. They become consequential when the revised value is large enough to change the baseline that analysis depends on, and this one is. So “2024 remittances” is not precise enough on its own when two official publications attach materially different values to that year. The publication vintage has to travel with the reference year. The shape of the series is a clue, not a crosswalk When the remittance series in the 2025 CBY-Aden report and the IMF’s 2025 Article IV series are each indexed to 2021 = 100, their paths through 2024 are almost identical: the largest difference in annual growth over 2022–2024 is 0.0032 percentage points. Their levels are not: in every year from 2021 to 2024 the CBY-Aden value is 1.838 times the IMF value. That regularity is useful. It suggests closely related trajectories compiled under different scopes or methods. It does not supply a conversion formula, and nothing public explains what the ratio represents. IMF documentation describes a reconstruction of Yemen’s external-sector statistics under severe data constraints, including a model of personal transfers where information on informal channels was limited. That is method context. It does not reveal the exact formula behind each value in the CBY-Aden annual report. A statistical clue is not yet a documented crosswalk. Why the revision matters Remittances matter at several levels at once: household livelihoods, the supply of foreign exchange, balance-of-payments analysis and the channels, formal and informal, through which money moves. A large revision to the macro series can therefore shift several analytical baselines without any new event in a single household. Read without both the reference year and the publication vintage, a statistical revision can be mistaken for growth or collapse. Read with both, the useful question becomes: what changed in the measurement, and what, if anything, changed in the economy? What this evidence does not tell us It does not show that one series is correct for every purpose and the other wrong, and it offers no general conversion factor between the CBY-Aden and IMF series. It says nothing about how remittances are distributed across households, governorates or channels. And net errors and omissions in the balance of payments cannot be relabelled as unrecorded remittances: the residual balances the accounts; it is not an observed flow. How to use the figures For trend analysis, use a consistent statistical vintage wherever possible, and where the vintage changes, show the break. For scenario work it is legitimate to keep more than one baseline, provided each result says which one it uses. In public communication, describe a same-year difference as a statistical restatement, not as movement from one year to the next. What would change this reading? A primary methodological note linking the restated CBY-Aden series to the external-sector reconstruction would change the analysis materially. The most useful note would set out the scope, the source inputs, the treatment of informal flows, the revision policy and how the old and new vintages relate. Until it exists, keep the vintage with the number. Trace the evidence Each statement this Reading relies on is backed by an Evidence Record. Where a record also rests on material with no public link to its original document, that material is not listed and no figure from it is shown.
