en/reforms/index.html.text: Explore / Are reforms and payment infrastructure turning into access, use, quality and outcomes? A reform can be real before its outcome is known. Recent reforms are documented at the rule, funding and institution stages: consumer-protection instructions announced in August 2023, a signed 2025 mobile e-money amendment, the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) approved in June 2025, and 2026 steps to build payment institutions. Evidence that they have changed access, use, service quality or outcomes is not yet available. This resource separates rule, funding, institution, implementation, operation, use, quality and outcome, shows the furthest stage the evidence supports for each reform, and leaves every later stage open until it is measured. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What reform evidence does not establish A rule does not prove implementation quality. A funded or procured component does not prove operation. A new institution does not prove adoption. A complaints architecture does not prove effective redress. Participation in a literacy activity does not prove capability. A target does not prove achievement. And missing downstream outcome evidence is not evidence that the reform failed. Where the reform evidence chain breaks The biggest gaps sit after formal or implementation milestones: go-live evidence and subsequent active rail use, service reliability, consumer complaint volumes and outcomes, provider compliance in practice, user awareness and capability, and comparable user-level outcomes. Those gaps determine how far each reform can be interpreted. 01 System context Each stage of the reform chain needs its own evidence This resource uses one transmission chain, from rule or funding to implementation or institution, operation, reachable access, actual use, quality and protection, and outcome. Each reform is placed at the furthest stage the evidence supports. Missing downstream evidence does not mean the reform failed; it means the later stage is not yet established. 02 Analysis Official guidance describes a complaint path; performance is unmeasured A 2024 consumer-protection brochure from the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) describes a provider complaint stage of up to 10 business days, possible extension under stated conditions, and escalation to the central bank within 14 business days. The legal text of the Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions, announced on 28 August 2023, has not been extracted here. Separately, the 2023 mobile e-money instructions set a 10-business-day maximum for complaint processing and require a complaint register. What remains open is actual complaint volume, resolution time, outcome quality, enforcement and consumer experience. 03 Evidence The e-money amendment changes rules, not observed usage The signed 2025 mobile e-money amendment permits specified foreign-currency e-money alongside YER and sets transaction and balance ceilings. Those are legal permissions and limits. They do not establish that a provider launched the product, that customers adopted it, what balances are held or how transactions are distributed. 04 Analysis FPS, RTGS and access support are different parts of the payment-infrastructure reform The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) separates three functions: a Fast Payment System (FPS), which the project supports in areas under the internationally recognized government; a Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS), to be managed by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) alongside a core-banking upgrade; and a separate access-and-use component covering access-point mapping, capacity building, merchant onboarding in underserved areas and outreach. The project links RTGS to large-value payments between financial institutions, while the FPS is the fast electronic-payment component. The 2026 sequence then adds a CBY-Aden board decision on what the source calls a national QR standard and e-wallet interconnection, unified-network integration work, and the establishment and governance of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC). These are different kinds of step — project design, architecture decision, integration and institution-building. None by itself proves go-live, reliability, user adoption, transaction coverage or an inclusion effect. The project’s results framework also records January 2025 baselines for its own project-defined indicators: 817 financial access points (2030 target: 1,021), 1,062,441 active bank accounts (200,898 of them owned by women), 375,252 active e-wallet accounts, 170 merchants accepting electronic payments and 65 agents of licensed financial institutions. These are project baselines that count access points, accounts, merchants and agents — not people — and they have not been reconciled with CBY-Aden’s payment-report totals or with survey measures of account ownership. 05 Regulatory evidence Adopting a rule and implementing it are different stages, each needing its own evidence The Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) announced its Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions on 28 August 2023. That establishes a documented regulatory action. It does not by itself establish provider compliance, supervisory effectiveness, consumer experience, or implementation across all relevant institutions and geographies. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. Analysis Financial-literacy activity is an output until capability is measured Global Money Week records of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) document activity during 2023–2025. Population financial capability is a different evidence class. Without a suitable baseline, endline or evaluation, this resource does not attribute capability levels or changes to those activities. Evidence The July 2026 SMP agreement is staff-level and conditional On 16 July 2026, IMF staff and Yemeni authorities announced staff-level agreement on policies and reforms that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program. The IMF stated that the agreement was subject to Management approval and would not result in Board discussion. It is not an IMF financing arrangement and should not be presented as Executive Board approval. Analysis Funding stages must be kept distinct when reading reforms and programmes Pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposit, amount made available, budget disbursement, FX-auction use, in-kind support and project cost are not interchangeable. A project target is likewise not an observed result. This resource labels the stage of each amount so that commitments, inputs and outputs do not become one cumulative total or an inclusion outcome by presentation alone. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading When does a payment reform become financial inclusion? A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced. Evidence Reading The payment arrived. What happened next? Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. Is digital finance becoming durable financial use — or do the available data still mainly measure infrastructure and transactions? What measurement would change the decision? Active and repeat digital use Provider/rail administrative data with deduplication rules and/or demand-side active-use measures. This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use. Open this measurement priority Consumer experience and redress outcomes Complaint and redress data from providers and the regulator, plus consumer-side evidence on experience, including fees, disclosure and trust. This evidence would allow redress performance and service quality to be assessed rather than inferred from the existence of rules. en/remittances/index.html.text: Explore / What do remittances and other money flows tell us about households’ connection to the financial system? Remittances: each figure depends on its source, concept and edition For the 2024 reference year, the 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gave remittances of US$6.245 billion, and its 2025 annual report restated the same year at about US$3.42 billion: a revision of the same year, not a fall. Macro inflows, corridor prices and household receipt channels answer different questions, so this resource keeps these evidence records separate and makes revisions visible. Explore questionsOpen evidence How numbers are presented Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment. What remittance evidence does not establish A macro remittance series does not equal informal hawala volume or household distribution. A source revision is not an economic fall. Similar paths after indexing to 2021 = 100 do not prove that two raw series have the same scope or reveal a conversion factor. Corridor prices are not a national cost average. A change in an external stock is not automatically a transaction, and BPM7, the updated international standard for balance-of-payments statistics, does not retroactively rewrite Yemen’s historical series without an explicit conversion. What remains unresolved The exact public crosswalk between key external-sector series of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and the IMF remains open. For 2024, CBY-Aden’s 2025 annual report gives remittances of about US$3.42 billion, while the IMF’s 2025 Article IV staff report gives US$1,861.7 million on the IMF’s analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government. Over 2021–2024 the two series differ by a roughly constant ratio of 1.838 and their indexed growth paths almost coincide; what that ratio represents is not established, so neither level can be converted into the other. Current household receipt and channel behaviour, and the scale of informal channels, are also not established by the macro and corridor evidence. 01 Analysis Reported history, estimates and projections are different kinds of evidence The IMF staff report gives 2018–2024 as reported history based on staff calculations; a later supplement to the same consultation gives 2025 as an estimate and 2026–2030 as projections. The series is kept apart where the source document changes: reported history is never extended through the forecast as if all years had the same status. A forecast revision is not an observed economic change, and the macro series is not a measure of informal hawala volume. Another view of the evidence Remittances — IMF-reported history, estimate and projections Text description of this view Analytical question: What does the IMF report for past remittance inflows, and what is only estimated or projected? What the evidence shows: For external-sector remittances, the IMF's 2025 Article IV staff report gives 2018–2024 as reported history based on staff calculations, including US$1,861.7 million in 2024. A later supplement to the same consultation gives US$1,977 million as the 2025 estimate and projections rising from US$2,159 million in 2026 to US$3,110 million in 2030. The two documents were published at different times, so the two parts are not joined into one continuous series. The series covers the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government, not the whole of Yemen. Estimates and projections are not observations, and the series is not a measure of informal hawala volume. Scope and time: 2018–2030 · IMF external-sector remittance series on the IMF’s analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government; each year labelled as reported history, estimate or projection, with its source document What not to conclude: Estimates and projections are not observations, and a forecast revision is not an economic change. The two IMF documents do not form one continuous series. The series is not a measure of informal hawala volume, and its level, which covers areas under the internationally recognized government, is not a figure for the whole of Yemen. Open evidence record → 02 Analysis The same reference year can change when the source publishes a new edition For the 2024 reference year, the 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gave US$6.245 billion, while its 2025 annual report restated 2024 at about US$3.42 billion. That is a same-year source revision, not a year-on-year fall. The later path also shows unusually similar growth rates across overlapping years; that invites method scrutiny but does not establish smoothing or interpolation. 03 Evidence A reconstruction effort is documented; the exact crosswalk is not IMF documents a 2024–2025 external-sector statistics reconstruction effort with the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and a July 2025 mission that produced balance-of-payments (BOP) and international investment position (IIP) statistics for 2014–2024. It also documents a demographic-behavioural personal-transfer model where informal-channel data were limited. This establishes method context, not the exact formula behind every value in CBY-Aden annual reports. The public CBY-Aden and IMF components tested here do not support a single conversion factor for all series. 04 Analysis Cost depends on corridor and transfer size In 2025 Q3, quoted averages for Saudi Arabia–Yemen were 2.70% at US$200 and 1.26% at US$500. For UAE–Yemen they were 7.53% and 5.62%. The difference shows why transfer size and corridor must stay visible. These quotes do not cover every provider or informal channel and must not be collapsed into one national remittance-cost rate. More evidence and context More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits. System context Household behaviour is a different evidence layer The 2014 weighted World Bank profile reported 18.3% of adults receiving domestic remittances. Among recipients—not all adults—31.1% reported a money-transfer operator, 2.0% a financial institution and 0.0% mobile phone. Those historical channel shares cannot be converted into current monetary-flow shares, but they provide a bounded people-side context for how remittances were received in that survey wave. Analysis Before ranking external flows, inspect the balancing residual In the 2025 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), net errors and omissions exceed the published remittance line in every year from 2021 through 2025; in 2025 the residual is about US$7.117 billion against US$3.614 billion in remittances, or 1.97 times the remittance line. Net errors and omissions are a balancing residual, not an observed flow and not a hidden-remittance estimate. Evidence Readings on this question Evidence Reading Same year, different number Successive annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden give very different remittance values for 2024. A revision of this size is a measurement event to be explained before it can be read as an economic story. Related questions These pages answer connected questions. A link between two pages is not evidence that a change in one causes a change in the other. Who is being left behind — and where are the measured gaps? What measurement would change the decision? A current people-side inclusion baseline New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency. A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population. en/rights/index.html.text: Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence Source and data rights How source rights affect what this resource shows and what you may republish. Start with a questionVerify evidence Understand → Explore → Verify This resource presents the strongest defensible answer while keeping scope, limits and source visible. 01 Citation, factual use and redistribution are separate A source may be valid evidence, and may be cited, even when its publisher has not granted permission to republish its file, table, figure, dataset or substantial text. This resource therefore treats evidence fitness, citation, factual use and redistribution as separate questions.
